It does the daily work of Tokkl's web app and adds what a PWA cannot: the running timer in a notification, a home screen widget, a Quick Settings tile, and starting and stopping timers with no connection to the server. A later version talks to Toggl Track through the same API.
Tokkl set itself a bar: if starting a timer is slower than in Toggl, the owner drifts back to Toggl. The same bar applies here, with the PWA as the thing to beat. The app has done its job when the owner no longer opens the PWA on the phone.
- Starting and stopping timers away from the laptop, often from the notification, widget or tile without opening the app.
- The first version targets Tokkl only. Toggl Track comes later by pointing the app at Toggl's base URL, because both speak the same API. The Toggl version hides the Tokkl-only features above.
5. **Loud look, plain function.** Tokkl's sixth principle applies as written: any style that costs a readable number, a reachable control or a passing test gets dropped.
- **Colour.** Always Tokkl's palette, never the wallpaper. Light theme: sand background, ink text, sunset orange primary, aqua secondary, hot pink and lime for states. Dark theme: navy background with the neon counterparts. The source of truth is the colour tokens in `../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css`. Dynamic color is off, at most an opt-in setting.
| T1 | Start and stop the timer, and edit the running entry: description, project, task, tags, billable. |
| M1 | Add a past entry by start and end or by duration, with Tokkl's parsing: `9`, `930`, `9:30`, `4pm`, entries across midnight, and durations like `1h 30m`, `90`, `1,5h`. |
### 5.6 Projects, clients, tags and tasks
| P1 | Pick a project, task and tags wherever an entry is edited, including archived items when an old entry uses them. |
| P5 | Create, edit and delete tasks within a project. |
| N1 | An ongoing notification while a timer runs, with the description, project, a ticking elapsed time and a Stop action. |
| O1 | Start, stop, create and edit entries with no route to the server. Each change waits in a queue on the phone, marked as not sent, and goes out in order when the server is reachable. A timer started offline keeps its real start time. |
| O2 | Cache what the app last loaded: projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and about two weeks of history. All of it can be read offline, and entries can be edited. |
| O4 | Send the queue in the background when the network comes back, with the app closed. |
- Room (SQLite) for the cache and the queue of unsent changes.
- A Kotlin port of the duration and time-of-day parsing in `../tokkl/packages/common`, checked against the same cases as the TypeScript tests.
Since Android 9 an app cannot use cleartext HTTP unless it opts in, and since Android 7 it trusts only system CAs by default ([network security configuration](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/security-config)). The app's network security config therefore permits cleartext (S4) and trusts user-added CAs (S2). The self-signed certificate in S3 is pinned in the app, separate from Android's trust store.
| Speed | A tap on Start or Stop in the app, notification, widget or tile changes the state on the phone without waiting for the server. Tests prove it with a network that never answers. Jetpack Macrobenchmark runs cold start (`StartupTimingMetric`) and tap-to-state (`TraceSectionMetric`) on the CI emulator and fails a build that is slower than the previous one. The goals are 200 ms from tap to new state and 1.5 s cold start on a mid-range phone; no real phone checks them, so they guide design but do not gate releases. |
| Tests | JVM unit tests, Compose UI tests, and instrumented tests on an emulator against a real Tokkl server from the `ghcr.io/e0ipso/tokkl` image, never a fake one. |

A commit marked as a breaking change then moves the app to 1.0.0.

8. Some phone makers restrict background work, which can delay sending the queue. To verify on real devices.
6. What does fully featured cover? The daily-use features: timer with favorites and continue, manual entry with Tokkl's time parsing, day-grouped history with edit, duplicate, split, undo and trash, the week calendar, projects, clients, tags and tasks, and the summary, detailed and weekly reports. Left to the web app: admin pages, Toggl CSV import, JSON export and restore, bulk edit.
17. Tests against a real Tokkl server? Yes, the `ghcr.io/e0ipso/tokkl` image, not a fake.
20. Version? Its own, independent of Tokkl's, starting at 0.1.0.
22. Speed targets and how to enforce them? Tap path never waits for the server, proven by tests; Macrobenchmark on the CI emulator catches regressions. No manual real-phone run before releases, so 200 ms and 1.5 s are goals, not gates.

# Turn off cloud backup and device transfer for all app data

## Problem

PRD S8 keeps every app file out of Android backup and device transfer (docs/PRD.md:97). The only backup rule in the tracker is TKA-0011's, and it excludes the secret store alone (.ai/sift/open/server-connection/hardening/TKA-0011--keystore-secrets.md:33). - [ ] The merged manifest sets `android:allowBackup="false"`.
- [ ] The `android:dataExtractionRules` file excludes `root`, `file`, `database`, `sharedpref` and `external` in both `<cloud-backup>` and `<device-transfer>`.

## Problem

Tokkl stops the running entry when a new one starts. Say the phone queued a start at 10:00 and the laptop started a timer at 10:30. ## Direction

- Before the sender posts a queued start (`POST /workspaces/{wid}/time_entries` with no `stop`), it fetches `GET /me/time_entries/current`.

- If nothing runs, or the running entry started earlier, post the start as queued. Tokkl stops the earlier entry itself.
- If the queue also holds a stop for the same local entry, that stop replaces the computed stop only when it is earlier.
- For the server side, see `stopRunning` in `../tokkl/packages/api/src/models/timeEntries.ts` (around line 242). It stops a running entry at "now" when the new start is earlier than the running entry's start.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An instrumented test queues a start at T, starts another timer on the server at T+30m through the API, then sends the queue. The phone's entry ends at T+30m and the server's timer still runs.
- [ ] With no timer running on the server, the queued start is sent and runs.
- [ ] With an earlier timer running, the queued start runs and the server stops the earlier one.
- [ ] Each queued start costs one extra GET and no more.

# Handle each server rejection of a queued change (409, 404, 400, 403)

## Problem

PRD O6 gives each server rejection of a queued change its own outcome (docs/PRD.md:174). TKA-0027 sorts rejections into two buckets: 401, 403 and 429 stop the drain and keep the change queued (.ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0027--change-queue.md:38), and any other 4xx marks it failed. TKA-0048 only lists the failed changes with their reason (.ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0048--sync-status.md:31). A stop that already happened elsewhere or an entry deleted on the web would sit in the queue forever. After a token reset, the queue would fail change after change on 403 with nothing asking the user to sign in again.

## Evidence

- docs/PRD.md:174
- .ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0027--change-queue.md:38
- .ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0048--sync-status.md:31

## Direction

In the queue sender:

- A 409 on a stop is dropped with no message, since the entry is stopped either way.
- A 404 is dropped, and the app shows "1 change discarded: the entry was deleted elsewhere". Aggregate the count and keep the text in a string resource.
- A 400 moves to a "needs attention" list that holds the server's message. The user opens it, edits and resends the change, or discards it. Later queued changes for the same entry wait behind it while the rest of the queue continues.
- A 403 pauses the whole queue, discards nothing, and prompts the user to sign in again through TKA-0016's flow. The queue resumes after sign-in.
- 5xx and network errors keep TKA-0037's backoff. 429 keeps TKA-0027's Retry-After handling.
- The "needs attention" list and the discard notice belong to this ticket. TKA-0048 stays a counter plus the last-answered time and links to the list.
- TKA-0027 will be edited separately to point here.
- Tests run against the real `ghcr.io/e0ipso/tokkl` server.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Instrumented tests against the real Tokkl server cover each status below.
- [ ] A 409 on a stop drops the change silently.
- [ ] A 404 drops the change and shows the discard notice.
- [ ] A 400 holds the change with the server's message and holds later changes to the same entry, while other changes are sent. Resending after a fix succeeds, and discarding removes the change.
- [ ] After `POST /me/reset_token`, the 403 pauses the queue and nothing is discarded. The queue drains after signing in with the new token.
EOF

# Send a queued start as stopped when a later timer already runs

## Problem

Tokkl stops the running entry when a new one starts. Say the phone queued a start at 10:00 and the laptop started a timer at 10:30. Replaying the start makes the server stop the laptop's timer at send time and leaves the phone's older entry running. PRD O3 now makes the queued start an exception to last-write-wins, and the timer started last wins (docs/PRD.md:171). TKA-0027 still applies plain last-write-wins to every change (.ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0027--change-queue.md:40).

## Evidence

- docs/PRD.md:171
- .ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0027--change-queue.md:40

## Direction

- Before the sender posts a queued start (`POST /workspaces/{wid}/time_entries` with no `stop`), it fetches `GET /me/time_entries/current`.
- If an entry runs and its start is later than the queued start, post the queued entry with `stop` set to that entry's start, and leave the running entry alone. Update the local cache so the phone shows the server's running entry.
- If nothing runs, or the running entry started earlier, post the start as queued. Tokkl stops the earlier entry itself.
- If the queue also holds a stop for the same local entry, that stop replaces the computed stop only when it is earlier.
- For the server side, see `stopRunning` in `../tokkl/packages/api/src/models/timeEntries.ts` (around line 242). It stops a running entry at "now" when the new start is earlier than the running entry's start.
- Tests run against the real `ghcr.io/e0ipso/tokkl` server from TKA-0006.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An instrumented test queues a start at T, starts another timer on the server at T+30m through the API, then sends the queue. The phone's entry ends at T+30m and the server's timer still runs.
- [ ] With no timer running on the server, the queued start is sent and runs.
- [ ] With an earlier timer running, the queued start runs and the server stops the earlier one.
- [ ] Each queued start costs one extra GET and no more.
EOF

# Handle each server rejection of a queued change (409, 404, 400, 403)

## Problem

PRD O6 gives each server rejection of a queued change its own outcome (docs/PRD.md:174). TKA-0027 sorts rejections into two buckets: 401, 403 and 429 stop the drain and keep the change queued (.ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0027--change-queue.md:38), and any other 4xx marks it failed. TKA-0048 only lists the failed changes with their reason (.ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0048--sync-status.md:31). A stop that already happened elsewhere or an entry deleted on the web would sit in the queue forever. After a token reset, the queue would fail change after change on 403 with nothing asking the user to sign in again.

## Evidence

- docs/PRD.md:174
- .ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0027--change-queue.md:38
- .ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0048--sync-status.md:31

## Direction

In the queue sender:

- A 409 on a stop is dropped with no message, since the entry is stopped either way.
- A 404 is dropped, and the app shows "1 change discarded: the entry was deleted elsewhere". Aggregate the count and keep the text in a string resource.
- A 400 moves to a "needs attention" list that holds the server's message. The user opens it, edits and resends the change, or discards it. Later queued changes for the same entry wait behind it while the rest of the queue continues.
- A 403 pauses the whole queue, discards nothing, and prompts the user to sign in again through TKA-0016's flow. The queue resumes after sign-in.
- 5xx and network errors keep TKA-0037's backoff. 429 keeps TKA-0027's Retry-After handling.
- The "needs attention" list and the discard notice belong to this ticket. TKA-0048 stays a counter plus the last-answered time and links to the list.
- TKA-0027 will be edited separately to point here.
- Tests run against the real `ghcr.io/e0ipso/tokkl` server.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Instrumented tests against the real Tokkl server cover each status below.
- [ ] A 409 on a stop drops the change silently.
- [ ] A 404 drops the change and shows the discard notice.
- [ ] A 400 holds the change with the server's message and holds later changes to the same entry, while other changes are sent. Resending after a fix succeeds, and discarding removes the change.
- [ ] After `POST /me/reset_token`, the 403 pauses the queue and nothing is discarded. The queue drains after signing in with the new token.
EOF

# Check the running entry every 15 minutes while a timer runs

## Problem

No push reaches the phone, so a timer stopped on another client keeps ticking in the phone's notification and widget until the app opens. PRD section 6.3 adds a WorkManager job that checks the running entry every 15 minutes while a timer runs (docs/PRD.md:208). The battery budget allows that one check and no other wakeups (docs/PRD.md:217). TKA-0047 says no timer triggers a network request (.ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0047--event-refresh.md:35), and TKA-0037 schedules no periodic work (.ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0037--background-send.md:33). As the tracker stands, both forbid the check.

## Evidence

- docs/PRD.md:208
- docs/PRD.md:217
- .ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0047--event-refresh.md:35
- .ai/sift/open/offline/feature/TKA-0037--background-send.md:33

## Direction

- When the local running entry starts, enqueue a unique `PeriodicWorkRequest` with a 15-minute interval (the WorkManager minimum) and a network constraint. Cancel it when the entry stops locally or when the check finds nothing running.
- The worker calls `GET /me/time_entries/current` once and writes the result to the Room cache that the notification (TKA-0054), widget (TKA-0060) and tile (TKA-0061) read. It does nothing else.
- If the queue holds unsent changes for the running entry, the worker leaves that entry as it is.
- No work is scheduled while no timer runs (section 7, Battery).
- TKA-0047 and TKA-0037 will be edited separately to allow this job.
- Tests run against the real `ghcr.io/e0ipso/tokkl` server.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Starting a timer schedules exactly one unique periodic job, and stopping it cancels the job.
- [ ] With no timer running and the queue empty, WorkManager holds no job from the app.
- [ ] A test with WorkManager's `TestDriver` against the real server shows a timer stopped on the server cleared from the cache, the notification and the widget at the next run.
- [ ] The worker does not overwrite unsent local changes.
EOF

A timer started on the laptop leaves the tile showing "not running". A tap then continues the last entry, and the server stops the laptop's timer. # Trust a self-signed certificate only by its pinned SHA-256 fingerprint after a disclaimer

## Problem

Users whose Tokkl server has a self-signed certificate cannot connect, because no system or user CA signed it. The PRD lets them trust that one certificate after reading a disclaimer that shows its SHA-256 fingerprint. The app must ask again when the certificate changes, and it must never accept a certificate without a check. The PRD puts this pin in a trust manager on the OkHttp client, separate from Android's trust store and the network security config.

## Evidence

- docs/PRD.md:90
- docs/PRD.md:190
- docs/PRD.md:197
- absent: app/src/main/

## Direction

- When the TLS handshake fails on an untrusted chain, show a disclaimer with the leaf certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint and subject. The handshake fails before any HTTP request, so no credential has gone out yet. Capture the server's chain during the failed check so the prompt can show the leaf.
- On accept, store the fingerprint with the server configuration.
- Add a custom `X509TrustManager` to the shared client from TKA-0009. It first delegates to the platform trust manager, which covers system and user CAs. If that fails, it accepts only a leaf whose SHA-256 matches the stored pin. Otherwise it fails with a certificate-changed error that routes back to the prompt.
- Hostname verification stays on.
- No trust-all trust manager or hostname verifier exists anywhere in the codebase, including debug builds and tests.
- Keep the disclaimer text in English string resources and give every control a TalkBack label. Meet WCAG AA contrast, never use colour as the only signal, and keep it usable at the largest font scale. TKA-0022 shows a stronger warning for plain `http://`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An untrusted certificate shows the disclaimer with its SHA-256 fingerprint before any credential is sent.
- [ ] After the user accepts, connections succeed only with that certificate.
- [ ] A changed certificate fails and prompts again.
- [ ] A certificate trusted by a system or user CA never prompts.
- [ ] A JVM test shows a different certificate with the same subject is rejected.
- [ ] An instrumented test passes against the real Tokkl container behind a self-signed TLS proxy.
- [ ] No trust-all code path exists in the codebase.
- [ ] The disclaimer meets the string resource, TalkBack, contrast, colour and font scale rules.
EOF

# Queue start, stop, create and edit offline and send them in order with real start times

## Problem

Tapping Start or Stop with no route to the server would fail, or lose the real start time when the request finally goes out. That breaks the offline-first principle. The PRD wants each change kept on the phone, marked not sent, and sent in order once the server is reachable. A timer started offline keeps its real start time. When the phone and another client both change an entry, the change that reaches the server last wins.

## Evidence

- docs/PRD.md:61
- docs/PRD.md:67
- docs/PRD.md:166
- docs/PRD.md:168
- docs/PRD.md:188
- docs/PRD.md:203
- absent: app/src/main/

## Direction

- Keep a FIFO of pending operations in Room. The operations are create or start, stop, update and delete. Only time entries go in the queue.
- Apply each operation to the cache at once and mark it unsent. Until it is sent, keep it applied over refreshed rows so the user still sees it.
- An entry created offline gets a local ID. Once the server creates it, map the local ID to the server ID, and later operations that reference it use the server ID.
- A sender drains the queue in order and stops at the first transient failure. A network failure, a 5xx, 401, 403 and 429 stop the drain and keep the operation queued.
- A permanent rejection, any 4xx other than 401, 403 and 429, marks that change failed for TKA-0048 to show. Changes that depend on it fail too. Independent changes keep sending.
- Send full field values. The last write to reach the server wins, and nothing merges.
- Taps never await the network. Start and stop times are the tap times.
- The notification, widget and tile read the running entry from this cache, so they change at once while the queue sends behind them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With the network hanging, an instrumented test shows Start and Stop update state at once and mark the change unsent.
- [ ] A timer started offline keeps its tap time as its start on the server after sending.
- [ ] Changes reach the server in the order made, including create, edit and stop of an entry created offline.
- [ ] When the web app edits the same entry, the last change to reach the server wins with no merge prompt.
- [ ] A permanent rejection marks that change and the changes that depend on it failed, and independent changes still send.
- [ ] The queue survives process death.
EOF

## Problem

To see or stop a running timer, the owner has to open the app. Goal 1 names the notification as one of the places to start and stop the timer, so the app falls short of that goal. A PWA cannot keep the running timer in a notification, and closing that gap is a reason this app exists.

## Direction

Post an ongoing notification whenever the running entry on the phone starts, and remove it when the entry stops. Drive it from the local running-entry state, not from each start path. Starts from the app, offline starts, and later starts from the widget, tile and shortcuts then show it with no extra wiring.

The notification shows the description, the project, and a system chronometer that counts from the entry's start time, set with `setUsesChronometer` and `setWhen`. The system ticks the chronometer, so the app needs no wakeups to update it.

A Stop action stops the timer on the phone and hands the change to the queue, without opening the app. Declare its receiver in AndroidManifest.xml. Tapping the notification opens the app. The channel name and description are English string resources, and the Stop action has a TalkBack label.

Asking for the notification permission belongs to TKA-0058, and the Live Update promotion belongs to TKA-0059.

- [ ] It shows the description, the project and a ticking elapsed time, and the app schedules no wakeups to update it.

Declare POST_NOTIFICATIONS in AndroidManifest.xml. On Android 13 and later, request it when the first timer starts in the app. The timer starts at once and the request shows after it, so starting never waits on the answer. If the owner denies it, show a non-blocking message. It says the running timer will not appear in the notification shade or as a Live Update, and it offers an action that opens the app's notification settings. The message and the action label are English string resources.

A runtime permission request needs the app on screen, and the widget and tile start timers without opening the app. If the first start comes from one of them, ask at the first start made in the app instead.

# Promote the running-timer notification to a Live Update on Android 16 and later

## Problem

Android 16 can show a running timer as a Live Update, as a chip in the status bar, at the top of the notification drawer and on the lock screen. The running-timer notification from TKA-0054 does not ask for that, so the owner gets a plain notification even where the system could do more. Support depends on the device and on the Android 16 release it runs, so the regular notification has to keep working without it.

## Evidence

- docs/PRD.md:156 defines N2. On Android 16 and later, promote the notification to a Live Update, shown as a status bar chip, at the top of the notification drawer and on the lock screen. Elsewhere it stays a regular ongoing notification.
- docs/PRD.md:255 lists risk 6. Live Updates depend on the device and on the Android 16 release it runs, and the notification has to work without them.
- absent: app/src/main/. No app source exists yet.

## Direction

On Android 16 and later, request promotion of the TKA-0054 notification with the platform's promoted ongoing notification API. Follow the current guide on developer.android.com and meet every requirement it lists for promotion. Check that the app may post promoted notifications before relying on it.

# Build the Tokkl Material 3 theme from the web colour tokens, light and dark

## Problem

No theme exists, so the app cannot show Tokkl's sand, ink and sunset orange in light or its navy and neon in dark. The PRD makes Tokkl's palette the default on Material 3 components, never the wallpaper. Every screen after this one needs the theme's colours, and the running and billable states need theirs. Principle 5 also means a colour that costs readable text gets dropped, so the mapping has to prove its contrast.

## Evidence

- docs/PRD.md:70 sets principle 5. Any style that costs a readable number, a reachable control or a passing test gets dropped.
- docs/PRD.md:74 picks Material 3 through Compose Material 3.
- docs/PRD.md:75 sets the colour direction. Always Tokkl's palette, with the styles.css colour tokens as the source of truth, and dynamic colour off or at most an opt-in.

- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css:164 sets `--text: light-dark(#1c1a2b, #f3f1ff)`.
- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css:167 sets `--primary: light-dark(#a8380a, #ff8c42)`.
- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css:169 sets `--secondary: light-dark(#00727c, #2ee6e6)`.
- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css:170 sets `--accent-pink: light-dark(#d81b72, #ff4fa8)`.
- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css:171 sets `--accent-lime: light-dark(#4f7a00, #b6ff3b)`.
- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css:187 sets `--state-running: var(--accent-pink)`.
- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css:189 sets `--state-billable: light-dark(#4a7c00, #b6ff3b)`.
- absent: app/src/main/res/values/themes.xml. No window theme exists.
- absent: app/src/main/. No app source exists yet.

## Direction

Build Compose Material 3 light and dark colour schemes from the styles.css tokens. In `light-dark()` the first value is the light one. Map them this way:

- background from `--bg`, styles.css:161
- text on background and surface from `--text`, styles.css:164
- primary from `--primary`, styles.css:167
- secondary from `--secondary`, styles.css:169
- the pink and lime accents from `--accent-pink` and `--accent-lime`, styles.css:170 and :171
- the running state from `--state-running`, styles.css:187, which resolves to the pink accent
- the billable state from `--state-billable`, styles.css:189, which differs from the lime accent in light

- [ ] The clock, totals and headings survive the largest font scale without clipping.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

=== map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session.md
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.
The manifest sets `android:allowBackup="false"` and points at `res/xml/backup_rules.xml` (Android 11 and earlier) and `res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml` (Android 12 and later). Both exclude all nine domains. In the data extraction rules a missing section leaves that transfer mode on for everything, so `cloud-backup`, `device-transfer` and `cross-platform-transfer platform="ios"` each list every domain. A new store therefore needs no backup rules of its own. `BackupRulesTest` (JVM) checks the merged manifest and both files.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Samples the peak RSS (VmHWM) of the qemu process booting AVD $1 every 5 s until $2 exists.

peak=0

    for pid in $(pgrep -f "qemu-system-x86_64.*-avd $avd( |$)"); do
        hwm=$(awk '/VmHWM/{print $2}' /proc/$pid/status 2>/dev/null)

        [ -n "$rss" ] && printf '%s pid=%s rss_kb=%s hwm_kb=%s\n' "$(date +%T)" "$pid" "$rss" "$hwm" >>"$out.samples"
    done
    echo "$peak" >"$out"
    sleep 5
done
EOF

    echo "$peak" >"$out"

done

# Find why the reports font scale test hangs on API 30

## Problem

`ReportsScreenTest.theScreenAndItsRangeDialogsFitAtTheLargestFontScale` never ends on tokkl-api30 (Android 11). Its process stops making progress, the run waits with no time limit, and only a force-stop of the app lets the other tests go on. ## Evidence

- Two full runs through `TOKKL_TEST_AVD=tokkl-api30 scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` on 2026-10-19 hung in this test: one started it at 08:22:33 and one at 08:54:16. Neither had moved on after more than six minutes, and `adb shell am force-stop com.github.e0ipso.tokkl` let each run continue.
- In both, logcat shows `IdlingPolicy: These resources are not idle: [Compose-Espresso link]` every five seconds for about 20 seconds after the screen opens, then nothing more from the test process.
- The test is app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/reports/ReportsScreenTest.kt:175. It passes on tokkl-api36, where all 146 tests passed on 2026-10-19.
- On API 30 apps draw with OpenGL, since HWUI aborts there with `skiavk` (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh, end of `boot_emulator`).

## Direction

Reproduce with `-Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.reports.ReportsScreenTest#theScreenAndItsRangeDialogsFitAtTheLargestFontScale` on tokkl-api30 and find the step that never returns, for example with thread dumps through `run-as` or log lines around each step. Fix the cause in the app or the test. If an infinite animation or a recomposition loop keeps Compose busy, that is an app bug to fix, not a test to skip. Give a waiting step a timeout if it has none, so a hang fails the test instead of the run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The test passes or fails within its own timeouts on tokkl-api30 and still passes on tokkl-api36.
- [ ] A full run on tokkl-api30 finishes with no force-stop.

# Stop failed assumptions from failing instrumented tests

## Problem

With the test orchestrator and Android Gradle Plugin 9.4.1, a JUnit assumption that fails counts as a failed test, not a skipped one, and fails `connectedDebugAndroidTest`. `WindowBackgroundTest` uses one to skip when the system's night mode follows a schedule, so on such a device it fails instead. Any later test that skips with `assumeTrue` will do the same.

## Evidence

- On 2026-10-19 on tokkl-api30, `LightScreenshotTest` skipped its eight tests with `assumeTrue` in a rule. TestRunner logged `assumption failed` for each, and the JUnit XML and HTML report under app/build listed all eight as failures and none as skipped. The screenshot classes now use `@SdkSuppress` instead (app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/screenshot/ScreenshotTest.kt, the four subclasses).
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/WindowBackgroundTest.kt:138 calls `assumeTrue("the system's night mode follows a schedule", fixed)`.
- gradle/libs.versions.toml:13-14 pins runner 1.7.0 and orchestrator 1.6.1. app/build.gradle.kts:148 runs the tests through the orchestrator.

## Direction

Find whether the orchestrator, the runner or AGP's test platform turns the assumption into a failure, and whether a version or option fixes it. If none does, replace the assumption in `WindowBackgroundTest`: set the system's night mode to a fixed value for the test and put it back afterwards, as `SystemFontScale` does for the font scale. Mention the behaviour in README.md "Build and test" so the next test does not use an assumption.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No instrumented test relies on an assumption to skip, or a failed assumption shows as skipped in the report.
- [ ] `WindowBackgroundTest` passes on a device whose night mode follows a schedule.
EOF

# Give pre-Android 12 emulator runs memory headroom and a run at API 26

## Problem

Below Android 12 apps on the emulator draw with OpenGL, because HWUI aborts with `skiavk` there, and qemu keeps memory after each test's process. A full run on tokkl-api30 peaked at 5.75 GB, against the 6 GB cap of the emulator's scope, so a few more tests will get it OOM-killed. On API 26, the app's minSdk, qemu grows faster still, so no full run fits there. That run matters: below API 30, `LargestFontScaleTest` crashed on `android.view.WindowInsets$Type`, an API 30 class, which tokkl-api30 cannot show.

## Evidence

- Full runs on tokkl-api30 on 2026-10-19 peaked at 5.75 GB VmHWM with 2560 MB of guest RAM and 5.64 GB with 2048 MB. qemu grew by 2.4 GB over the last 63 tests of the second. The cap is `EMULATOR_MEMORY_MAX=6G` in scripts/instrumented-tests.sh.
- With 20 to 22 UI tests, qemu grew by about 110 MB per test on API 26 and API 28 with `-gpu lavapipe`. On API 28 `swiftshader` and `host` hit the 6 GB cap within about 20 tests, and the `lavapipe` emulator segfaulted ("DisplaySurfaceGlContextHelper context was preempted").
- With `skiavk`, HWUI aborted every app at its first frame: on API 28 the image offers no Vulkan, and on API 30 its Vulkan lacks `VK_KHR_external_semaphore_fd`, with `lavapipe` and with `swiftshader`.
- The `WindowInsets$Type` crash came from LargestFontScaleTest.kt:459 on tokkl-api26. TKA-0131 moved it to `WindowInsetsCompat`.
- Emulator 37.2.12, the newest in the SDK repository on 2026-10-19.

## Direction

Measure again with each new emulator release. If the growth stays, let scripts/instrumented-tests.sh split a run on a pre-Android 12 AVD into batches of classes, with a fresh emulator for each batch, and keep the classes whose tests depend on each other, such as the `*RestartTest` steps, in one batch. Then add a tokkl-api26 AVD on `system-images;android-26;default;x86_64` and document it beside tokkl-api30. Do not raise the 6 GB cap without measuring what else the machine needs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A full run on tokkl-api30 peaks at least 1 GB under the emulator's cap.
- [ ] The full suite runs on an API 26 emulator through scripts/instrumented-tests.sh, and README.md says how.
EOF

test: run the instrumented suite on an API 30 emulator too

switch is hidden, and android:allowBackup alone keeps the app out of
backup. CI's instrumented job runs API 30 as a second matrix entry, and
the README names both images and the command for each.

grew by about 110 MB a test on both, too fast for the emulator's 6 GB

skiavk only on Android 12 and later. The SDK repository has no plain
AOSP image for API 36.1 or later, so the cross-platform-transfer rules
still run on no device.

The older images found test bugs that API 36 hid. LargestFontScaleTest
read the keyboard through WindowInsets.Type, an API 30 class, and now
uses WindowInsetsCompat. The queue tests parsed Tokkl's +00:00 times
with Instant.parse, which API 30 refused. The TLS sign-in tests clicked
the sign-in button without scrolling to it, and timed out on API 30.

BackupRefusedTest asks the backup manager to back the app up and
expects a refusal. WindowBackgroundTest checks that launches below
Android 12 keep the system's night mode and still show the chosen
background. The screenshot classes carry @SdkSuppress for API 36, where
their references come from: AGP reported a failed assumption as a
failed test.

Refs: TKA-0131

 * Launch shows the chosen scheme's background from the starting window on, so starting the app
 * Android draws the starting window before the app runs, from the manifest theme and the night
 * So each test launches twice. The first launch hands the mode to Android. The second has to
 * start in it, in the same configuration Android draws a cold start's starting window in. Below
 * Android 12 the app hands Android nothing, and one test checks that instead.
class WindowBackgroundTest {
     * the starting window Android draws before it, keeps the system's mode. Once the activity
     * starts, the window and the content still take the chosen scheme's background.
    @Test
    fun belowAndroid12LaunchesKeepTheSystemsNightModeAndShowTheChosenBackground() {
        val background = if (systemDark) TokklLightColorScheme.background else TokklDarkColorScheme.background
                assertBackgrounds(which, activity, background)
        val background = if (dark) TokklDarkColorScheme.background else TokklLightColorScheme.background
            assertBackgrounds("first launch", activity, background)
            assertBackgrounds("next launch", activity, background)

`ReportsServer` takes the account's default workspace from `GET /api/v9/me` and its rounding from `GET /api/v9/workspaces/{id}`. It pages `POST /reports/api/v3/workspace/{id}/search/time_entries`, following `X-Next-Row-Number`, and the phone sums the entries. The summary endpoints will not do: Tokkl's v3 totals send `rates: []`, and its v3 summary groups carry seconds only, with no billable time or amount. Each search asks for the workspace's `rounding` and `rounding_minutes`, because the Reports API rounds only when asked while the web app always rounds. `ReportsScreenTest` checks the summary against `POST /api/app/report`, the web app's own call.
Report data stays in memory. Offline, or on a 502, 503 or 504 from a proxy that cannot reach Tokkl, the screen says reports need the server and shows no numbers. When the app comes back to the foreground, after an `ON_STOP` that was not a configuration change, the model asks for the range again and shows no numbers until the answer comes. Adding the lifecycle observer replays `ON_START` at once, and the model ignores that one. A configuration change keeps the report and sends nothing.
Read the timezone, first day of the week and `time_resolution_minutes` from `GET /api/v9/me`, and use the account timezone everywhere (S7). Resolve its name with `time.parseTimeZone`, never `ZoneId.of`. Tokkl accepts what JavaScript's Intl accepts, such as `europe/madrid` in any case and ICU-only names like `IST`, and rejects some names `ZoneId.of` takes, such as `Z` or `GMT+5`. A name it cannot resolve gives null. Never fall back to the device's zone. Screens take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime`, and `NoDeviceZoneTest` fails on any read of the device's zone (see the account settings node). Show stopped entries as the server returns them, after it snaps them to `time_resolution_minutes` (T3). The phone snaps entries it has not sent yet in the account timezone, so their times do not change when the server answers. History and queue code calls `snapUnsent` in `time/Snap.kt`, never `snapSpan` directly. The server cuts both ends to whole seconds before it snaps (`snapToResolution` in `../tokkl/packages/api/src/models/timeEntries.ts`), and `snapUnsent` does the same. With no `time_resolution_minutes` in `/me` it returns the span unchanged. Never pass it the running entry, whose clock is not snapped.
Manual entry accepts times like `9`, `930`, `9:30` and `4pm`, entries across midnight, and durations like `1h 30m`, `90` and `1,5h` (M1). The parsing is a Kotlin port of Tokkl's `parseDuration` in `../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts` and `parseTimeOfDay` in `../tokkl/packages/web/src/lib/timeOfDay.ts`, checked against the cases in the `.test.ts` file next to each. The time-of-day parser lives in the web package, not in `packages/common`. Both ports live in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time`, and their tests copy the TypeScript cases verbatim at a recorded tokkl commit (see the porting practice node). The ports can still drift when the TypeScript changes later. Sharing the test cases between the two repos would catch that.

Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). `MainActivity` calls `WindowCompat.enableEdgeToEdge` and sets the system bar icon colours itself in `showSystemBarIconsFor`. androidx.activity 1.13's `enableEdgeToEdge` reapplies its first call's styles after every configuration change, which gave dark mode the wrong status bar icons. With `SystemBarStyle.auto` it also turns on the system's navigation bar contrast enforcement, which paints a translucent band over a three-button navigation bar; no scrim colour causes that band. `ScrollingScreenInsets` in `ui/theme/ScreenInsets.kt` keeps the status bar and the sides outside a scrolling screen, and the screen puts `navigationBarsPadding` inside its scroll, so text scrolls under the transparent navigation bar and the last line can still scroll clear of it. `MainActivity` declares `android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize"`, so Android does not pan the window when the keyboard opens, and a form makes room with `imePadding`.
`session/AccountSettings` holds the `GET /api/v9/me` fields that decide how the app shows and reads times: `timezone`, `beginning_of_week` and Tokkl's optional `time_resolution_minutes`. It holds no credential. Sign-in stores them from its own `/me`. A `/me` without `timezone` or `beginning_of_week`, or with a week start outside 0 to 6, fails sign-in as `SignInResult.NotTokkl`. Toggl Track and older Tokkl servers leave out `time_resolution_minutes` and do not snap, so it stays null for them. `durationFormat` comes from `duration_format` in `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` and, as in the web app, reads as improved when the key is missing, null or names another format. Screens write durations with `AccountSettings.formatDuration(Long)`.
`session/AccountSettingsSource` is the one place screens read the settings from. `TokklApplication.accountSettings` builds it over `AccountSettingsStore`, which keeps them in the private preferences file `account_settings`, so screens have them offline and after a restart. `MainActivity.onStart` and each sign-in call `refresh()`, so a change made in the web app reaches the phone. A refresh sends `GET /api/v9/me?with_related_data=true` and `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` once and hands both answers to its `onRefresh`, where the capabilities and the cache refresh from them. A second `refresh()` while one runs gets the running job instead of sending another request. A failed request or write keeps what is stored, failed preferences keep the stored duration format, and a refresh drops its answer when sign-in stored newer settings while the request ran.
`AccountSettings.time()` gives a `time/AccountTime`: the account's zone, a clock in that zone, `now()`, `today()`, `local(instant)`, `startOfWeek(date)` and `snapUnsent(start, stop)`. It returns null when `parseTimeZone` cannot resolve the name, as when the server's Intl knows a zone that the phone's tz database lacks. There is no fallback to the device's zone or to UTC. A screen without an `AccountTime` must show no clock times or dates, take no time input and name the zone it does not know. Durations, the running clock, Start and Stop need no zone and keep working.
`NoDeviceZoneTest`, a JVM test, reads the constant pool of every compiled app class through `ClassReferences` and fails on `ZoneId.systemDefault`, `TimeZone.getDefault` (java.util and ICU), `Clock.systemDefaultZone`, a `now()` without arguments on the java.time date and time types, and a `Calendar` or `GregorianCalendar` built without a zone. Its `ALLOWED` set is empty, and a class added there needs a comment saying why the account's zone will not do. Take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime` instead.

The duration rounds up to a multiple of the resolution, so the padding is always less than one step. The start moves to the nearest grid point, and the stop follows it by the rounded duration. The response returns the stored values, so `stop - start` equals `duration`. A running entry keeps its exact start until it stops. When a new timer stops it, its stored stop lands up to half a step before the new start or up to one and a half steps after it. A timer that has run for more than 999 hours, the longest entry the API accepts, stops at 999 hours. CSV import and JSON restore keep the times in the file, and existing entries change only when they are next edited.

- Task `tracked_seconds` is in milliseconds, because Toggl documents it that way.
- `since` filters retained records on `/me/clients`, `/me/projects`, `/me/tags`, `/me/tasks`, `/me/workspaces`, workspace projects and workspace tasks.     private fun assertTextsFit() {

# Port Tokkl's duration and time-of-day parsing to Kotlin and test it against the TypeScript cases
Manual entry needs Tokkl's parsing of `9`, `930`, `9:30`, `4pm`, entries across midnight, and durations like `1h 30m`, `90` and `1,5h` (docs/PRD.md:110). PRD section 6.1 asks for a Kotlin port checked against the same cases as the TypeScript tests (docs/PRD.md:191), and the test plan runs JVM unit tests (docs/PRD.md:215). The duration parser is `parseDuration` (../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts:16) with its cases at ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.test.ts:6, and TKA-0002 records where the time-of-day parser lives. The app has no source or tests yet, since neither `app/src/main/` nor `app/src/test` exists. Without a Kotlin port tested against the TypeScript cases, the phone reads input differently from the web app, which is PRD risk 5 (docs/PRD.md:254).
- ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts:16
- ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.test.ts:6
- absent: app/src/test
- A port of `parseDuration` from ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts:16. It returns whole seconds, or null for input it rejects, as the original does.
Match the TypeScript output wherever Kotlin and JavaScript differ. One trap: the original calls `replace(',', '.')` on a string (../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts:17), which in JavaScript replaces only the first comma, while Kotlin's `String.replace` replaces every one.
JVM tests under `app/src/test` replay every case from the TypeScript test files, starting with ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.test.ts:6. Copy the cases verbatim as data and do not edit them. A comment at the top of each test file names the TypeScript source file and the tokkl commit the cases came from, so a later diff against tokkl shows drift (docs/PRD.md:254). The tests run as plain JVM unit tests (docs/PRD.md:215).
- [ ] Every case from ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.test.ts passes in a JVM test, including the ones that expect null.
- [ ] Every time-of-day case from the test file TKA-0002 names passes in a JVM test.
- [ ] Each test file records the TypeScript file and the tokkl commit its cases came from.
- [ ] The parser source has no Android dependencies and its tests run without a device or emulator.

# Propose to Tokkl that parseDuration reject a unit named constructor instead of returning NaN

## Problem

Tokkl's `parseDuration` looks units up in a plain object literal, so `UNIT_SECONDS['constructor']` finds `Object.prototype.constructor` and the `undefined` check lets it through. `parseDuration('1 constructor')` then returns NaN, which is neither seconds nor the null that callers check for. The web app treats NaN as a valid duration, and the Kotlin port from TKA-0012 returns null for that input, so the two disagree (PRD risk 5). This repo cannot edit `../tokkl`, so the human has to submit the change there.

## Evidence

- ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts:3 declares `UNIT_SECONDS` as a `Record<string, number>` object literal, which inherits from `Object.prototype`.
- ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts:35-36 reads `UNIT_SECONDS[match[2]!]` and rejects only `undefined`. `constructor` is the only `Object.prototype` key made of lowercase letters alone, which is what the unit pattern captures.
- Node 24.21.0 importing ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts at tokkl commit ec84de60087b32e8279c74197bdc94e52164579b returns NaN for `'1 constructor'`. In a corpus of 159,150 generated duration inputs, 1,865 gave NaN.
- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/components/TimeFields.tsx:24-25 checks only `parsed === null`, so NaN goes to `onCommit`. ../tokkl/packages/web/src/components/EntryEditor.tsx:109 builds `new Date(start.getTime() + seconds * 1000).toISOString()` after a `seconds !== null` check, which throws a RangeError for NaN. ../tokkl/packages/api/src/services/importCsv.ts:237 has the same `!== null` check. These effects come from reading the code; none was run in a browser or against the API.
- This repo's port, app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/time/Duration.kt, returns null for this input and documents the difference in its KDoc.

## Direction

- In ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts, make the unit lookup see only its own keys, with `Object.hasOwn(UNIT_SECONDS, unit)`, a `Map`, or an object built with `Object.create(null)`.
- Add `['1 constructor', null]` to the cases in ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.test.ts so the Kotlin replay in TKA-0012's DurationTest picks it up on the next sync.
- The human submits this. Do not edit ../tokkl from this repo.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In Tokkl, `parseDuration('1 constructor')` and `parseDuration('1h 2constructor')` return null.
- [ ] Every existing case in ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.test.ts still passes.
- [ ] ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.test.ts has a case for a unit named `constructor` that expects null.

A screen without an `AccountTime` must show no clock times or dates, take no time input and name the zone it does not know. Durations, the running clock, Start and Stop need no zone and keep working.
`NoDeviceZoneTest`, a JVM test, reads the constant pool of every compiled app class through `ClassReferences` and fails on `ZoneId.systemDefault`, `TimeZone.getDefault` (java.util and ICU), `Clock.systemDefaultZone`, a `now()` without arguments on the java.time date and time types, and a `Calendar` or `GregorianCalendar` built without a zone. Tapping Start or Stop never fails because the server is out of reach. A tap in the app, notification, widget or tile changes the state on the phone without waiting for the server. The notification, widget and tile read the running entry from the phone, so they react at once, and the queue sends the change behind them.
Each offline change waits in a queue on the phone, marked as not sent, and goes out in order when the server is reachable. A timer started offline keeps its real start time. 166:The script clones the commit twice, runs `./gradlew --no-daemon assembleRelease` in each clone without the signing variables below, and compares the two unsigned APKs byte for byte. It builds committed work only. The clones sit at paths of different lengths. The second build runs on at most two CPU cores and gets its own Gradle user home, which reads downloaded dependencies from yours but redoes every transform. So an embedded path, output that depends on the core count, and a transform that differs from run to run all show up as differences. When the APKs differ, the script lists the zip entries that differ and keeps both APKs. On this machine the two builds take about four minutes and use up to about 700 MB under `build/`, which the script removes at the end. CI runs the script on pull requests to `main` and on pushes to `main`.

feat: detect Tokkl-only capabilities from /me and a trash probe

A persisted Capabilities model holds four flags. Time resolution is on
when GET /me carries time_resolution_minutes, and favorites when it
carries Tokkl's role, so a fresh Tokkl account without saved favorites
still gets them. One GET /api/app/trash decides trash and undo of a
delete: a list turns both on, a 404 or a body that is not a list turns
both off, and any other answer keeps them. Nothing probes the restore
endpoint and nothing compares server versions.

The flags refresh with the account settings' /me and persist in their
own preferences file. The cache asks for favorites only when the server
has them.

Refs: TKA-0024
EOF

title: Port Tokkl's TypeScript with JavaScript semantics and verbatim test cases
  rules, return null for NaN, and reuse the .test.ts cases verbatim.
  - testing
The ports in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time` (`Duration.kt` for `parseDuration` and `formatDuration`, `TimeOfDay.kt` for `parseTimeOfDay`, `Snap.kt` for `snapSpan`, and `TimeZone.kt`, which accepts the timezone names Intl accepts) behave like the TypeScript they port, including where Kotlin differs from JavaScript. `JsSemantics.kt` has the helpers. JavaScript's `\s` and `String.prototype.trim` use the ECMAScript WhiteSpace and LineTerminator characters, while Java's `\s` matches only ASCII and Kotlin's `trim()` uses yet another set. `Math.round` rounds halves up and `kotlin.math.round` rounds them to even. JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.
A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.
`DurationTest` and `TimeOfDayTest` hold the cases of the matching `.test.ts` file verbatim, and their header names the tokkl commit they were copied at. To follow an upstream change, copy the cases again and update that commit. `DurationJsSemanticsTest` pins the JavaScript traps in its own file, since they are not in `duration.test.ts` and a later diff against tokkl leaves them alone. Its expected values come from running the TypeScript file in Node 24, where `node file.mts` strips the types.
`formatDuration` uses JavaScript's double arithmetic, and `DurationTest` holds the `formatDuration` cases of `duration.test.ts` too. `jsToFixed` in `JsSemantics.kt` is `Number.prototype.toFixed`, which rounds the double's exact binary value: `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is `1.00` and `(2.55).toFixed(1)` is `2.5`. `Intl.NumberFormat` rounds the shortest decimal string of the double instead and gives `1.01` and `2.6` (Node 24.21). So `jsToFixed` ports a `toFixed` call only, never an `Intl.NumberFormat` one. `sharePercent` in `reports/ReportFormat.kt` uses it for percentages that the web app writes with `Intl.NumberFormat`, and differs from the web app at halves until TKA-0148.
Where the TypeScript throws a RangeError, `snapSpan` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Within hours of the end of a JavaScript Date's range, near the year 275760, the TypeScript can also return an invalid Date. An `Instant` has no such value, so the port throws there too, and `SnapJsDateRangeTest` pins that edge.
`ReportsServer` takes the account's default workspace from `GET /api/v9/me` and its rounding from `GET /api/v9/workspaces/{id}`. It pages `POST /reports/api/v3/workspace/{id}/search/time_entries`, following `X-Next-Row-Number`, and the phone sums the entries. The summary endpoints will not do: Tokkl's v3 totals send `rates: []`, and its v3 summary groups carry seconds only, with no billable time or amount. Each search asks for the workspace's `rounding` and `rounding_minutes`, because the Reports API rounds only when asked while the web app always rounds. `ReportsScreenTest` checks the summary against `POST /api/app/report`, the web app's own call.
Report data stays in memory. Offline, or on a 502, 503 or 504 from a proxy that cannot reach Tokkl, the screen says reports need the server and shows no numbers. When the app comes back to the foreground, after an `ON_STOP` that was not a configuration change, the model asks for the range again and shows no numbers until the answer comes. Adding the lifecycle observer replays `ON_START` at once, and the model ignores that one. A configuration change keeps the report and sends nothing.

A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a message only when `@commitlint/is-ignored` (a declared dependency in `package.json`) matches its first line and the message passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. Because only the header goes to `isIgnored`, a body line such as `Merge branch y` no longer lets a non-Conventional message skip the format rules. `npm test` (`node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
The hook never sees the message that `git revert` or `git cherry-pick` writes (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), a commit made with `--no-verify`, or one from a tree without `npm install`. The `commitlint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` catches those. It lints the pull request's commits, or the pushed range on `main`, and falls back to `commitlint --last` when a force push removed the old tip. Then it runs `npm test`.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes it, and tests call `DeviceShell.closeSystemDialogs()` in `app/src/androidTest`, which sends the same broadcast.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

Raise `targetSdk` together with the emulator image, not to silence lint.
`gradle.properties` allows for the other services on this machine. `org.gradle.jvmargs` caps the daemon heap at `-Xmx2g` and metaspace at 768m, and `kotlin.compiler.execution.strategy=in-process` compiles Kotlin inside the Gradle daemon instead of a second long-lived Kotlin daemon.

The launch screen opens a settings screen with three theme modes:
follow the system (the default), light and dark. On Android 12 and
later it also has a wallpaper colours switch, off by default. With the
switch off the app keeps Tokkl's palette in every mode.

The settings live in their own private preferences file, written with
commit() the way ServerConfigStore writes the server URL. The existing
backup rules already leave out every domain, so they stay on the phone.
TokklApplication reads them once per process, before the first frame,
and holds them in a model that TokklTheme reads, so a change redraws at
once without restarting the activity. The write runs off the main
thread in an application scope, so leaving the app cannot cancel it. If
the write fails, the screen goes back to the stored choice.

chosen scheme. Before Android 12 the switch is hidden.

restart, the switch default and its Android 12 cut-off, wallpaper
colours on and off, TalkBack labels and roles, string resources and the
largest font scale. WindowBackgroundTest now resets the theme setting so
it keeps following the system.

## Problem

title: Port Tokkl's TypeScript with JavaScript semantics and verbatim test cases
  rules, return null for NaN, and reuse the .test.ts cases verbatim.
  - testing
The ports in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time` (`Duration.kt` for `parseDuration`, `TimeOfDay.kt` for `parseTimeOfDay`, `Snap.kt` for `snapSpan`, and `TimeZone.kt`, which accepts the timezone names Intl accepts) behave like the TypeScript they port, including where Kotlin differs from JavaScript. `JsSemantics.kt` has the helpers. JavaScript's `\s` and `String.prototype.trim` use the ECMAScript WhiteSpace and LineTerminator characters, while Java's `\s` matches only ASCII and Kotlin's `trim()` uses yet another set. `Math.round` rounds halves up and `kotlin.math.round` rounds them to even. JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.
A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.
`DurationTest` and `TimeOfDayTest` hold the cases of the matching `.test.ts` file verbatim, and their header names the tokkl commit they were copied at. To follow an upstream change, copy the cases again and update that commit. `DurationJsSemanticsTest` pins the JavaScript traps in its own file, since they are not in `duration.test.ts` and a later diff against tokkl leaves them alone. Its expected values come from running the TypeScript file in Node 24, where `node file.mts` strips the types.
Where the TypeScript throws a RangeError, `snapSpan` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Within hours of the end of a JavaScript Date's range, near the year 275760, the TypeScript can also return an invalid Date. An `Instant` has no such value, so the port throws there too, and `SnapJsDateRangeTest` pins that edge.
title: 'Account settings: AccountSettingsSource, AccountTime and NoDeviceZoneTest'
`AccountSettings.time()` gives a `time/AccountTime`: the account's zone, a clock in that zone, `now()`, `today()`, `local(instant)`, `startOfWeek(date)` and `snapUnsent(start, stop)`. It returns null when `parseTimeZone` cannot resolve the name, as when the server's Intl knows a zone that the phone's tz database lacks. There is no fallback to the device's zone or to UTC. A screen without an `AccountTime` must show no clock times or dates, take no time input and name the zone it does not know. Durations, the running clock, Start and Stop need no zone and keep working.
`NoDeviceZoneTest`, a JVM test, reads the constant pool of every compiled app class through `ClassReferences` and fails on `ZoneId.systemDefault`, `TimeZone.getDefault` (java.util and ICU), `Clock.systemDefaultZone`, a `now()` without arguments on the java.time date and time types, and a `Calendar` or `GregorianCalendar` built without a zone. Its `ALLOWED` set is empty, and a class added there needs a comment saying why the account's zone will not do. Take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime` instead.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot. CI's emulator step sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` itself.

The light theme has a sand background, ink text, a sunset orange primary, an aqua secondary, and hot pink and lime for states. The dark theme has a navy background with the neon counterparts.
In the app, `ui/theme/Color.kt` defines the Material 3 roles and the running and billable state colours, each with a comment naming its token in the first `:root` block of `styles.css`. Find a token by name, not by line. `TokklTheme` has dynamic colour off by default. `Theme.Tokkl` in `res/values` and `res/values-night` sets `android:windowBackground` to the scheme's background (`@color/window_background`), so launch shows no flash of another colour before Compose draws. When a token changes, update `Color.kt` and `window_background` together. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, `syncApplicationNightMode` in `settings/ApplicationNightMode.kt` passes the stored theme mode to `UiModeManager.setApplicationNightMode` on every start and every change, off the main thread: light is `MODE_NIGHT_NO`, dark `MODE_NIGHT_YES` and system `MODE_NIGHT_AUTO`. Android picks `res/values` or `res/values-night` for the starting window by that mode, so a cold start shows the chosen theme's colours. `MainActivity` declares `android:configChanges="uiMode"`, so the sync does not recreate it. Below Android 12 the starting window still follows the system's dark mode, and the window theme never knows the wallpaper's colours. So `MainActivity` still repaints the window background and picks the system bar icon colours from the chosen theme each time the setting changes. Wallpaper colours are an opt-in switch on the settings screen, shown only on Android 12 (API 31) and later.
The font is upstream Anybody 1.114, the variable TTF with width and weight axes, at `res/font/anybody_wdth_wght.ttf`. `res/font` accepts only font files, so the OFL (`anybody_ofl.txt`) and the source note with commit, URL and SHA-256 (`anybody_font_source.txt`) live in `res/raw`. No code reads the source note, so `res/raw/keep.xml` marks it `tools:keep`. `ui/theme/Type.kt` gives Anybody its own `Font` entries for weights 800 and 900 at width 85 and sizes the Material type roles from Tokkl's web scale.
Contrast meets WCAG AA as in Tokkl: 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for non-text elements. Colour is never the only signal for a state. Every control has a TalkBack label, and layouts survive the largest font scale. `ThemeContrastTest` checks the theme's colour pairs. Draw chart marks on surface, not surface-2: in light, `--chart-other` falls under 3:1 on surface-2, which is why Tokkl's `styles.css` keeps its chart off surface-2. The reports chart's bar track is still `surfaceVariant`, which is surface-2 (TKA-0150). Tokkl's sixth principle applies as written. Any style that costs a readable number, a reachable control or a passing test gets dropped.
=== map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session.md
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.
`ReportsServer` takes the account's default workspace from `GET /api/v9/me` and its rounding from `GET /api/v9/workspaces/{id}`. It pages `POST /reports/api/v3/workspace/{id}/search/time_entries`, following `X-Next-Row-Number`, and the phone sums the entries. The summary endpoints will not do: Tokkl's v3 totals send `rates: []`, and its v3 summary groups carry seconds only, with no billable time or amount. Each search asks for the workspace's `rounding` and `rounding_minutes`, because the Reports API rounds only when asked while the web app always rounds. `ReportsScreenTest` checks the summary against `POST /api/app/report`, the web app's own call.
Report data stays in memory. Offline, or on a 502, 503 or 504 from a proxy that cannot reach Tokkl, the screen says reports need the server and shows no numbers. When the app comes back to the foreground, after an `ON_STOP` that was not a configuration change, the model asks for the range again and shows no numbers until the answer comes. Adding the lifecycle observer replays `ON_START` at once, and the model ignores that one. A configuration change keeps the report and sends nothing.

fix: treat an empty 2xx body as success for calls that expect no content

Tokkl answers every DELETE with 200 and an empty body. The client decoded

body. send and get still decode, so an empty or malformed body there is

Since Android 9 an app cannot use cleartext HTTP unless it opts in, and since Android 7 it trusts only system CAs by default ([network security configuration](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/security-config)). The app's network security config therefore permits cleartext (S4) and trusts user-added CAs (S2). The self-signed certificate in S3 is pinned in the app, separate from Android's trust store.
- No push reaches the phone, so it can miss a timer started or stopped on another client. Two more events cover that. Opening the notification shade makes the tile fetch `GET /me/time_entries/current`, at most once a minute (N4); the cap keeps Toggl's 30 requests an hour for `/me` endpoints in reach (risk 2). While a timer runs, a WorkManager job checks the running entry every 15 minutes, the shortest periodic interval WorkManager allows, and clears the notification and widget if the timer stopped elsewhere. Otherwise the phone learns of a timer started elsewhere only on one of these events.
| Speed | A tap on Start or Stop in the app, notification, widget or tile changes the state on the phone without waiting for the server. Tests prove it with a network that never answers. Jetpack Macrobenchmark runs cold start (`StartupTimingMetric`) and tap-to-state (`TraceSectionMetric`) on the CI emulator and fails a build that is slower than the previous one. fix: keep the 429 sign-in cooldown across process death

The deadline after a 429 lived only in SignInModel's memory, so a model
recreated within Retry-After, after the process died, let the user send
attempts again. It now persists in SignInCooldownStore, one entry per
server origin holding the deadline and nothing else. The model loads the
entries when it starts, and submit waits for that load. It drops an entry
once its deadline passes or a sign-in to that server succeeds. It still
never retries on its own.

The deadline is wall-clock time, not elapsed realtime, because Tokkl's
lockout runs on the server's clock and a reboot of the phone does not
lift it. ServerUrl.origin gives the scheme://host:port key, the same form
the host guard reports.

Refs: TKA-0103
EOF
git log --oneline -4

connection button that opens the prompt again. Other network failures stay
quiet, and an answer from the server clears the refusal.

can host them. Sign-in still shows its own.

EOF

mkdir -p ~/.local/libexec/android-env && cat > ~/.local/libexec/android-env/tool-wrapper <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# Wrapper for JDK and Android SDK tools, installed as ~/.local/bin/<tool>
# symlinks. Agent shells put ~/.local/bin on PATH but read neither ~/.profile
# nor the PATH set in ~/.bashrc, so this runs the real tool from the paths in
# ~/.config/android-env.sh. Symlinking the tools directly does not work:
# sdkmanager and avdmanager find the SDK from their own path.
env_file="$HOME/.config/android-env.sh"
if [ ! -f "$env_file" ]; then
    echo "android-env: $env_file is missing" >&2
    exit 127
fi
. "$env_file"

tool=$(basename "$0")
case $tool in
    java) dir=${JAVA_HOME:-}/bin; base=${JAVA_HOME:-} ;;
    adb) dir=${ANDROID_HOME:-}/platform-tools; base=${ANDROID_HOME:-} ;;
    sdkmanager|avdmanager) dir=${ANDROID_HOME:-}/cmdline-tools/latest/bin; base=${ANDROID_HOME:-} ;;
    emulator) dir=${ANDROID_HOME:-}/emulator; base=${ANDROID_HOME:-} ;;
    *) echo "android-env: unknown tool '$tool'" >&2; exit 127 ;;
esac
if [ -z "$base" ] || [ ! -x "$dir/$tool" ]; then
    echo "android-env: $tool is not installed; see $env_file" >&2
    exit 127
fi
exec "$dir/$tool" "$@"
EOF
chmod 755 ~/.local/libexec/android-env/tool-wrapper && for t in java adb sdkmanager avdmanager emulator; do test -e ~/.local/bin/$t && echo "EXISTS $t" || ln -s ../libexec/android-env/tool-wrapper ~/.local/bin/$t; done; ls -la ~/.local/bin | grep tool-wrapper; sh -n ~/.local/libexec/android-env/tool-wrapper && echo "syntax ok"

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes it, and tests call `DeviceShell.closeSystemDialogs()` in `app/src/androidTest`, which sends the same broadcast.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

The parsing is a Kotlin port of Tokkl's `parseDuration` in `../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts` and `parseTimeOfDay` in `../tokkl/packages/web/src/lib/timeOfDay.ts`, checked against the cases in the `.test.ts` file next to each. The time-of-day parser lives in the web package, not in `packages/common`. Both ports live in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time`, and their tests copy the TypeScript cases verbatim at a recorded tokkl commit (see the porting practice node). The ports can still drift when the TypeScript changes later. Sharing the test cases between th
The time parsers in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time` (`Duration.kt` for `parseDuration`, `TimeOfDay.kt` for `parseTimeOfDay`) behave like the TypeScript they port, including where Kotlin differs from JavaScript. `JsSemantics.kt` has the helpers. JavaScript's `\s` and `String.prototype.trim` use the ECMAScript WhiteSpace and LineTerminator characters, while Java's `\s` matches only ASCII and Kotlin's `trim()` uses yet another set. `Math.round` rounds halves up and `kotlin.math.round` rounds them to even. JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.
A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.
`DurationTest` and `TimeOfDayTest` hold the cases of the matching `.test.ts` file verbatim, and their header names the tokkl commit they were copied at. To follow an upstream change, copy the cases again and update that commit. `DurationJsSemanticsTest` pins the JavaScript traps in its own file, since they are not in `duration.test.ts` and a later diff against tokkl leaves them alone. Its expected values come from running the TypeScript file in Node 24, where `node file.mts` strips the types.
