source: "sift-drain wave 4 sitting w4-a2, found while building TKA-0015"
# Show the chosen theme's background in the starting window, not the system's
TKA-0015 lets the owner pin the app to light or dark. The app's own window follows that choice from its first frame, but Android draws the starting window from the manifest theme before the app runs. That theme takes its background from `res/values` or `res/values-night`, which match the system's mode. With the app pinned to dark on a light system, a cold start should show a sand starting window and then switch to navy, the flash that `WindowBackgroundTest` guards against when the app follows the system. Nobody has reproduced it on a device yet; the code paths below predict it.
A cold start shows the chosen theme's background from the starting window on, in every theme mode, as `WindowBackgroundTest` checks for the follow-the-system mode.
- app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:20 gives the application `@style/Theme.Tokkl`, which Android uses for the starting window.
- app/src/main/res/values/themes.xml:10 and app/src/main/res/values-night/themes.xml:4 set `android:windowBackground` to `@color/window_background`, picked by the system's night mode.
- `grep -rn setApplicationNightMode app/src/main` finds nothing; only `WindowBackgroundTest` calls it.
Reproduce first and record what the recording shows. On Android 12 and later, `UiModeManager.setApplicationNightMode` tells the system the app's night mode, which the starting window also uses: map light to `MODE_NIGHT_NO`, dark to `MODE_NIGHT_YES` and follow the system to `MODE_NIGHT_AUTO`. Call it when the setting changes and keep the stored setting as the source of truth. Check whether the call recreates the activity and whether the settings screen stays open when it does. `WindowBackgroundTest` sets the application night mode itself, so decide whether the app syncs it at start and adapt that test to drive the setting instead. Below Android 12 there is no such API; record whether that case stays as it is.

- [ ] On Android 12 and later, a cold start with a pinned light or dark mode shows that mode's background from the starting window on.
- [ ] Following the system still matches the system, and `WindowBackgroundTest` passes.

# Draw edge to edge in both themes with no navigation bar scrim

## Problem

With three-button navigation, the system draws a near-white band under the sand screen in light mode. Its pixels read 254,253,250, which is exactly what a 0xE6 white scrim gives over the sand background, and dark mode shows a lighter navy band. The comment at MainActivity.kt:78 says those scrims draw only on Android 9 and earlier, so the comment and the screen disagree. Each screen also applies the scaffold's `innerPadding` outside `verticalScroll`, so scrolled text is cut off at the bar's top edge instead of passing under it. The owner approved fixing this after seeing the screenshots.

## Expected behaviour

In light and dark mode the navigation bar area shows the screen's own background. Scrolling content passes under a transparent bar, and the bar's inset becomes padding inside the scrolling content.

## Steps to reproduce

1. On an API 36 device or emulator, switch the system to three-button navigation.
2. Open the app in light mode and sample a pixel in the navigation bar area.
3. Switch the app to dark mode in Settings and sample the same pixel.
4. Open Licences and scroll to the end. The text stops at the top edge of the navigation bar.

## Evidence

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/MainActivity.kt:41 calls `enableEdgeToEdge()` with its defaults before `setContent`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/MainActivity.kt:71 calls `enableEdgeToEdge` again with `navigationBarStyle = SystemBarStyle.auto(LIGHT_SCRIM, DARK_SCRIM)`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/MainActivity.kt:77-81 sets `LIGHT_SCRIM` to `argb(0xe6, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)` and `DARK_SCRIM` to `argb(0x80, 0x1b, 0x1b, 0x1b)`, under a comment at :78 saying only Android 9 and earlier draw them.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/settings/SettingsScreen.kt:68 applies `innerPadding` before `verticalScroll` at :69.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/licences/LicencesScreen.kt:41 applies `innerPadding` before `verticalScroll` at :42.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/signin/SignInScreen.kt:134 applies `innerPadding` before `imePadding` at :136 and `verticalScroll` at :137.

## Direction

Find out which mechanism paints the band before changing anything. It is either the scrim that `enableEdgeToEdge` passes at MainActivity.kt:71, or the system's navigation bar contrast enforcement, which `window.isNavigationBarContrastEnforced = false` turns off. Fix it at the cause, keep or drop `LIGHT_SCRIM` and `DARK_SCRIM` at MainActivity.kt:77-81 to match, and rewrite the comment at MainActivity.kt:78 so it states the real cause. MainActivity.kt:41 runs before the theme is known, so check that the first frame shows no band either.

On sign-in, Settings and Licences, take the system-bar insets out of the outer padding and give them to the scrolling content as content padding. Text then scrolls under the transparent bar, and the last line can still scroll clear of it. Sign-in keeps its IME padding. Keep `consumeWindowInsets` at SignInScreen.kt:135, or an equivalent, so `imePadding` does not add the navigation bar inset twice. The status bar icons keep following the chosen theme mode, as `SystemBarStyle.auto` at MainActivity.kt:70 does now. Do not change any theme colour.

TKA-0107 changes the padding on the same column modifiers, so whichever ticket lands second keeps both changes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With three-button navigation on API 36, the pixels under the navigation bar match the screen background in light and dark mode, checked with a screenshot or a pixel sample.
- [ ] On Licences, scrolled text passes under the navigation bar and the last line can scroll fully above it.
- [ ] Settings and sign-in pass scrolled content under the navigation bar the same way, and sign-in still keeps the focused field above the keyboard.
- [ ] The comment at MainActivity.kt:78 states the real cause.
- [ ] Gesture navigation still shows no band.
EOF

# Render the OFL readably, at body size and with separators that do not wrap

## Problem

The OFL is the longest text in the app and the only one set in `bodySmall`, 12sp, which is a caption size. The Licences screen shows it as one proportional `Text` with soft wrap. Each long dashed separator line therefore wraps onto a stray second line of dashes. The owner approved fixing this after seeing the screenshots.

## Expected behaviour

The licence reads at body size, and each separator line shows as a single rule at every width and font scale.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open Licences on a phone at font scale 1.0.
2. Scroll to the OFL title. The dashed lines above and below it each wrap onto a second line of dashes.

## Evidence

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/licences/LicencesScreen.kt:33-36 reads res/raw/anybody_ofl.txt into one string and only turns CRLF into LF.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/licences/LicencesScreen.kt:70 shows that string as one `Text` in `MaterialTheme.typography.bodySmall`.

## Direction

Set the licence text in `bodyMedium`. Replace the OFL's dashed separator lines with a `HorizontalDivider` at render time, by splitting the text read at LicencesScreen.kt:33-36 on lines made only of dashes, or show those lines in a style that cannot wrap. res/raw/anybody_ofl.txt:8 and :10 are the two separators, 59 dashes each. Keep res/raw/anybody_ofl.txt byte-identical, since the OFL must ship unchanged.

Keep the existing Licences tests passing. LicencesScreenTest.kt:35-42 finds the one node whose text contains the OFL title and compares its lines, dashes included, with the shipped file. Splitting the text across several `Text` nodes fails that check unless one node still exposes the full text to semantics.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The licence text uses `bodyMedium`.
- [ ] No dashed separator wraps onto a second line at 1x or the largest font scale.
- [ ] res/raw/anybody_ofl.txt is unchanged.
- [ ] LicencesScreenTest still passes.
EOF

# Add a spacing scale, one screen margin and a content width cap, and use them on every screen

## Problem

Sign-in and home pad 24dp on every side, while Settings and Licences pad 16dp across and 8dp down. The http warning and the certificate prompt space their content 16dp and 8dp apart. The theme names no spacing values, so every screen picks its own literals and the content edge jumps from screen to screen. No screen caps its width either. On the tablets and foldables the PRD names, the sign-in form and the Settings rows stretch across the whole window.

## Evidence

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/MainActivity.kt:92 pads the home screen with `padding(24.dp)`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/signin/SignInScreen.kt:138 pads sign-in with `padding(24.dp)`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/settings/SettingsScreen.kt:70 pads Settings with `padding(horizontal = 16.dp, vertical = 8.dp)`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/licences/LicencesScreen.kt:43 pads Licences with `padding(horizontal = 16.dp, vertical = 8.dp)`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/signin/SignInScreen.kt:304 spaces the http warning with `Arrangement.spacedBy(16.dp)`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/signin/SignInScreen.kt:353 spaces the certificate prompt with `Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp)`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/signin/SignInScreen.kt:130-140 builds the sign-in column with `fillMaxSize()`, no width limit and `spacedBy(16.dp)` between fields.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/settings/SettingsScreen.kt:66 starts the Settings column's modifier chain, which has no width limit.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/licences/LicencesScreen.kt:39 starts the Licences column's modifier chain, which has no width limit.
- docs/PRD.md:80 says layouts adapt to tablets and foldables.
- absent: app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/Spacing.kt. ui/theme holds only Color.kt, Theme.kt and Type.kt.

## Direction

Add ui/theme/Spacing.kt with Tokkl's spacing scale, taken from `--space-1` to `--space-8` in ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32 and 48dp. Expose it through the theme object next to `TokklTheme.extraColors`. Name the rhythm on top of the scale: 24dp between groups, 8dp inside a group and 16dp under the top bar.

Define one screen margin, 16dp on compact widths and 24dp on medium and wider, using Material's window size class breakpoints. Define a 600dp content width cap that centres the content on wider windows. Apply both on home, sign-in, Settings, Licences and both sign-in dialogs. The dialogs use the scale's in-group gap of 8dp and between-group gap of 24dp. Replace the literal dp values at the cited sites with the tokens.

This caps single-column content only. TKA-0056 still owns the navigation rail and multi-pane layouts. TKA-0105 moves the system-bar insets on the same column modifiers, so whichever ticket lands second keeps both changes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] ui/theme/Spacing.kt defines the scale and the theme exposes it.
- [ ] Every cited site uses the tokens instead of literal dp values.
- [ ] Home, sign-in, Settings and Licences share one horizontal margin on a phone.
- [ ] On a window wider than 600dp plus margins, content is capped at 600dp and centred, checked by a test with a wide window size.
- [ ] Existing JVM tests pass, and instrumented tests pass through scripts/instrumented-tests.sh.
EOF

# Set Tokkl's navigation bar item colours in the theme before the first NavigationBar

## Problem

Material's `NavigationBar` paints the active item's indicator in `secondaryContainer`, which Color.kt maps to `--state-selected`, a pale fill. Tokkl's web marks the active item as a primary block with an on-primary icon and label. The timer and history screens will add the first bottom bar. Unless the theme sets the item colours once, that bar will not look like Tokkl.

## Evidence

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/Color.kt:96 maps `secondaryContainer`, the default indicator colour, to `--state-selected`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/Color.kt:121 maps `surfaceContainer`, the bar's default container colour, to `--surface`.

## Direction

Add a theme-level `NavigationBarItemColors` default that later screens use, through a small composable or a defaults object, and keep Material 3's `NavigationBarItem`. The active indicator is a primary block behind the icon only, with the icon in on-primary. The active label sits below the indicator, on the bar's surface, in primary at weight 700, the button and label role weight. Inactive icons and labels use on-surface-variant, with labels at the normal label weight. The indicator shape and the bold label are the cues that do not depend on colour.

Tokkl's web puts the label inside the primary block (the `.nav-link.active` rule in ../tokkl/packages/web/src/styles.css). Material 3's item layout draws the label below the indicator, on the bar's surface, where on-primary text would be unreadable. That is why the active label takes primary instead.

In ThemeContrastTest, check these pairs in light and dark. The bar surface is `surfaceContainer`, which Color.kt:121 maps to `--surface`.

- On-primary icon on the primary indicator, 3:1 for non-text.
- Primary active label on the bar surface, 4.5:1 for text.
- On-surface-variant inactive icon on the bar surface, 3:1.
- On-surface-variant inactive label on the bar surface, 4.5:1.

Do not add a `NavigationBar` to any screen. TKA-0056 and the screen tickets own navigation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The theme provides Tokkl navigation bar item colours for `NavigationBarItem`. The active item has a primary indicator behind the icon, an on-primary icon, and a primary label at weight 700. Inactive items use on-surface-variant for icon and label.
- [ ] The default replaces `secondaryContainer` (Color.kt:96) as the active indicator colour without changing the colour scheme mapping.
- [ ] ThemeContrastTest checks all four pairs above in both themes, and they pass.
- [ ] No screen gains a navigation bar in this ticket.
EOF

### Build and test
Build the debug APK, run lint and run the JVM unit tests:
./gradlew assembleDebug lint testDebugUnitTest
`./gradlew check` runs the same lint and unit tests, plus `:app:checkDeniedDependencies`. That task fails when the release runtime classpath holds a module from a group listed in `gradle/denied-dependency-groups.txt`, such as Google Play Services, Firebase or an analytics SDK. The failure names each module and the dependencies that pulled it in.
The instrumented tests, including the Compose UI tests, run against a real Tokkl server, never a fake one. One command runs them. It needs Docker, `curl`, `jq` and `openssl`:
scripts/instrumented-tests.sh
[credential-related line omitted]
If no device is attached, the script boots `tokkl-api36` as in the previous section, with 2.5 GB of guest RAM, 4 cores and the `lavapipe` renderer, and stops it and the adb server at the end. When your systemd user manager is running, the emulator runs in a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` and at most 6 GB of memory. If the kernel's OOM killer ends qemu, the script fails and says so, and systemd leaves the session that started it alone. On an emulator it boots, the script also turns on `hide_error_dialogs` and closes open system dialogs, because a fresh headless boot often leaves "System UI isn't responding" in front of the app. It also sets the font scale to 1.0, because the AVD keeps the last scale a test set across boots. It turns on `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` too, since otherwise the soft keyboard never opens on the headless emulator. It sets `debug.hwui.renderer` to `skiavk`, so apps draw with Vulkan: qemu kept about 100 MB after every app process that drew with OpenGL, and the test orchestrator starts one per test, so a full run took qemu to 11 GB instead of 3.5 GB. It changes no setting on an emulator that was already running, and that emulator keeps running. Arguments go to Gradle, so one class runs with:
scripts/instrumented-tests.sh \
  -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest
Without the script, `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails the tests that need the server. `gradle.properties` caps the Gradle heap at 2 GB and compiles Kotlin inside the Gradle daemon, so no separate Kotlin daemon starts. The Gradle daemon itself stays in memory after the build. Stop it when you finish:
### Screenshot tests
`app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/screenshot/` captures sign-in with each method, home, Settings, Licences, Reports, the http warning and the certificate prompt, in the light and the dark theme, at font scale 1.0 and 2.0. Each capture shrinks to a third in each direction and is compared with its reference image in `app/src/androidTest/assets/screenshots/`. The references come from `tokkl-api36`, because density and system fonts change the pixels. Run all four classes with:
scripts/instrumented-tests.sh \
  -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.package=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.ui.screenshot

The capture and a diff, with the differing pixels in magenta, land in `actual/` and `diff/` under `app/build/outputs/connected_android_test_additional_output/debugAndroidTest/connected/<device>/screenshots/`. README.md:140:If no device is attached, the script boots `tokkl-api36` as in the previous section, with 2.5 GB of guest RAM, 4 cores and the `lavapipe` renderer, and stops it and the adb server at the end. When your systemd user manager is running, the emulator runs in a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` and at most 6 GB of memory. If the kernel's OOM killer ends qemu, the script fails and says so, and systemd leaves the session that started it alone. On an emulator it boots, the script also turns on `hide_error_dialogs` and closes open system dialogs, because a fresh headless boot often leaves "System UI isn't responding" in front of the app. It also sets the font scale to 1.0, because the AVD keeps the last scale a test set across boots. It turns on `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` too, since otherwise the soft keyboard never opens on the headless emulator. It sets `debug.hwui.renderer` to `skiavk`, so apps draw with Vulkan: qemu kept about 100 MB after every app process that drew with OpenGL, and the test orchestrator starts one per test, so a full run took qemu to 11 GB instead of 3.5 GB. It changes no setting on an emulator that was already running, and that emulator keeps running. Arguments go to Gradle, so one class runs with:

README.md:263:Commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). `npm install` sets up a commit-msg hook that runs commitlint, which needs Node 22.12 or later. The hook lives in `.husky/_`, which git ignores, so run `npm install` once in every new clone or git worktree. Until you do, commits there skip the check. The hook rejects a ticket ID such as `TKA-0001` in the subject; put it in a `Refs: TKA-0001` trailer instead. It also rejects commits that credit an AI tool or a co-author (`Co-authored-by:`, "Generated with Claude Code" and the like). `npm test` checks these rules, and runs the hook against real commits and merges in a throwaway repository. Since Android 9 an app cannot use cleartext HTTP unless it opts in, and since Android 7 it trusts only system CAs by default ([network security configuration](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/security-config)). The app's network security config therefore permits cleartext (S4) and trusts user-added CAs (S2). The self-signed certificate in S3 is pinned in the app, separate from Android's trust store.
- No push reaches the phone, so it can miss a timer started or stopped on another client. Two more events cover that. Opening the notification shade makes the tile fetch `GET /me/time_entries/current`, at most once a minute (N4); the cap keeps Toggl's 30 requests an hour for `/me` endpoints in reach (risk 2). While a timer runs, a WorkManager job checks the running entry every 15 minutes, the shortest periodic interval WorkManager allows, and clears the notification and widget if the timer stopped elsewhere. Otherwise the phone learns of a timer started elsewhere only on one of these events.

            val instant = Instant.parse(iso)

            assertEquals("$iso $zone 12", expected.second, formatTime(instant, ZoneId.of(zone), twelveHour = true))
        }

        }

package com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.calendar

import com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.cache.CachedTimeEntry
import com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.cache.EntryWithSendState
import com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.session.AccountSettings
import java.time.Clock
import java.time.DayOfWeek

import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOf

import org.junit.After
import org.junit.Assert.assertEquals
import org.junit.Before
import org.junit.Test

/**
 * The calendar lays out the week in the account's timezone and from its first day of the week,
 * never the device's. The device runs in Los Angeles here, and the account in Tokyo, 16 hours
 * ahead in October, so a wrong zone moves every block to another hour and most to another day.
 */
class CalendarTimeZoneTest {

    private lateinit var deviceZone: TimeZone

    @Before
    fun putTheDeviceInAnotherZone() {
        deviceZone = TimeZone.getDefault()
        TimeZone.setDefault(TimeZone.getTimeZone("America/Los_Angeles"))
    }

    @After
    fun restoreTheDeviceZone() {
        TimeZone.setDefault(deviceZone)
    }

    @Test
    fun theWeekAndItsBlocksFollowTheAccountTimezone() = runBlocking {
        val model = CalendarModel(
            entries = flowOf(listOf(EntryWithSendState(LATE_CALL, unsent = false))),
            projects = flowOf(emptyList()),
            tasks = flowOf(emptyList()),
            accountSettings = MutableStateFlow(TOKYO_SUNDAY),
            client = { null },
            scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Unconfined),
            io = Dispatchers.Unconfined,
            clock = NOW,
        )

        val state = model.state.first { it is CalendarState.Shown } as CalendarState.Shown

        assertEquals("today in Tokyo, while Los Angeles is still on the 13th", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 14), state.today)
        assertEquals("the account's week starts on Sunday", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 11), state.weekStart)
        assertEquals(WeekSource.Cached, state.week)
        val blocks = calendarBlocks(state.entries, state.weekDays, state.zone, NOW.instant())
        // 14:30 to 16:00 UTC is 23:30 to 01:00 in Tokyo, across midnight, while in Los Angeles it
        // would be 07:30 to 09:00 on the 13th.
        assertEquals(
            listOf(
                Triple(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 13), 23 * 60 + 30.0, 24 * 60.0),
                Triple(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 14), 0.0, 60.0),
            ),
            blocks.map { Triple(it.day, it.top, it.bottom) },
        )
        assertEquals(5400L, dayTotalSeconds(state.entries, LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 13), state.zone, NOW.instant()))
        assertEquals(0L, dayTotalSeconds(state.entries, LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 14), state.zone, NOW.instant()))
    }

    private companion object {
        val TOKYO_SUNDAY = AccountSettings("Asia/Tokyo", DayOfWeek.SUNDAY, timeResolutionMinutes = null)

        /** Noon on Wednesday 14 October in Tokyo, 20:00 on Tuesday the 13th in Los Angeles. */
        val NOW: Clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-10-14T03:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC)

        val LATE_CALL = CachedTimeEntry(
            id = 1,
            workspaceId = 1,
            projectId = null,
            taskId = null,
            description = "Late call",
            start = Instant.parse("2026-10-13T14:30:00Z"),
            stop = Instant.parse("2026-10-13T16:00:00Z"),
            billable = false,
            tags = emptyList(),
            tagIds = emptyList(),
        )
    }
}

# Give the Calendar view room on a phone held sideways

## Problem

PRD K1 shows the week view in landscape, but on a phone held sideways the week grid gets almost no height. The Timer page keeps its brand heading and the List and Calendar switch fixed above the calendar, and the bottom bar sits below it, so on tokkl-api36 turned to landscape (411dp tall) the calendar's toolbar and day heads fill the space and the grid shows about one hour row. At the largest font scale the toolbar and heads alone are taller than that space. The grid still scrolls, but a user sees one hour of the week at a time.

## Evidence

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/timer/TimerScreen.kt:66-73 draws `Brand(BrandSize.MEDIUM)` and the view switch above a `weight(1f)` box that holds the calendar, and none of them scroll away.

- docs/PRD.md:131 asks for the week view in landscape.

## Direction

On a window of compact height, under 480dp by Material's window size classes, let the Timer page's heading and view switch scroll away or collapse as the calendar scrolls, so the grid gets most of the window. Keep the calendar's day heads in view while the grid scrolls. Leave the width to TKA-0056, which gives the week calendar the extra width on expanded windows and moves navigation to a rail. Keep the layout usable at the largest font scale and keep every control reachable with TalkBack.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On tokkl-api36 in landscape, the Calendar view shows at least four hour rows of the week at font scale 1.0.
- [ ] At font scale 2.0 in landscape, the grid shows at least one whole hour row and every toolbar control stays reachable.

The light theme has a sand background, ink text, a sunset orange primary, an aqua secondary, and hot pink and lime for states. The dark theme has a navy background with the neon counterparts.
In the app, `ui/theme/Color.kt` defines the Material 3 roles and the running and billable state colours, each with a `styles.css:<line> --token` comment naming its source. `TokklTheme` has dynamic colour off by default. `Theme.Tokkl` in `res/values` and `res/values-night` sets `android:windowBackground` to the scheme's background (`@color/window_background`), so launch shows no flash of another colour before Compose draws. When a token changes, update `Color.kt` and `window_background` together. Those resources follow only the system's dark mode, and the settings screen can choose light or dark against it. So `MainActivity` repaints the window background and picks the system bar icon colours from the chosen theme each time the setting changes. Wallpaper colours are an opt-in switch on the settings screen, shown only on Android 12 (API 31) and later.
The font is upstream Anybody 1.114, the variable TTF with width and weight axes, at `res/font/anybody_wdth_wght.ttf`. `res/font` accepts only font files, so the OFL (`anybody_ofl.txt`) and the source note with commit, URL and SHA-256 (`anybody_font_source.txt`) live in `res/raw`. No code reads the source note, so `res/raw/keep.xml` marks it `tools:keep`. `ui/theme/Type.kt` defines `ClockTextStyle` and `TotalTextStyle` in Anybody.
Contrast meets WCAG AA as in Tokkl: 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for non-text elements. Colour is never the only signal for a state. Every control has a TalkBack label, and layouts survive the largest font scale. Tokkl's sixth principle applies as written. `session/AccountSettings` holds the `GET /api/v9/me` fields that decide how the app shows and reads times: `timezone`, `beginning_of_week` and Tokkl's optional `time_resolution_minutes`. It holds no credential. Sign-in stores them from its own `/me`. A `/me` without `timezone` or `beginning_of_week`, or with a week start outside 0 to 6, fails sign-in as `SignInResult.NotTokkl`. Toggl Track and older Tokkl servers leave out `time_resolution_minutes` and do not snap, so it stays null for them.

`session/AccountSettingsSource` is the one place screens read the settings from. `TokklApplication.accountSettings` builds it over `AccountSettingsStore`, which keeps them in the private preferences file `account_settings`, so screens have them offline and after a restart. `MainActivity.onStart` calls `refresh()`, so a change made in the web app reaches the phone. A second `refresh()` while one runs gets the running job instead of sending another request. A failed request or write keeps what is stored, and a refresh drops its answer when sign-in stored newer settings while the request ran.

`AccountSettings.time()` gives a `time/AccountTime`: the account's zone, a clock in that zone, `now()`, `today()`, `local(instant)`, `startOfWeek(date)` and `snapUnsent(start, stop)`. It returns null when `parseTimeZone` cannot resolve the name, as when the server's Intl knows a zone that the phone's tz database lacks. There is no fallback to the device's zone or to UTC. A screen without an `AccountTime` shows no clock times or dates, takes no time input and names the zone it does not know. Durations, the running clock, Start and Stop need no zone and keep working.

`NoDeviceZoneTest`, a JVM test, reads the constant pool of every compiled app class through `ClassReferences` and fails on `ZoneId.systemDefault`, `TimeZone.getDefault` (java.util and ICU), `Clock.systemDefaultZone`, a `now()` without arguments on the java.time date and time types, and a `Calendar` or `GregorianCalendar` built without a zone. Its `ALLOWED` set is empty, and a class added there needs a comment saying why the account's zone will not do. Take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime` instead.
EOF
wc -c $tmp/account.md

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URLs and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, in the Tokkl container's network namespace. As a TLS proxy it serves a self-signed certificate that `openssl` makes for each run, with IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. On another port the proxy serves Tokkl over http under the path prefix `/tokkl` and answers 404 to every other path there, so a client that drops the prefix fails. Tests reach it as `tokklPrefixedBaseUrl`, through `TokklTestServer.prefixedUrl`.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD`, by default `tokkl-api36`, sets it up as the emulator node describes, and kills it at the end. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot.
[credential-related line omitted]
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `-Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`, one test with `class=<class>#<method>`. A comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list works too. AGP hands the runner all its arguments in one comma-joined string and splits it at every comma, so a raw `class=A,B` ran only `A` and still passed. The script writes such a list to a `tokkl-test-filter-*` file beside the credentials file, one entry per line, and passes its path as `testFile`. It refuses a comma in any other runner argument, and a `testFile` of your own beside a list.
Below Android 12, a run with no runner argument on an emulator the script boots goes in batches, because qemu keeps memory after every OpenGL process there. The script has the runner list the tests first, which leaves out what `@SdkSuppress` leaves out. Then it runs whole classes, at most 20 tests a batch, the script's `BATCH_TESTS`, each batch on a freshly booted emulator against the same server, and keeps each batch's results in `app/build/outputs/androidTest-results/batches/<n>/`. The run fails when a batch fails and when a batch ran a different number of tests than the runner listed. On API 26 AGP once passed a batch it could not install, `INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS`, with no test run.
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. A run with a filter, or on a device the script did not boot, runs as one, with no count check. There and outside the script, read the test count, not the BUILD line.
`app/build.gradle.kts` sets `execution = "ANDROIDX_TEST_ORCHESTRATOR"`, so every test runs in a new app process. The `*RestartTest` classes need that to prove state survives a process restart.

A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a message only when `@commitlint/is-ignored` (a declared dependency in `package.json`) matches its first line and the message passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. Because only the header goes to `isIgnored`, a body line such as `Merge branch y` no longer lets a non-Conventional message skip the format rules. `npm test` (`node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
The hook never sees the message that `git revert` or `git cherry-pick` writes (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), a commit made with `--no-verify`, or one from a tree without `npm install`. The `commitlint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` catches those. It lints the pull request's commits, or the pushed range on `main`, and falls back to `commitlint --last` when a force push removed the old tip. Then it runs `npm test`.

=== practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script.md
Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot. CI's emulator step sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` itself.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.
The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

`TokklNavHost` is the whole navigation: a back stack of `Destination`s held in `rememberSaveable`, so it survives configuration changes and process death. The destinations are `SIGN_IN`, `HOME`, `SETTINGS`, `LICENCES` and `REPORTS`. Home is still a placeholder that shows the `Brand` and links to the others. The app uses no navigation library. It starts at sign-in until a server and token are stored, and at the home screen after that. Contrast meets WCAG AA as in Tokkl: 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for non-text elements. Colour is never the only signal for a state. === map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session.md
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.

In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. fix(trust): explain a certificate that does not name the server's host

A self-signed certificate whose subjectAltName lists another host, or
none, as a plain `openssl req -x509` makes, got the trust prompt. After
the user trusted it, OkHttp's host name check refused it with
SSLPeerUnverifiedException, and sign-in said "Can't reach the server".
Signed in, the same failure stayed quiet.

PinningTrustManager now asks OkHttp's own host name check before it
offers an unpinned certificate. A leaf that does not name the host fails
with CertificateHostMismatchException instead of
UntrustedCertificateException, so the prompt never offers a certificate

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. title: Build with --no-daemon in parallel worktrees and never run --stop
  ./gradlew --stop ends every daemon of that Gradle version for the user,
kk_id: practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees
Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.
title: Run npm install in every new clone or worktree to turn on the commit hook
  The commit-msg hook lives in git-ignored .husky/_, so a clone or worktree that
A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a message only when `@commitlint/is-ignored` (a declared dependency in `package.json`) matches its first line and the message passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. Because only the header goes to `isIgnored`, a body line such as `Merge branch y` no longer lets a non-Conventional message skip the format rules. `npm test` (`node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
The hook never sees the message that `git revert` or `git cherry-pick` writes (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), a commit made with `--no-verify`, or one from a tree without `npm install`. The `commitlint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` catches those. It lints the pull request's commits, or the pushed range on `main`, and falls back to `commitlint --last` when a force push removed the old tip. Then it runs `npm test`.

title: An OOM kill inside an agent session's scope ends the whole session
  Agent sessions run in t3code-claude-*.scope with OOMPolicy=stop, so one
  OOM-killed process stops the session and its background agents.
kk_id: map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.

Tapping Start or Stop never fails because the server is out of reach. A tap in the app, notification, widget or tile changes the state on the phone without waiting for the server. The notification, widget and tile read the running entry from the phone, so they react at once, and the queue sends the change behind them.
Each offline change waits in a queue on the phone, marked as not sent, and goes out in order when the server is reachable. A timer started offline keeps its real start time. The queue sends in the background when the network comes back, even with the app closed. The app shows how many changes are not sent and when the server last answered (O1 to O5). Some phone makers restrict background work, which can delay sending the queue.
The app has no sync engine and no full local copy of the account. The server is the source of truth. The phone keeps a cache of what it last loaded and the queue of unsent changes. The cache holds projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and about two weeks of history, all readable and editable offline. When the phone and another client both changed an entry, the change that reaches the server last wins. Signing out warns when unsent changes would be lost, then clears the cache and the queue.
The HTTP code lives in `app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/api/`. `SharedHttpClient.instance` is the app's only `OkHttpClient`, so its connection pool, dispatcher and security settings apply to every request. New security settings, such as the trust manager for a pinned self-signed certificate, go into its `build()`, never into a second client. `SingleHttpClientTest` reads the constant pool of every compiled app class through `ClassReferences`, the class-file reader in `app/src/test` that `NoDeviceZoneTest` shares, and fails when any class but `SharedHttpClient` builds an HTTP client, so an import alias or a fully qualified name cannot hide one.
`TogglApiClient.get` and `send` decode a 2xx body with a kotlinx.serialization deserializer, and an empty body fails to decode. Calls that expect no content use `sendNoContent`, which treats any 2xx as success and ignores the body. Tokkl's DELETE routes for time entries, tasks, clients and tags answer 200 with an empty body, while the project DELETE answers 200 with the project id as JSON (`../tokkl/packages/api/src/routes/togglV9.ts`). `sendNoContent` handles both.
Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.

In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. feat(cache): queue time entry changes on the phone and send them in order

Start, Stop, create, edit and delete now change the cached entry at once
and queue the change in the same Room transaction, so a tap never waits
for the network and the change survives the process. The cache marks an
entry unsent while a change to it is queued, and a refresh applies the
queued changes over the server's rows until they are sent.

ChangeQueue is the API the timer and the entry screens will call.
Start and Stop take the tap time; Start also stops a cached running
entry at that time, as the server would. An entry created on the phone
gets a negative local id, and once the server answers the create,
every queued change to it and the cached row take the server's id.

ChangeSender drains the queue oldest first. A create is a POST, an
update or stop a PUT with every field, so the stop keeps the tap time
that Tokkl's PATCH .../stop would replace with the server's clock, and
the last change to reach the server wins. A network failure, a 5xx, a
429 or any other failure stops the drain and keeps the change queued;
after a 429 the next try waits for Retry-After, or 60 seconds without
one. The drain runs when a change is queued, after each refresh and
when the wait ends, and the account refreshes after a drain that sent
something.

The database moves to version 2 through an auto-migration that adds
pending_changes and entry_ids, with the exported schema, and never
drops the file.

Refs: TKA-0027
EOF

Start, Stop, create, edit and delete now change the cached entry at once
and queue the change in the same Room transaction, so a tap never waits
for the network and the change survives the process. The cache marks an
entry unsent while a change to it is queued, and a refresh applies the
queued changes over the server's rows until they are sent.

ChangeQueue is the API the timer and the entry screens will call.
Start and Stop take the tap time; Start also stops a cached running
entry at that time, as the server would. An entry created on the phone
gets a negative local id, and once the server answers the create,
every queued change to it and the cached row take the server's id.

ChangeSender drains the queue oldest first. A create is a POST, an
update or stop a PUT with every field, so the stop keeps the tap time
that Tokkl's PATCH .../stop would replace with the server's clock, and
the last change to reach the server wins. A network failure, a 5xx, a
429 or any other failure stops the drain and keeps the change queued;
after a 429 the next try waits for Retry-After, or 60 seconds without
one. The drain runs when a change is queued, after each refresh and
when the wait ends, and the account refreshes after a drain that sent
something.

The database moves to version 2 through an auto-migration that adds
pending_changes and entry_ids, with the exported schema, and never
drops the file.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. title: 'Test on the plain AOSP API 36 emulator, headless, and stop it afterwards'
  AVD tokkl-api36 uses the AOSP image, since ATD images drop SystemUI and the
  launcher. Boot it with -no-window -accel on and kill it after.
  - testing
  - map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session
  - practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions
  - practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script
The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

kk_id: practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees
Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. # Test on an Android 12 emulator instead of Android 11 and 8.0, and drop the batched runs
With minSdk 31 (TKA-0191) the app no longer installs on the tokkl-api30 and tokkl-api26 emulators, but the script, README and CI still use them. The script splits full runs below Android 12 into batches on fresh emulators, because apps there draw with OpenGL and qemu leaks memory. That code only serves versions the app drops. The oldest supported version, Android 12, has never had a test run, and the skiavk renderer rule the script applies from API 31 has only been exercised on API 36.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:42, :110 (`BATCH_TESTS=20`), :154, :348, :571 (`run_in_batches`), :667: the batching below Android 12.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:362: `setprop debug.hwui.renderer skiavk` from API 31.
- README.md:106-114 and :156-165: tokkl-api30 and tokkl-api26, and the batches.
- Wave 7 gate close run on tokkl-api30 (/tmp/sift-drain.7oM4Ky/gate-w7/close/instrumented-api30.log): HistoryServerTest's two server tests failed because `Instant.parse` rejects Tokkl's `+00:00` offset on API 30 (HistoryServerTest.kt:116-117, :193-194; other tests use OffsetDateTime.parse for this), and ProjectsServerTest#createEditArchiveAndRestoreAProjectAndTheCacheFollowsEachChange timed out after 30 s waiting for the UI.
- Create a tokkl-api31 AVD from the plain AOSP image (system-images;android-31;default;x86_64), like the others, and make it the second test target. Check that skiavk works there (no HWUI abort) and measure qemu's peak in a full run under the 6 GB scope cap.
- Remove run_in_batches, BATCH_TESTS and their README text. Keep the guard that a run fails when a device went away.
- Remove the tokkl-api30 and tokkl-api26 AVDs and their system images with avdmanager and sdkmanager, after the API 31 run passes.
- Make HistoryServerTest parse server times with OffsetDateTime.parse, as ChangeQueueServerTest does.
- Run ProjectsServerTest on tokkl-api31. If the timeout reproduces, find the cause and fix it in the app or file it; if not, record that it was specific to Android 11.
- Run the reports range dialog on tokkl-api31 to confirm whether FillScreenWindow is still needed there.
- [ ] A full run with no arguments on tokkl-api31 passes, with qemu's peak recorded, and tokkl-api36 still passes with the 64 screenshot references.
- [ ] The script has no batching code, and README documents tokkl-api36 and tokkl-api31 only.
- [ ] HistoryServerTest parses offsets with OffsetDateTime, and ProjectsServerTest's Android 11 timeout is explained or fixed.
- [ ] The tokkl-api30 and tokkl-api26 AVDs and images are removed from this machine.

# Fail an instrumented run that Gradle passes without running its tests
On an API 26 device that already has the app installed, AGP 9.4.1's test task cannot install the app, runs no test and still reports BUILD SUCCESSFUL. For a run that is not batched, scripts/instrumented-tests.sh returns Gradle's status, so it would exit 0. A run killed before AGP removes the app at its end can leave it on the AVD, whose data survives a boot with -no-snapshot, so the next run on tokkl-api26 could pass with nothing tested. Batched runs already compare each batch's count with the runner's list; single runs have no such check.
- First batched run on tokkl-api26 on 2026-10-19 (TKA-0168 sitting), batch 1: Gradle logged "AndroidTestRunner failed on emulator-5554 ... Failed to install APK .../app-debug.apk ... INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS: Attempt to re-install com.github.e0ipso.tokkl without first uninstalling", then "BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 15s", and left no JUnit XML report. The listing step had installed the app; on tokkl-api30 the same sequence installed over it and ran every test.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh `run_tests` fails only on Gradle's status or a device that went away; `run_in_batches` checks each batch's count.
After a single run, fail when Gradle's output has an "AndroidTestRunner failed" line, or when the JUnit XML under app/build/outputs/androidTest-results/connected/debug/ is missing or reports 0 tests. Alternatively uninstall the app and the test APK before the run on an emulator the script booted. Check that a run with the app preinstalled on tokkl-api26 then fails or runs every test.
- [ ] A run on tokkl-api26 that starts with the app installed either fails with a message or runs every test.
- [ ] A normal run on tokkl-api36 is unaffected.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URLs and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, in the Tokkl container's network namespace. As a TLS proxy it serves a self-signed certificate that `openssl` makes for each run, with IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. On another port the proxy serves Tokkl over http under the path prefix `/tokkl` and answers 404 to every other path there, so a client that drops the prefix fails. Tests reach it as `tokklPrefixedBaseUrl`, through `TokklTestServer.prefixedUrl`.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD`, by default `tokkl-api36`, sets it up as the emulator node describes, and kills it at the end. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot.
[credential-related line omitted]
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `-Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`, one test with `class=<class>#<method>`. A comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list works too. AGP hands the runner all its arguments in one comma-joined string and splits it at every comma, so a raw `class=A,B` ran only `A` and still passed. The script writes such a list to a `tokkl-test-filter-*` file beside the credentials file, one entry per line, and passes its path as `testFile`. It refuses a comma in any other runner argument, and a `testFile` of your own beside a list.
Below Android 12, a run with no runner argument on an emulator the script boots goes in batches, because qemu keeps memory after every OpenGL process there. The script has the runner list the tests first, which leaves out what `@SdkSuppress` leaves out. Then it runs whole classes, at most 20 tests a batch, the script's `BATCH_TESTS`, each batch on a freshly booted emulator against the same server, and keeps each batch's results in `app/build/outputs/androidTest-results/batches/<n>/`. The run fails when a batch fails and when a batch ran a different number of tests than the runner listed. On API 26 AGP once passed a batch it could not install, `INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS`, with no test run.
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. A run with a filter, or on a device the script did not boot, runs as one, with no count check. There and outside the script, read the test count, not the BUILD line.
`app/build.gradle.kts` sets `execution = "ANDROIDX_TEST_ORCHESTRATOR"`, so every test runs in a new app process. The `*RestartTest` classes need that to prove state survives a process restart.

ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both. `tokkl-api36` runs Android 16, the version the app targets, and its captures are the screenshot references. `tokkl-api30` runs Android 11 and covers the code paths before Android 12. `tokkl-api26` runs Android 8.0, the oldest version the app supports, and catches a call to an API newer than the device. There is no API 28 AVD: there the `swiftshader` and `host` renderers reached 6 GB within 20 tests, and `lavapipe` crashed after about 20. The SDK repository has no plain AOSP image for API 36.1 or later. README "Run the emulator" has the `avdmanager` commands.
Let `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` boot the emulator, picked with `TOKKL_TEST_AVD`. It runs `emulator -avd <avd> -memory 2560 -cores 4 -gpu lavapipe -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. The emulator raises any smaller `-memory` to 2560 MB for an API 34 or later image, so asking for 2048 saves nothing. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
qemu keeps about 100 MB each time an app process that drew with OpenGL ends, with `lavapipe` and with `swiftshader`. The test orchestrator starts a process for every test, so one full run took qemu to 11 GB. A process that draws with Vulkan leaves about 5 MB. So on Android 12 and later the script runs `setprop debug.hwui.renderer skiavk` after boot, and a full run on tokkl-api36 peaks at about 3.5 GB. Below Android 12 HWUI aborts every app at its first frame with `skiavk`: the API 28 image has no Vulkan, and the API 30 image's Vulkan lacks `VK_KHR_external_semaphore_fd`. Apps there draw with OpenGL, and a full run there goes in batches, each on a fresh emulator. CI's emulator step sets the same property from API 31 on.
When the systemd user manager answers, the emulator runs in a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue`, `MemoryMax=6G` and `MemorySwapMax=0`, and the scope is `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process with no cap. Runs take turns through a `flock` on `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/tokkl-instrumented-tests-<uid>.lock`, and a waiting run prints the PID, start time and directory of the run that holds it. Without the lock a second run would test on the first run's emulator, which the first run's cleanup stops.
Never start an emulator or an adb server by hand for a test run, not even to poll for readiness. The lock covers only runs of the script, an emulator started by hand gets no scope or memory cap, and an OOM kill of it ends the whole agent session. The script stops the adb server at the end only when it was not running before, so a server started by hand stays up and later runs reuse it.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. The script does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard on the headless emulator. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot. CI's emulator step sets `hide_error_dialogs` and `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` itself.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. After a run outside the script, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

source: "sift-drain wave 4 sitting w4-a2, found while building TKA-0015"
# Show the chosen theme's background in the starting window, not the system's
TKA-0015 lets the owner pin the app to light or dark. The app's own window follows that choice from its first frame, but Android draws the starting window from the manifest theme before the app runs. That theme takes its background from `res/values` or `res/values-night`, which match the system's mode. With the app pinned to dark on a light system, a cold start should show a sand starting window and then switch to navy, the flash that `WindowBackgroundTest` guards against when the app follows the system. Nobody has reproduced it on a device yet; the code paths below predict it.
A cold start shows the chosen theme's background from the starting window on, in every theme mode, as `WindowBackgroundTest` checks for the follow-the-system mode.
- app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:20 gives the application `@style/Theme.Tokkl`, which Android uses for the starting window.
- app/src/main/res/values/themes.xml:10 and app/src/main/res/values-night/themes.xml:4 set `android:windowBackground` to `@color/window_background`, picked by the system's night mode.
- `grep -rn setApplicationNightMode app/src/main` finds nothing; only `WindowBackgroundTest` calls it.
Reproduce first and record what the recording shows. On Android 12 and later, `UiModeManager.setApplicationNightMode` tells the system the app's night mode, which the starting window also uses: map light to `MODE_NIGHT_NO`, dark to `MODE_NIGHT_YES` and follow the system to `MODE_NIGHT_AUTO`. Call it when the setting changes and keep the stored setting as the source of truth. Check whether the call recreates the activity and whether the settings screen stays open when it does. `WindowBackgroundTest` sets the application night mode itself, so decide whether the app syncs it at start and adapt that test to drive the setting instead. Below Android 12 there is no such API; record whether that case stays as it is.
- [ ] A recording or test shows whether the starting window flashes the system's colour with a pinned mode, before and after the change.
- [ ] On Android 12 and later, a cold start with a pinned light or dark mode shows that mode's background from the starting window on.
- [ ] Following the system still matches the system, and `WindowBackgroundTest` passes.

The sign-in method radios, the Settings theme radios and the http warning's checkbox each build the same row by hand. ## Evidence

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/signin/SignInScreen.kt:237 builds the sign-in method row, 48dp minimum and `selectable` with `Role.RadioButton`, with a 12dp spacer before the label.

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/signin/SignInScreen.kt:307-317 builds the http warning's checkbox row, `toggleable` with `Role.Checkbox`, also 48dp with a 12dp spacer.

## Direction

Add one option-row composable in `ui/`. It can offer a radio variant and a checkbox variant, or take the control as a slot. Keep `selectableGroup` on the radio groups' parent columns. Use the row at all three sites and keep the existing tests passing unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The sign-in method radios, the Settings theme radios and the http warning checkbox all use the shared row.
- [ ] Each row is 48dp minimum and clickable across its width with a radio or checkbox role.
- [ ] SignInScreenTest, including its http warning tests, and SettingsScreenTest pass through scripts/instrumented-tests.sh.
EOF

# Give filled buttons a 48dp pill and a weight-700 label

Add Tokkl button defaults for filled and ghost buttons, as a `TokklButton` composable or a `ButtonDefaults` wrapper. Following the shared decisions, both are pills at least 48dp tall. Keep that parity by giving both buttons in a dialog the same variant, so the restyle does not make the risky choice the loudest one. Keep every label at 4.5:1 against its fill in both themes.

Tokkl's wordmark is the owner's graffiti artwork, and the web app ships it as an image named "Tokkl" in the brand block that opens every page. The app has no wordmark drawable at all. The home screen sets "Tokkl" as plain Anybody text with no heading semantics, so no screen shows the brand. In dark mode the artwork's navy outline also needs the halo the web draws around it, or the outline is lost against the navy background.

## Evidence

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/MainActivity.kt:96-100 sets the home title as the `app_name` string in `headlineLarge`, Anybody text with no heading semantics.
- absent: app/src/main/res/drawable-xxxhdpi/tokkl_wordmark.png. That folder holds only the launcher icon layers.
- ../tokkl/scripts/icons.ts:17 defines Tokkl's wordmark crop, `WORDMARK_CROP = '1645x709+80+91'`.
- ../tokkl/scripts/icons.ts:57-64 derives the 640 px tokkl-wordmark.png and the web's wordmark-260.png and wordmark-520.png by cropping the 1774x887 ../tokkl/docs/brand/tokkl-wordmark-v3.png with that crop, then resizing.

## Direction

The largest is 260dp at 4x, 1040 px, which is under the crop's 1645 px, so nothing is upscaled. Do not start from the 640 px tokkl-wordmark.png, which is too small for the 260dp size at xxhdpi and xxxhdpi. Record the source, the crop and the steps next to the images, as TKA-0085 did for the icon in app/src/main/res/mipmap-anydpi/ic_launcher.xml:2-36. If the icon needs its own image rather than the launcher layers, record its source and steps the same way. Respect TKA-0111's bundled-assets rule.

Add a Brand composable that draws the icon beside the wordmark in three sizes, the icon at 24, 30 or 48dp with the wordmark at 84, 130 or 260dp wide. Name the wordmark "Tokkl" for TalkBack and keep the icon decorative, as the web's Brand component does. In dark mode draw a 1dp halo around the wordmark in TKA-0109's --wordmark-halo colour, which the web draws as four 1px drop shadows. Use the Brand on the home screen in place of the Anybody "Tokkl" text, and on the sign-in screen above the form. TKA-0124 builds the full sign-in scene around it.

title: Run npm install in every new clone or worktree to turn on the commit hook
