A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a default-ignored message only when it passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. `npm test` (`node --test`, `test/commitlint.test.js`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
Two gaps remain. `git revert` never runs the commit-msg hook (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), so only a CI check could catch a bad revert message, and the repo has no CI workflow yet. And a body line such as `Merge branch y` makes commitlint treat a non-Conventional message as a merge and skip the format rules. The two custom rules still apply to it, so it is rejected when the header has a ticket ID or the message carries a credit line.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

title: 'Test on the plain AOSP API 36 emulator, headless, and stop it afterwards'
  AVD tokkl-api36 uses the AOSP image, since ATD images drop SystemUI and the
  launcher. Boot it with -no-window -accel on and kill it after.
  - testing
  - practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions
The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running.
- Related: [practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions](practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions.md)
CI on GitHub copies Tokkl's setup. One `ci.yml` workflow runs on pull requests and pushes to `main`. Every action is pinned to a commit SHA with its version in a comment, and Dependabot updates them. Jobs cover the Gradle build, lint and unit tests, and instrumented tests on an emulator. GitHub's Ubuntu runners need a udev rule before the emulator can use KVM.

When a token changes, update `Color.kt` and `window_background` together. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, `syncApplicationNightMode` in `settings/ApplicationNightMode.kt` passes the stored theme mode to `UiModeManager.setApplicationNightMode` on every start and every change, off the main thread: light is `MODE_NIGHT_NO`, dark `MODE_NIGHT_YES` and system `MODE_NIGHT_AUTO`. title: Build with --no-daemon in parallel worktrees and never run --stop
  ./gradlew --stop ends every daemon of that Gradle version for the user,
kk_id: practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees
Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.

# Check text and wordmark-halo contrast on the texture and scene colours

## Problem

TKA-0109 added the texture, scene and wordmark-halo colours to the theme. ThemeContrastTest still checks no pair that uses them, so TKA-0121, TKA-0123 and TKA-0124 can put text or the wordmark on those gradients with no test behind the contrast. Tokkl's styles.css records these pairs in its contrast table, and the app's WCAG AA rule applies to them.

## Evidence

- app/src/test/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/ThemeContrastTest.kt:40 builds the pairs from the colour scheme and, through `x`, the running, billable and lime colours. No texture, scene or halo colour is among them.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/Color.kt:179 defines `TokklExtraColors`, which holds the seven colours since TKA-0109.
- styles.css lists the rows "text on texture-glow", "muted on texture-glow" and the same for swell and stripe, "text on scene-glow", swell and stripe, and "wordmark-halo on bg, surface, texture and scene (worst)". It reads them as 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for the halo.
- I computed every one of these pairs from the theme's values on 2026-10-18. The lowest text ratio is 4.69:1 (muted on texture-stripe, dark) and the lowest halo ratio is 4.69:1 (halo on texture-stripe, dark), so the tests pass as written.

## Direction

In ThemeContrastTest, add these pairs to both themes, taking the colours from `TokklExtraColors`:

- onSurface and onSurfaceVariant on `textureGlow`, `textureSwell` and `textureStripe`, as text (4.5:1).
- onSurface on `sceneGlow`, `sceneSwell` and `sceneStripe`, as text.
- In dark only, `wordmarkHalo` on background, surface, and each texture and scene colour, as non-text (3:1). The light halo is transparent and has no pair.

Do not add the "overlap (worst case)" rows. styles.css derives them from channel extremes where gradients overlap, and a drawing ticket owns that check.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] ThemeContrastTest checks the text pairs on the six texture and scene colours in light and dark.
- [ ] It checks the wordmark halo on background, surface and the six colours in dark.
- [ ] The tests pass with the current values.
EOF

# Start every instrumented run on the test emulator at font scale 1.0
The tokkl-api36 emulator keeps the system font scale at 2.0 across boots. Every instrumented class that does not set its own scale runs at 200%, so a screen test meant for the default size checks the largest size instead. Screenshots taken at the default scale also come out at 200%. SystemFontScale puts back whatever value it read before the test, so once one run leaves 2.0 behind, later runs keep restoring it. The script resets other settings on an emulator it boots, but not the font scale.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace.   AVD tokkl-api36 uses the AOSP image, since ATD images drop SystemUI and the
  launcher. Boot it with -no-window -accel on and kill it after.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a message only when `@commitlint/is-ignored` (a declared dependency in `package.json`) matches its first line and the message passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. Because only the header goes to `isIgnored`, a body line such as `Merge branch y` no longer lets a non-Conventional message skip the format rules. `npm test` (`node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
The hook never sees the message that `git revert` or `git cherry-pick` writes (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), a commit made with `--no-verify`, or one from a tree without `npm install`. The `commitlint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` catches those. It lints the pull request's commits, or the pushed range on `main`, and falls back to `commitlint --last` when a force push removed the old tip. Then it runs `npm test`.

  ./gradlew --stop ends every daemon of that Gradle version for the user,
kk_id: practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees
Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.

## Commit messages
Commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). `npm install` sets up a commit-msg hook that runs commitlint, which needs Node 22.12 or later. The hook lives in `.husky/_`, which git ignores, so run `npm install` once in every new clone or git worktree. Until you do, commits there skip the check. The hook rejects a ticket ID such as `TKA-0001` in the subject; put it in a `Refs: TKA-0001` trailer instead. README.md:180:Commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). `npm install` sets up a commit-msg hook that runs commitlint, and CI lints every PR's commits and every push to main. Commits that credit an AI tool or a co-author (`Co-authored-by:`, "Generated with Claude Code" and the like) are rejected. Every push to main runs the checks, the KDE companion's included, and then semantic-release. `feat`, `fix`, `perf`, `refactor` and `revert` commits cut a release (a breaking change cuts a major one): a version bump, a changelog entry, a GitHub release with the KDE companion's DEB and RPM attached (see [desktop/kde/README.md](desktop/kde/README.md#ci-and-releases)), the macOS companion's DMG, which a later job attaches to the same release (see [desktop/macos/README.md](desktop/macos/README.md#releases)), the GNOME companion's DEB, RPM and extension zip, also attached by later jobs (see [desktop/gnome/README.md](desktop/gnome/README.md#releases)), and a container image. `docs`, `build`, `ci`, `test`, `style` and `chore` commits do not.
- One `ci.yml` workflow on pull requests and pushes to `main`, with every action pinned to a commit SHA and its version in a comment, and Dependabot for updates.
- Jobs for the Gradle build, lint and unit tests, and for instrumented tests on an emulator. GitHub's Ubuntu runners need a udev rule before the emulator can use KVM ([android-emulator-runner](https://github.com/ReactiveCircus/android-emulator-runner)).
- The app has its own version, independent of Tokkl's, with its own `v*` tags and changelog, starting at 0.1.0. semantic-release does not support a first release below 1.0.0 ([FAQ](https://semantic-release.gitbook.io/semantic-release/support/faq)), so the first release is a hand-made `v0.1.0` tag and semantic-release counts on from it. A commit marked as a breaking change then moves the app to 1.0.0.

`app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/screenshot/` holds the abstract `ScreenshotTest` and one subclass per theme and font scale: `LightScreenshotTest`, `DarkScreenshotTest`, `LightLargestFontScreenshotTest` and `DarkLargestFontScreenshotTest`. `ReferenceImages` shrinks each capture to a third in each direction, averaging 3x3 blocks, and compares it with its PNG in `app/src/androidTest/assets/screenshots/`. A pixel counts as different when any channel differs by more than 8, and up to 20 such pixels pass. The README section "Screenshot tests" has the run command and the copy step.
Record and compare the references only on the AVD `tokkl-api36` (medium_phone, 420 dpi, the android-36 `default` x86_64 image at revision 2), because density and system fonts change the pixels. Two runs on freshly booted tokkl-api36 emulators matched pixel for pixel. Nobody has compared the CI emulator's captures with the references yet (TKA-0087). A change to how a screen looks updates its references in the same commit, after a look at every diff and capture.
- Related: [practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script](practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script.md)
`MainActivity` calls `WindowCompat.enableEdgeToEdge` and sets the system bar icon colours itself in `showSystemBarIconsFor`. androidx.activity 1.13's `enableEdgeToEdge` reapplies its first call's styles after every configuration change, which gave dark mode the wrong status bar icons. With `SystemBarStyle.auto` it also turns on the system's navigation bar contrast enforcement, which paints a translucent band over a three-button navigation bar; no scrim colour causes that band. `ScrollingScreenInsets` in `ui/theme/ScreenInsets.kt` keeps the status bar and the sides outside a scrolling screen, and the screen puts `navigationBarsPadding` inside its scroll, so text scrolls under the transparent navigation bar and the last line can still scroll clear of it. `MainActivity` declares `android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize"`, so Android does not pan the window when the keyboard opens, and a form makes room with `imePadding`.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot. CI's emulator step sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` itself.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.
The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.

screenshot references pass unchanged.

# Close the SystemUI ANR dialog after the harness boots the emulator
A fresh headless boot of `tokkl-api36` often leaves an "Application Not Responding: com.android.systemui" dialog holding window focus. Any key the instrumented tests inject, such as system back, goes to that dialog instead of the app, so the test fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the app. The wave 3 e2e pass worked around it inside the tests with a `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` broadcast. Every later UI test that injects keys would need the same workaround, and a test that forgets it fails only on a fresh boot.
- The wave 3 e2e specialist saw `dumpsys window` report `mCurrentFocus=Window{… Application Not Responding: com.android.systemui}` after a fresh boot; pressing back by hand with the app focused worked.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/DeviceShell.kt:20 sends `am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` as the test-side workaround.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh boots the AVD in `boot_emulator` and waits only for `sys.boot_completed`.
- In `boot_emulator`, after `sys.boot_completed`, dismiss system dialogs once and keep error dialogs from taking focus on the AVD the script boots, for example `settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` plus a `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` broadcast. Only change settings on an emulator the script booted itself, never on a device that was already attached.
- Then drop the per-test workaround if no test needs it any more, keeping `DeviceShell` if other tests use it.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes it, and tests call `DeviceShell.closeSystemDialogs()` in `app/src/androidTest`, which sends the same broadcast.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

=== practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees.md
title: Build with --no-daemon in parallel worktrees and never run --stop
  ./gradlew --stop ends every daemon of that Gradle version for the user,
kk_id: practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees
Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.

title: Boot the harness emulator in its own systemd scope so an OOM kill cannot end the agent session
labels: [testing, emulator, memory, agents]
source: "sift-drain wave 4, coordinator investigation of three session losses on 2026-10-18"
# Boot the harness emulator in its own systemd scope so an OOM kill cannot end the agent session
`scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` starts the emulator as a child of whatever runs it. When an agent runs the script, qemu lands in that agent session's systemd scope (`t3code-claude-*.scope`), which has `OOMPolicy=stop`. On this 16 GB machine qemu holds 3 to 4 GB, and the kernel's OOM killer picks it first (`oom_score_adj` 800). systemd then stops the whole scope, which kills Claude Code and every background agent of the drain. That happened three times on 2026-10-18 and lost hours of agent time each time.
- `journalctl -k`: OOM kills of `qemu-system-x86` at 02:09:39 (anon-rss 3,991,664 kB), 11:19:20 (2,855,740 kB) and 13:15:47 (2,953,340 kB), each with `task_memcg=.../app-t3code-agents.slice/.../t3code-claude-<id>.scope`.
- `journalctl --user` at 02:09:40: `t3code-claude-6bf4c3bb.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`, after 2 h 4 min of CPU time.
- `systemctl --user show 't3code-claude-*.scope' -p OOMPolicy` prints `OOMPolicy=stop`.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:79 starts `emulator -avd ...` in the background of the script's own process tree.
- When `systemd-run` is available and a user manager is running, start the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope` (or `--unit` with `--collect`) and `-p OOMPolicy=continue`, so an OOM kill takes only qemu and the script fails cleanly instead of the caller's session dying. Fall back to the current launch when `systemd-run --user` is not usable, such as in CI.
- Cap the guest RAM explicitly (`-memory 2048` or the AVD's `hw.ramSize`) and record the measured qemu RSS before and after.
- Keep the cleanup trap working: the script must still stop the emulator it started, including when the scope or unit outlives the shell.
- If the emulator is OOM-killed, the script exits non-zero with a message that says so.
- [ ] An emulator started by the script runs in its own systemd scope or unit, not in the caller's (check `/proc/<qemu pid>/cgroup`).
- [ ] Killing qemu with SIGKILL during a run ends the script with a clear error and leaves the calling shell and agent session alive.
- [ ] CI (no user systemd manager) still boots the emulator through the fallback.

The instrumented tests, including the Compose UI tests, run against a real Tokkl server, never a fake one. One command runs them. It needs Docker, `curl` and `jq`:

`gradle.properties` caps the Gradle heap at 2 GB and compiles Kotlin inside the Gradle daemon, so no separate Kotlin daemon starts. The Gradle daemon itself stays in memory after the build. Stop it when you finish:

The script clones the commit twice, runs `./gradlew --no-daemon assembleRelease` in each clone without the signing variables below, and compares the two unsigned APKs byte for byte. It builds committed work only. The clones sit at paths of different lengths. The second build runs on at most two CPU cores and gets its own Gradle user home, which reads downloaded dependencies from yours but redoes every transform. So an embedded path, output that depends on the core count, and a transform that differs from run to run all show up as differences. When the APKs differ, the script lists the zip entries that differ and keeps both APKs. On this machine the two builds take about four minutes and use up to about 700 MB under `build/`, which the script removes at the end.

F-Droid asks to keep that file and to build the release APK from a clean checkout of the tagged commit. So build the GitHub release APK once the release commit and its tag exist, never from a tree with uncommitted changes, such as one where the release step has just rewritten `gradle/version.properties`.
- The ART baseline profile, `assets/dexopt/baseline.prof` and `baseline.profm`, stays in the APK because it speeds up start-up and came out the same on 8 and on 2 cores. Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.
`compileSdk` is 37 because Compose UI 1.12 declares `minCompileSdk` 37 in its AAR metadata, and a lower value fails AGP's AAR metadata check. `targetSdk` stays at 36, the API level of the emulator `tokkl-api36`, so lint reports `OldTargetApi` and the project accepts that warning. Raise `targetSdk` together with the emulator image, not to silence lint.
`gradle.properties` allows for the other services on this machine. `org.gradle.jvmargs` caps the daemon heap at `-Xmx2g` and metaspace at 768m, and `kotlin.compiler.execution.strategy=in-process` compiles Kotlin inside the Gradle daemon instead of a second long-lived Kotlin daemon.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot. CI's emulator step sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` itself.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. `MainActivity` calls `WindowCompat.enableEdgeToEdge` and sets the system bar icon colours itself in `showSystemBarIconsFor`. androidx.activity 1.13's `enableEdgeToEdge` reapplies its first call's styles after every configuration change, which gave dark mode the wrong status bar icons. With `SystemBarStyle.auto` it also turns on the system's navigation bar contrast enforcement, which paints a translucent band over a three-button navigation bar; no scrim colour causes that band. `ScrollingScreenInsets` in `ui/theme/ScreenInsets.kt` keeps the status bar and the sides outside a scrolling screen, and the screen puts `navigationBarsPadding` inside its scroll, so text scrolls under the transparent navigation bar and the last line can still scroll clear of it. `MainActivity` declares `android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize"`, so Android does not pan the window when the keyboard opens, and a form makes room with `imePadding`.
`cache/` keeps what the app last loaded from the server in the Room database `account_cache.db` (`CacheDatabase`): projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and the time entries of `HistoryWindow`, which is today and the 13 days before it, counted in the account's timezone. Screens read the flows of `AccountCache`, which come from the phone and never wait for the network. The account settings are not cached here; `AccountSettingsSource` stays their one source.
One refresh feeds all of this. `AccountSettingsSource.refresh`, called from `MainActivity.onStart`, after sign-in and after an accepted trust prompt, sends `GET /api/v9/me?with_related_data=true` and `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` once. Its `onRefresh`, wired in `TokklApplication`, refreshes the capabilities with the trash probe and then the cache, which adds `GET /api/v9/me/time_entries` for the history window. A feature that needs `/me` data takes it from this refresh instead of sending its own request. `MePreferences` keeps the raw JSON object, and each reader decodes only its own key, `duration_format` for the settings and `favorites` for the cache, so a malformed key fails that reader alone.

A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a message only when `@commitlint/is-ignored` (a declared dependency in `package.json`) matches its first line and the message passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. Because only the header goes to `isIgnored`, a body line such as `Merge branch y` no longer lets a non-Conventional message skip the format rules. `npm test` (`node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
The hook never sees the message that `git revert` or `git cherry-pick` writes (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), a commit made with `--no-verify`, or one from a tree without `npm install`. The `commitlint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` catches those. It lints the pull request's commits, or the pushed range on `main`, and falls back to `commitlint --last` when a force push removed the old tip. Then it runs `npm test`.

A new tag can be typed offline: the queue sends tags by name, and Tokkl creates the missing ones (`resolveTagNames` in `../tokkl/packages/api/src/models/tags.ts`). Creating a project, client or task needs the server; offline, the picker offers what is cached and says so. |
176:| O1 | Start, stop, create, edit and delete entries with no route to the server. Each change waits in a queue on the phone, marked as not sent, and goes out in order when the server is reachable. A timer started offline keeps its real start time. |
177:| O2 | Cache what the app last loaded: projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and about two weeks of history. All of it can be read offline, and entries can be edited. |
178:| O3 | When the phone and another client both changed an entry, the change that reaches the server last wins. A queued start is the exception, because Tokkl stops the running entry when a new one starts (Tokkl T2). Before sending a queued start, the app fetches the running entry. If that entry started after the queued start, the app sends the queued entry as stopped at that entry's start, and the later timer keeps running. The timer started last is the one the user meant. |

# Reload the projects, clients and tags pages when the app comes back to the foreground

## Problem

The projects, clients and tags pages load their list from the server when the page opens, on Try again, and when the network comes back. They do not load again when the app returns to the foreground. A project edited in the web app while the phone sat in the background stays stale on the open page. The project form then saves every field it shows, so a save from that stale form overwrites the web app's change. The clients page's project counts go stale the same way.

## Expected behaviour

Coming back to the foreground with one of these pages open loads its list again, as the Reports screen does, and a form opened afterwards starts from the server's current values. Turning the phone sends no extra request.

## Evidence

- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/catalog/CatalogModel.kt:94 (open), :101 (retry) and :106 (reconnected) are the only loads.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/projects/ProjectsScreen.kt:61 and :65, clients/ClientsScreen.kt:60 and :64, tags/TagsScreen.kt:70 and :74 call only open and reconnected.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/reports/ReportsScreen.kt:68-69 reloads on ON_START after an ON_STOP that is not a configuration change.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/projects/ProjectsServer.kt:67-68 sends the whole form with PUT.
- .ai/kenkeep/nodes/practice-refresh-on-events-no-polling.md: refresh when the app opens, after a change and when the network returns.

## Direction

Give CatalogModel the reports model's pair: wentToBackground on a stop that is not a configuration change, and cameToForeground on the next start, which loads again. Wire it once for the three pages, for example in CatalogPage or a shared effect. Keep an open form's typed values; reload the list behind it. No timer.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With a page open, sending the app to the background and back loads its list again, and a rotation sends no request.
- [ ] A change made on the server while the app was in the background shows on the page after it returns.
- [ ] A unit test covers the background and foreground pair on CatalogModel.
EOF

title: Port Tokkl's TypeScript with JavaScript semantics and verbatim test cases
  rules, return null for NaN, and reuse the .test.ts cases verbatim.
  - testing
The time parsers in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time` (`Duration.kt` for `parseDuration`, `TimeOfDay.kt` for `parseTimeOfDay`) behave like the TypeScript they port, including where Kotlin differs from JavaScript. `JsSemantics.kt` has the helpers. JavaScript's `\s` and `String.prototype.trim` use the ECMAScript WhiteSpace and LineTerminator characters, while Java's `\s` matches only ASCII and Kotlin's `trim()` uses yet another set. `Math.round` rounds halves up and `kotlin.math.round` rounds them to even. JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.
A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.
`DurationTest` and `TimeOfDayTest` hold the cases of the matching `.test.ts` file verbatim, and their header names the tokkl commit they were copied at. To follow an upstream change, copy the cases again and update that commit. `DurationJsSemanticsTest` pins the JavaScript traps in its own file, since they are not in `duration.test.ts` and a later diff against tokkl leaves them alone. Its expected values come from running the TypeScript file in Node 24, where `node file.mts` strips the types.
title: Build with --no-daemon in parallel worktrees and never run --stop
  ./gradlew --stop ends every daemon of that Gradle version for the user,
kk_id: practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees
Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.

## Commit messages
Commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). `npm install` sets up a commit-msg hook that runs commitlint, which needs Node 22.12 or later. The hook lives in `.husky/_`, which git ignores, so run `npm install` once in every new clone or git worktree. Until you do, commits there skip the check. The hook rejects a ticket ID such as `TKA-0001` in the subject; put it in a `Refs: TKA-0001` trailer instead. It also rejects commits that credit an AI tool or a co-author (`Co-authored-by:`, "Generated with Claude Code" and the like). `npm test` checks these rules, and runs the hook against real commits and merges in a throwaway repository. The local hook never sees a commit made with `git revert` or `--no-verify`, so the commitlint job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` also lints the commits of every pull request and push to `main`, and runs `npm test`.

title: 'Account settings: AccountSettingsSource, AccountTime and NoDeviceZoneTest'
  Sign-in and each refresh store timezone, week start, resolution and duration
`session/AccountSettings` holds the `GET /api/v9/me` fields that decide how the app shows and reads times: `timezone`, `beginning_of_week` and Tokkl's optional `time_resolution_minutes`. It holds no credential. Sign-in stores them from its own `/me`. A `/me` without `timezone` or `beginning_of_week`, or with a week start outside 0 to 6, fails sign-in as `SignInResult.NotTokkl`. Toggl Track and older Tokkl servers leave out `time_resolution_minutes` and do not snap, so it stays null for them. `durationFormat` comes from `duration_format` in `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` and, as in the web app, reads as improved when the key is missing, null or names another format. Screens write durations with `AccountSettings.formatDuration(Long)`.
`session/AccountSettingsSource` is the one place screens read the settings from. `TokklApplication.accountSettings` builds it over `AccountSettingsStore`, which keeps them in the private preferences file `account_settings`, so screens have them offline and after a restart. `MainActivity.onStart` and each sign-in call `refresh()`, so a change made in the web app reaches the phone. A refresh sends `GET /api/v9/me?with_related_data=true` and `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` once and hands both answers to its `onRefresh`, where the capabilities and the cache refresh from them. A second `refresh()` while one runs gets the running job instead of sending another request. A failed request or write keeps what is stored, failed preferences keep the stored duration format, and a refresh drops its answer when sign-in stored newer settings while the request ran.
`AccountSettings.time()` gives a `time/AccountTime`: the account's zone, a clock in that zone, `now()`, `today()`, `local(instant)`, `startOfWeek(date)` and `snapUnsent(start, stop)`. It returns null when `parseTimeZone` cannot resolve the name, as when the server's Intl knows a zone that the phone's tz database lacks. There is no fallback to the device's zone or to UTC. A screen without an `AccountTime` must show no clock times or dates, take no time input and name the zone it does not know. Durations, the running clock, Start and Stop need no zone and keep working.
`NoDeviceZoneTest`, a JVM test, reads the constant pool of every compiled app class through `ClassReferences` and fails on `ZoneId.systemDefault`, `TimeZone.getDefault` (java.util and ICU), `Clock.systemDefaultZone`, a `now()` without arguments on the java.time date and time types, and a `Calendar` or `GregorianCalendar` built without a zone. Its `ALLOWED` set is empty, and a class added there needs a comment saying why the account's zone will not do. Take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime` instead.
  Room cache and the capability flags that screens read offline.
  - room
`cache/` keeps what the app last loaded from the server in the Room database `account_cache.db` (`CacheDatabase`): projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and the time entries of `HistoryWindow`, which is today and the 13 days before it, counted in the account's timezone. Screens read the flows of `AccountCache`, which come from the phone and never wait for the network. The account settings are not cached here; `AccountSettingsSource` stays their one source.
One refresh feeds all of this. `AccountSettingsSource.refresh`, called from `MainActivity.onStart`, after sign-in and after an accepted trust prompt, sends `GET /api/v9/me?with_related_data=true` and `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` once. Its `onRefresh`, wired in `TokklApplication`, refreshes the capabilities with the trash probe and then the cache, which adds `GET /api/v9/me/time_entries` for the history window. A feature that needs `/me` data takes it from this refresh instead of sending its own request. `MePreferences` keeps the raw JSON object, and each reader decodes only its own key, `duration_format` for the settings and `favorites` for the cache, so a malformed key fails that reader alone.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot. CI's emulator step sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` itself.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.

# Cut the test emulator's host memory with a pinned GPU mode, core count and an effective RAM cap
The script launches the emulator with `-memory 2048` and sets neither `-gpu` nor `-cores` (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:151-152), and its header says qemu holds up to 5 GB (:32). The last local boot was launched with `-memory 2048`, yet the AVD ran with hw.ramSize 2560, 4 cores and the lavapipe software GPU. CI already passes `-gpu swiftshader_indirect`. qemu reached about 4 GB of anon RSS and the kernel OOM-killed it three times (TKA-0099). On this 16 GB always-on homelab, every OOM kill puts the agent session and other services at risk.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:151-152 starts `emulator -avd "$AVD" -port "$port" -memory 2048 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`, with no `-gpu` or `-cores`.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:32 says qemu holds up to 5 GB.
- ~/.android/avd/tokkl-api36.avd/emu-launch-params.txt shows the last boot was launched with `-memory 2048`.
- ~/.android/avd/tokkl-api36.avd/hardware-qemu.ini:2-3 shows `hw.cpu.ncore = 4` and `hw.ramSize = 2560`.
- ~/.android/avd/tokkl-api36.avd/hardware-qemu.ini:75-76 shows `hw.gpu.enabled = true` and `hw.gpu.mode = lavapipe`.
- .ai/sift/archive/foundation/hardening/TKA-0099--emulator-own-scope-oom.md:26 records three OOM kills of qemu, the largest at 3,991,664 kB anon RSS.

- Pin a GPU mode in the launch at scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:151-152 that keeps the tests passing with less host memory. Compare `swiftshader_indirect`, which CI uses (.github/workflows/ci.yml:105), with lavapipe, which the last local boot picked (hardware-qemu.ini:75-76).
- Pin a core count with `-cores`. The last boot used 4 (hardware-qemu.ini:2).
- Make the guest RAM cap apply. `-memory 2048` did not stop the AVD running with hw.ramSize 2560 (emu-launch-params.txt, hardware-qemu.ini:3). Set hw.ramSize in the AVD's config.ini from the script, or document the setting next to the AVD setup if the script should not edit the AVD.

The script runs the tests on every device adb lists and boots its own emulator only when none is attached (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:26-30, :134-136, :175-177, :275-279). A second run that starts while the first is active finds the first run's emulator, skips booting its own and runs its tests there. When the first run ends, its cleanup kills that emulator (:113). If adb was not running when the first run started (:71), the cleanup also stops the shared adb server (:120-121). Two agents or sittings running tests at once break each other, so only one sitting at a time can use the emulator, and that serialises most of each wave.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:26-30 says the tests run on the devices adb lists, the script boots an AVD only with no device attached, and it stops the adb server if that was not running before.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:71 records whether adb was running at start.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:113 kills the emulator the run started, in cleanup.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:120-121 kills the adb server in cleanup when it was not running at start.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:134-136 lists every attached device.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:175-177 boots an emulator only when `ANDROID_SERIAL` is unset and no device is attached.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:275-279 picks `ANDROID_SERIAL` or every attached device as the test devices.
- Isolate. Each run boots its own read-only instance of the AVD on its own port, sets `ANDROID_SERIAL` for itself instead of using every device adb lists (:134-136, :275-279), and never kills an adb server or emulator it did not start (:71, :113, :120-121).
- Keep the emulator's own systemd scope from TKA-0099 and the check from TKA-0101 that every test device is still online after Gradle.
- [ ] Starting a second run while one is active either waits or fails clearly, or runs safely on its own emulator.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. title: An OOM kill inside an agent session's scope ends the whole session
  Agent sessions run in t3code-claude-*.scope with OOMPolicy=stop, so one
  OOM-killed process stops the session and its background agents.
kk_id: map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.

=== practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees
Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.

# Propose to Tokkl the commitlint fix for default ignores skipping the ticket-ID and credit rules

## Problem

Tokkl's `commitlint.config.js` is where this repo's rules came from, and it has the gap TKA-0078 fixed here. commitlint skips every rule for `Revert "..."`, `fixup!`, `squash!` and merge messages, so a revert or fixup can carry a `TT-` ID in the subject or a `Co-authored-by` or AI credit trailer and still pass. Tokkl's CI lints the pushed commit range with the same config, so it does not catch them either. This repo cannot edit `../tokkl`, so the human has to submit the change there.

## Evidence

- ../tokkl/commitlint.config.js:35-36 exports a config with `extends` and no `defaultIgnores` or `ignores` key. A grep for `defaultIgnores\|ignores` in that file finds nothing.
- ../tokkl/commitlint.config.js:33 defines the ID pattern as `/\bTT-\d+\b/`; this repo's copy also matches `TKA-`.
- ../tokkl/.github/workflows/ci.yml:34 runs `npx --no -- commitlint --from "$FROM" --to "$TO"`, which applies the same default ignores.
- Both packages are `^21.2.3` in ../tokkl/package.json:30-31, the version TKA-0078 was fixed and tested against. Nothing was run inside ../tokkl, so the gap there is read from the config, not reproduced.
- The fix here is in commitlint.config.js:1 (import), :38-59 (helpers and the ignore function) and :63-64 (`defaultIgnores: false`, `ignores`). Before it, `Revert "feat: implement TKA-0001"` plus a `Co-Authored-By` line exited 0 from `npx --no -- commitlint`; after it, that exits 1.

## Direction

- Apply the same change to ../tokkl/commitlint.config.js, keeping the `TT-` pattern: extract `findForbiddenContent` and `findTicketId` helpers, set `defaultIgnores: false`, and add one `ignores` function that returns `isIgnored(message) && passesCustomChecks(message)`. - Do not change the rules' patterns.
- The human submits this. Do not edit ../tokkl from this repo.

[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On
`ReportsServer` takes the account's default workspace from `GET /api/v9/me` and its rounding from `GET /api/v9/workspaces/{id}`. It pages `POST /reports/api/v3/workspace/{id}/search/time_entries`, following `X-Next-Row-Number`, and the phone sums the entries. The summary endpoints will not do: Tokkl's v3 totals send `rates: []`, and its v3 summary groups carry seconds only, with no billable time or amount. Each search asks for the workspace's `rounding` and `rounding_minutes`, because the Reports API rounds only when asked while the web app always rounds. `ReportsScreenTest` checks the summary against `POST /api/app/report`, the web app's own call.
Report data stays in memory. Offline, or on a 502, 503 or 504 from a proxy that cannot reach Tokkl, the screen says reports need the server and shows no numbers. When the app comes back to the foreground, after an `ON_STOP` that was not a configuration change, the model asks for the range again and shows no numbers until the answer comes. Adding the lifecycle observer replays `ON_START` at once, and the model ignores that one. A configuration change keeps the report and sends nothing.

result_evidence: docs/PRD.md:239:- Every API write that stores a stopped entry (create, update, stop, bulk `PATCH`, stopping the running entry when a new one starts, and undoing the delete of a running entry while another one runs) snaps it to the instance time resolution on the clock of the owner's timezone. The start moves to the nearest grid point. For a typed or edited span (create, update and bulk `PATCH`), the duration rounds up to a multiple of the resolution, so the padding is always less than one step, and the stop follows the start by the rounded duration. A running entry keeps its exact start until it stops. A stopping timer ends on the grid point nearest the moment it stops, or on its start if that point is earlier. A new timer's start snaps to that same point, so when a new timer stops the old one, the two are stored back to back. The stop endpoint stores at least one step; a new timer that starts within half a step of the old one's snapped start leaves the old entry with zero length. A stopped timer still lasts a multiple of the resolution, but it is not always at least as long as the real time: either end can move by up to half a step. A stop and a start sent as two requests seconds apart can leave a gap of one step when they fall on either side of a half-step mark, but never an overlap. The response returns the stored values, so `stop - start` equals `duration`. A timer that has run for more than 999 hours, the longest entry the API accepts, stops at 999 hours. CSV import and JSON restore keep the times in the file, and existing entries change only when they are next edited.

fix(calendar): show entries that start before a week and run into it

The calendar asked the server only for entries that start from the day
before a week, and drew the two cached weeks from the cache alone. The
server finds entries by their start, so an entry that started two days
before an older week, or the evening before the cache's first day, was
missing from the week it runs into.

Tokkl stores stopped entries of up to 999 hours. A week outside the
cache now asks for the entries that start from 999 hours before it and
keeps those that run into it. A cached week also asks the server for the
entries that start in those 999 hours before the cache and run into it,
one request shared by both cached weeks, and adds them to what the
phone keeps. The cache keeps holding only entries that start in its two
weeks, so the history's days and the refresh's request stay as they
were. Offline, a cached week draws from the cache and shows no error.

Refs: TKA-0179
EOF

# Propose to Tokkl that parseDuration reject a unit named constructor instead of returning NaN
Tokkl's `parseDuration` looks units up in a plain object literal, so `UNIT_SECONDS['constructor']` finds `Object.prototype.constructor` and the `undefined` check lets it through. `parseDuration('1 constructor')` then returns NaN, which is neither seconds nor the null that callers check for. The web app treats NaN as a valid duration, and the Kotlin port from TKA-0012 returns null for that input, so the two disagree (PRD risk 5). This repo cannot edit `../tokkl`, so the human has to submit the change there.
- ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts:3 declares `UNIT_SECONDS` as a `Record<string, number>` object literal, which inherits from `Object.prototype`.
- ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts:35-36 reads `UNIT_SECONDS[match[2]!]` and rejects only `undefined`. `constructor` is the only `Object.prototype` key made of lowercase letters alone, which is what the unit pattern captures.
- Node 24.21.0 importing ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts at tokkl commit ec84de60087b32e8279c74197bdc94e52164579b returns NaN for `'1 constructor'`. In a corpus of 159,150 generated duration inputs, 1,865 gave NaN.
- This repo's port, app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/time/Duration.kt, returns null for this input and documents the difference in its KDoc.
- In ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts, make the unit lookup see only its own keys, with `Object.hasOwn(UNIT_SECONDS, unit)`, a `Map`, or an object built with `Object.create(null)`.
- Add `['1 constructor', null]` to the cases in ../tokkl/packages/common/duration.test.ts so the Kotlin replay in TKA-0012's DurationTest picks it up on the next sync.
- [ ] In Tokkl, `parseDuration('1 constructor')` and `parseDuration('1h 2constructor')` return null.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. The ports in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time` (`Duration.kt` for `parseDuration`, `TimeOfDay.kt` for `parseTimeOfDay`, `Snap.kt` for `snapSpan`, and `TimeZone.kt`, which accepts the timezone names Intl accepts) behave like the TypeScript they port, including where Kotlin differs from JavaScript. `JsSemantics.kt` has the helpers. JavaScript's `\s` and `String.prototype.trim` use the ECMAScript WhiteSpace and LineTerminator characters, while Java's `\s` matches only ASCII and Kotlin's `trim()` uses yet another set. `Math.round` rounds halves up and `kotlin.math.round` rounds them to even. JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.
A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.
`DurationTest` and `TimeOfDayTest` hold the cases of the matching `.test.ts` file verbatim, and their header names the tokkl commit they were copied at. To follow an upstream change, copy the cases again and update that commit. `DurationJsSemanticsTest` pins the JavaScript traps in its own file, since they are not in `duration.test.ts` and a later diff against tokkl leaves them alone. Its expected values come from running the TypeScript file in Node 24, where `node file.mts` strips the types.
Where the TypeScript throws a RangeError, `snapSpan` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. The user unit `t3-update.timer` has `OnCalendar=daily`, `RandomizedDelaySec=1h` and `Persistent=true`. It starts `t3-update.service`, a oneshot that runs `t3 update` and then `systemctl --user restart t3.service` through `ExecStartPost`. The restart happens even when T3 is already current. T3 stops all running agent sessions when the service stops, and the stop logs `stoppedSessions: <count>`.
An agent run or background agent still going between about 00:00 and 01:00 local time is cut off this way. A missed timer fires at the next boot. A run that stops in that window was interrupted, not failed, so start it again.
== map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session.md
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.
