`cache/` keeps what the app last loaded from the server in the Room database `account_cache.db` (`CacheDatabase`): projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and the time entries of `HistoryWindow`, which is today and the 13 days before it, counted in the account's timezone. Screens read the flows of `AccountCache`, which come from the phone and never wait for the network. The account settings are not cached here; `AccountSettingsSource` stays their one source.

`AccountCache.refresh` replaces the rows with one `ServerSnapshot`. A list that is null, because its request failed or the server does not offer it, keeps its rows, and an `SQLiteException` during the write keeps the whole cache as it was. When the phone cannot resolve the account's timezone, the refresh reads no entries and prunes none. A server without favorites, such as Toggl Track, gets an empty favorites list.

`capabilities/Capabilities` holds the Tokkl-only flags `trash`, `restore`, `favorites` and `timeResolution`. `favorites` follows Tokkl's `role` in `/me`, and `timeResolution` its `time_resolution_minutes`. `probeTrash` sends `GET /api/app/trash`: a list is `PRESENT`, a 404 or a 2xx that is not a list is `ABSENT`, and anything else is `UNKNOWN`, which keeps the trash and restore flags as they were. Restore lives in the same router as the trash, so the trash probe decides it too. `CapabilitiesStore` keeps the flags in the private preferences file `capabilities`, and features read them from `CapabilitiesSource`.

One refresh feeds all of this. `AccountSettingsSource.refresh`, called from `MainActivity.onStart`, after sign-in and after an accepted trust prompt, sends `GET /api/v9/me?with_related_data=true` and `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` once. Its `onRefresh`, wired in `TokklApplication`, refreshes the capabilities with the trash probe and then the cache, which adds `GET /api/v9/me/time_entries` for the history window. A feature that needs `/me` data takes it from this refresh instead of sending its own request. `MePreferences` keeps the raw JSON object, and each reader decodes only its own key, `duration_format` for the settings and `favorites` for the cache, so a malformed key fails that reader alone.

Nothing calls `AccountCache.clear()` or `CapabilitiesStore.clear()` yet. Sign-out has to.
EOF

The summary endpoints will not do: Tokkl's v3 totals send `rates: []`, and its v3 summary groups carry seconds only, with no billable time or amount. Adding the lifecycle observer replays `ON_START` at once, and the model ignores that one. A configuration change keeps the report and sends nothing.

Every page of the detailed search is one request. Against Toggl Track's hourly quotas that will cost more than one summary call.
EOF

`ui/theme/Spacing.kt` is Tokkl's spacing scale, `--space-1` to `--space-8` (4 to 48dp), read as `TokklTheme.spacing`. Every gap, padding and margin on a screen is one of its values or named rhythms such as `betweenGroups`, `inGroup` and `underTopBar`. `Modifier.screenContent()` lays out a screen's single column: a 16dp margin on each side when the width the screen gets is under 600dp, 24dp from there, and at most 600dp of content, centred. It reads the available width, not the window's, so it needs a bounded width.

`ui/theme/Shape.kt` passes Tokkl's corners to `MaterialTheme`: `--radius-md`, 10dp, for fields and menus, and `--radius-lg`, 16dp, for cards, sheets and dialogs. Shapes set corners only, and a card or dialog draws Tokkl's 2dp frame (`FrameWidth`) itself. `ui/theme/Type.kt` sizes Material's roles from Tokkl's web scale. Display, headline and title roles are Anybody at width 85, and body and label roles keep the system font. Anybody has its own `Font` entries for weights 800 and 900, because the variable font's default instance is Thin and a role asking for 900 would get 800. The named styles include `ClockTextStyle` (36sp), `PageTitleTextStyle` and `TotalTextStyle` (28sp) and `DayTotalTextStyle` (22sp); the number styles use tabular figures.

`ui/OptionRow.kt` has `RadioOptionRow` and `CheckboxOptionRow`, which sign-in, Settings, the reports range and the http warning use. The whole row is the touch target, at least 48dp high, `selectable` or `toggleable` with the radio button or checkbox role, and 12dp sits between control and label. The control inside gets a null handler, so TalkBack reads one node. Put the radio rows of one choice in a parent with `selectableGroup`.

`ui/Brand.kt` draws Tokkl's icon beside the owner's wordmark in `BrandSize.SMALL`, `MEDIUM` and `LARGE`, each with its own PNGs, so none is drawn scaled down from a larger one. The brand is one semantics node, read once as "Tokkl". In dark mode a 1dp halo in `--wordmark-halo` traces the wordmark. The images are cut from `../tokkl/docs/brand/tokkl-wordmark-v3.png` with Tokkl's `WORDMARK_CROP`, 1645x709+80+91, and `res/raw/brand_images_source.txt` records the ImageMagick steps. Lint warns about these PNGs with IconDuplicates and IconDensities, and the gate passes with those warnings.

`MainActivity` calls `WindowCompat.enableEdgeToEdge` and sets the system bar icon colours itself in `showSystemBarIconsFor`. androidx.activity 1.13's `enableEdgeToEdge` reapplies its first call's styles after every configuration change, which left dark mode with the light theme's status bar icons. With `SystemBarStyle.auto` it also turns on the system's navigation bar contrast enforcement, which paints a translucent band over a three-button navigation bar; no scrim colour causes that band. `ScrollingScreenInsets` in `ui/theme/ScreenInsets.kt` keeps the status bar and the sides outside a scrolling screen, and the screen puts `navigationBarsPadding` inside its scroll, so text scrolls under the transparent navigation bar and the last line can still scroll clear of it. `MainActivity` declares `android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize"`, so Android does not pan the window when the keyboard opens, and a form makes room with `imePadding`.

`licences/LicenceReflow.kt` joins the OFL's hard-wrapped lines at display time and leaves out its dash rules, which the screen draws as dividers. `res/raw/anybody_ofl.txt` stays byte-identical to Tokkl's `OFL.txt`, so never rewrap the file itself.

=== practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script.md
Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.

Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.

=== map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session.md
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.
A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a message only when `@commitlint/is-ignored` (a declared dependency in `package.json`) matches its first line and the message passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. Because only the header goes to `isIgnored`, a body line such as `Merge branch y` no longer lets a non-Conventional message skip the format rules. `npm test` (`node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
The hook never sees the message that `git revert` or `git cherry-pick` writes (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), a commit made with `--no-verify`, or one from a tree without `npm install`. The `commitlint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` catches those. It lints the pull request's commits, or the pushed range on `main`, and falls back to `commitlint --last` when a force push removed the old tip. Then it runs `npm test`.

`gradle.properties` allows for the other services on this machine. `org.gradle.jvmargs` caps the daemon heap at `-Xmx2g` and metaspace at 768m, and `kotlin.compiler.execution.strategy=in-process` compiles Kotlin inside the Gradle daemon instead of a second long-lived Kotlin daemon.

JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.
A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.

Where the TypeScript throws a RangeError, `snapSpan` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. # Propose to Tokkl per-currency rates in its Reports API v3 totals and summary

## Problem

The app's summary report pages through every entry of the range with the v3 detailed search and adds them up on the phone (TKA-0026). Tokkl's v3 totals and summary answers would be cheaper, but they lack three things the web app's summary shows: billable time per bucket, the amount in each currency and the amount per group. A year of entries means several detailed pages of about a thousand rows each, where totals and summary would need about three requests. Against Toggl later, the page count also counts against its hourly quotas. This repo cannot edit `../tokkl`, so the human has to propose the change there.

## Evidence

- ../tokkl/packages/api/src/services/reportJobs.ts:205 answers totals with `rates: []`, and :206 gives each graph point `billable_amount_in_cents: 0` and an empty `by_rate`.
- ../tokkl/packages/api/src/services/reportJobs.ts:107-120 (`summaryGroup`) sends a group's id, colour, sub-groups and seconds, with no billable seconds and no amount.
- ../tokkl/docs/PRD.md line 261 lists rate splitting through `distinguish_rates` as not implemented.

The time parsers in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time` (`Duration.kt` for `parseDuration`, `TimeOfDay.kt` for `parseTimeOfDay`) behave like the TypeScript they port, including where Kotlin differs from JavaScript. `JsSemantics.kt` has the helpers. JavaScript's `\s` and `String.prototype.trim` use the ECMAScript WhiteSpace and LineTerminator characters, while Java's `\s` matches only ASCII and Kotlin's `trim()` uses yet another set. `Math.round` rounds halves up and `kotlin.math.round` rounds them to even. JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.
A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.

Its expected values come from running the TypeScript file in Node 24, where `node file.mts` strips the types.
Manual entry accepts times like `9`, `930`, `9:30` and `4pm`, entries across midnight, and durations like `1h 30m`, `90` and `1,5h` (M1). The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.

When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

=== map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session.md
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.

# Give pre-Android 12 emulator runs memory headroom and a run at API 26
Below Android 12 apps on the emulator draw with OpenGL, because HWUI aborts with `skiavk` there, and qemu keeps memory after each test's process. A full run on tokkl-api30 peaked at 5.5 GiB, against the 6 GB cap of the emulator's scope, so a few more tests will get it OOM-killed. On API 26, the app's minSdk, qemu grows faster still, so no full run fits there. That run matters: below API 30, `LargestFontScaleTest` crashed on `android.view.WindowInsets$Type`, an API 30 class, which tokkl-api30 cannot show.
- Full runs on tokkl-api30 on 2026-10-19 peaked at 5.49 and 5.50 GiB VmHWM with 2560 MB of guest RAM, and at 5.38 GiB with 2048 MB. qemu grew by 2.2 GiB over the last 63 tests of the 2048 MB run. The cap is `EMULATOR_MEMORY_MAX=6G` in scripts/instrumented-tests.sh.
- With 20 to 22 UI tests, qemu grew by about 110 MB per test on API 26 and API 28 with `-gpu lavapipe`. On API 28 `swiftshader` and `host` hit the 6 GB cap within about 20 tests, and the `lavapipe` emulator segfaulted ("DisplaySurfaceGlContextHelper context was preempted").
- The `WindowInsets$Type` crash came from `awaitKeyboardTop` in app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/LargestFontScaleTest.kt (line 459 at f0e9ade) on tokkl-api26 and tokkl-api28. TKA-0131 moved it to `WindowInsetsCompat`, and the class then passed on tokkl-api26.
Measure again with each new emulator release. If the growth stays, let scripts/instrumented-tests.sh split a run on a pre-Android 12 AVD into batches of classes, with a fresh emulator for each batch, and keep the classes whose tests depend on each other, such as the `*RestartTest` steps, in one batch. === practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script.md
Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot. CI's emulator step sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` itself.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

=== map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session.md
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.

# Take the network away in tests on Android 8 and 9 without cmd connectivity

## Problem

Five instrumented tests cut the network with `cmd connectivity airplane-mode enable`. Android adds that shell command in Android 10, so on Android 8.0 and 9 it does nothing, and each test waits 30 seconds for the network to go and fails. A full run on tokkl-api26, the app's minSdk, cannot pass while they do.

## Evidence

- Two batched full runs on tokkl-api26 on 2026-10-19 (TKA-0168 sitting) failed these five every time: `AccountCacheServerTest#afterOneRefreshEveryCachedKindReadsInAirplaneMode` and both airplane mode tests of `EntityPickerServerTest` with "the network did not go", `ReportsForegroundTest#offlineAfterTheBackgroundShowsTheMessageAndNoNumbers` with "timed out: the server is out of reach", and `ReportsScreenTest#offlineTheScreenSaysSoAndShowsNoNumbers` with "the server still answers". All five pass on tokkl-api30 and tokkl-api36.
- AOSP `services/core/java/com/android/server/ConnectivityService.java` has no `airplane-mode` shell command at tag android-8.0.0_r1 and has it at android-10.0.0_r1.
- Call sites: app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/cache/AccountCacheServerTest.kt:128, picker/EntityPickerServerTest.kt:235, reports/ReportsForegroundTest.kt:90 and 117, reports/ReportsScreenTest.kt:113 and 169.

## Direction

Give the five tests one helper that takes the server out of the app's reach on every API level the app supports. One way is to point the app at a relay the test can close, as `LoopbackRelay` and `HangingRelay` already do for other tests. If a test needs the system's own offline state, keep `cmd connectivity airplane-mode` from Android 10 and find a shell-user way below it, checking that the network really went. Do not skip the tests below Android 10.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The five tests pass on tokkl-api26 through scripts/instrumented-tests.sh.
- [ ] They still pass on tokkl-api30 and tokkl-api36.
EOF

# Find why ReportsForegroundTest gets a new MainActivity back on Android 8.0

## Problem

`ReportsForegroundTest#theForegroundAsksOnceAndARotationAsksNothing` sends the app home and brings its task back, and expects the same `MainActivity` to return. On tokkl-api26 a new instance came back in both full runs, so the test fails before it checks the reports. Either the test's way of returning differs from a user's on Android 8.0, or the app loses its activity there when it goes to the background, which a user would notice.

## Evidence

- Two batched full runs on tokkl-api26 on 2026-10-19 (TKA-0168 sitting) failed it with "the same activity came back, not a new one expected same:<com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.MainActivity@...> was not:<...>". It passes on tokkl-api30 and tokkl-api36.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/reports/ReportsForegroundTest.kt:197-201: `bringBack` runs `am start -W -n <component> -f 0x10020000` (NEW_TASK and REORDER_TO_FRONT, line 275) and asserts the same activity at line 201. `sendToBackground` (line 189) presses HOME.

## Direction

On tokkl-api26, find out whether the old activity was destroyed (for example by a configuration change while the launcher showed) or whether the `am start` flags start a new one on top. Check what a user gets when returning from the launcher icon and from Recents. If the user keeps the activity, return the way the user does in the test. If the user gets a new activity, file the app bug with what the screen loses.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The cause is recorded in the resolution.
- [ ] The test passes on tokkl-api26, tokkl-api30 and tokkl-api36, or an app bug is filed for what Android 8.0 users get.
EOF

# Fail an instrumented run that Gradle passes without running its tests

## Problem

On an API 26 device that already has the app installed, AGP 9.4.1's test task cannot install the app, runs no test and still reports BUILD SUCCESSFUL. scripts/instrumented-tests.sh then exits 0 for a run that is not batched. A run killed before AGP's own uninstall leaves the app on the AVD, so the next run on tokkl-api26 could pass with nothing tested. Batched runs already compare each batch's count with the runner's list; single runs have no such check.

## Evidence

- First batched run on tokkl-api26 on 2026-10-19 (TKA-0168 sitting), batch 1: Gradle logged "AndroidTestRunner failed on emulator-5554 ... Failed to install APK .../app-debug.apk ... INSTALL_FAILED_ALREADY_EXISTS: Attempt to re-install com.github.e0ipso.tokkl without first uninstalling", then "BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 15s", and the JUnit XML held 0 tests. The listing step had installed the app; on tokkl-api30 the same sequence installed over it and ran every test.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh `run_tests` fails only on Gradle's status or a device that went away; `run_in_batches` checks each batch's count.

## Direction

After a single run, fail when Gradle's output has an "AndroidTestRunner failed" line, or when the JUnit XML under app/build/outputs/androidTest-results/connected/debug/ is missing or reports 0 tests. Alternatively uninstall the app and the test APK before the run on an emulator the script booted. Check that a run with the app preinstalled on tokkl-api26 then fails or runs every test.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A run on tokkl-api26 that starts with the app installed either fails with a message or runs every test.
- [ ] A normal run on tokkl-api36 is unaffected.
EOF

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.

  launcher. Boot it with -no-window -accel on and kill it after.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

title: 'Test on the plain AOSP API 36 emulator, headless, and stop it afterwards'
  AVD tokkl-api36 uses the AOSP image, since ATD images drop SystemUI and the
  launcher. Boot it with -no-window -accel on and kill it after.
  - testing
  - map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session
  - practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions
  - practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script
The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

title: Run npm install in every new clone or worktree to turn on the commit hook
  The commit-msg hook lives in git-ignored .husky/_, so a clone or worktree that
A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a message only when `@commitlint/is-ignored` (a declared dependency in `package.json`) matches its first line and the message passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. Because only the header goes to `isIgnored`, a body line such as `Merge branch y` no longer lets a non-Conventional message skip the format rules. `npm test` (`node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
The hook never sees the message that `git revert` or `git cherry-pick` writes (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), a commit made with `--no-verify`, or one from a tree without `npm install`. The `commitlint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` catches those. It lints the pull request's commits, or the pushed range on `main`, and falls back to `commitlint --last` when a force push removed the old tip. Then it runs `npm test`.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot. CI's emulator step sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` itself.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. title: Run npm install in every new clone or worktree to turn on the commit hook
  The commit-msg hook lives in git-ignored .husky/_, so a clone or worktree that
A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a default-ignored message only when it passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. `npm test` (`node --test`, `test/commitlint.test.js`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
Two gaps remain. `git revert` never runs the commit-msg hook (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), so only a CI check could catch a bad revert message, and the repo has no CI workflow yet. And a body line such as `Merge branch y` makes commitlint treat a non-Conventional message as a merge and skip the format rules. The two custom rules still apply to it, so it is rejected when the header has a ticket ID or the message carries a credit line.

239:- Every API write that stores a stopped entry (create, update, stop, bulk `PATCH`, stopping the running entry when a new one starts, and undoing the delete of a running entry while another one runs) snaps it to the instance time resolution on the clock of the owner's timezone. The duration rounds up to a multiple of the resolution, so the padding is always less than one step. The start moves to the nearest grid point, and the stop follows it by the rounded duration. The response returns the stored values, so `stop - start` equals `duration`. A running entry keeps its exact start until it stops. When a new timer stops it, its stored stop lands up to half a step before the new start or up to one and a half steps after it. A timer that has run for more than 999 hours, the longest entry the API accepts, stops at 999 hours. CSV import and JSON restore keep the times in the file, and existing entries change only when they are next edited.
259:- Catalog deletions are permanent. Catalog `since` queries cannot return deleted projects, clients, tags or tasks as tombstones, and workspace `since` does not track membership changes. Use full catalog refreshes to discover removals. Deleted time entries do have tombstones through `/me/time_entries?since=...`.

The light theme has a sand background, ink text, a sunset orange primary, an aqua secondary, and hot pink and lime for states. The dark theme has a navy background with the neon counterparts.
In the app, `ui/theme/Color.kt` defines the Material 3 roles and the running and billable state colours, each with a `styles.css:<line> --token` comment naming its source. `TokklTheme` has dynamic colour off by default. `Theme.Tokkl` in `res/values` and `res/values-night` sets `android:windowBackground` to the scheme's background (`@color/window_background`), so launch shows no flash of another colour before Compose draws. When a token changes, update `Color.kt` and `window_background` together. Those resources follow only the system's dark mode, and the settings screen can choose light or dark against it. So `MainActivity` repaints the window background and picks the system bar icon colours from the chosen theme each time the setting changes. Wallpaper colours are an opt-in switch on the settings screen, shown only on Android 12 (API 31) and later.
The font is upstream Anybody 1.114, the variable TTF with width and weight axes, at `res/font/anybody_wdth_wght.ttf`. `res/font` accepts only font files, so the OFL (`anybody_ofl.txt`) and the source note with commit, URL and SHA-256 (`anybody_font_source.txt`) live in `res/raw`. A feature that needs `/me` data takes it from this refresh instead of sending its own request. `MePreferences` keeps the raw JSON object, and each reader decodes only its own key, `duration_format` for the settings and `favorites` for the cache, so a malformed key fails that reader alone.
title: 'Account settings: AccountSettingsSource, AccountTime and NoDeviceZoneTest'
  Sign-in and each refresh store timezone, week start, resolution and duration
`session/AccountSettings` holds the `GET /api/v9/me` fields that decide how the app shows and reads times: `timezone`, `beginning_of_week` and Tokkl's optional `time_resolution_minutes`. It holds no credential. Sign-in stores them from its own `/me`. A `/me` without `timezone` or `beginning_of_week`, or with a week start outside 0 to 6, fails sign-in as `SignInResult.NotTokkl`. Toggl Track and older Tokkl servers leave out `time_resolution_minutes` and do not snap, so it stays null for them. `durationFormat` comes from `duration_format` in `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` and, as in the web app, reads as improved when the key is missing, null or names another format. Screens write durations with `AccountSettings.formatDuration(Long)`.
`session/AccountSettingsSource` is the one place screens read the settings from. `TokklApplication.accountSettings` builds it over `AccountSettingsStore`, which keeps them in the private preferences file `account_settings`, so screens have them offline and after a restart. `MainActivity.onStart` and each sign-in call `refresh()`, so a change made in the web app reaches the phone. A refresh sends `GET /api/v9/me?with_related_data=true` and `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` once and hands both answers to its `onRefresh`, where the capabilities and the cache refresh from them. A second `refresh()` while one runs gets the running job instead of sending another request. A failed request or write keeps what is stored, failed preferences keep the stored duration format, and a refresh drops its answer when sign-in stored newer settings while the request ran.
`AccountSettings.time()` gives a `time/AccountTime`: the account's zone, a clock in that zone, `now()`, `today()`, `local(instant)`, `startOfWeek(date)` and `snapUnsent(start, stop)`. It returns null when `parseTimeZone` cannot resolve the name, as when the server's Intl knows a zone that the phone's tz database lacks. There is no fallback to the device's zone or to UTC. A screen without an `AccountTime` must show no clock times or dates, take no time input and name the zone it does not know. Durations, the running clock, Start and Stop need no zone and keep working.
`NoDeviceZoneTest`, a JVM test, reads the constant pool of every compiled app class through `ClassReferences` and fails on `ZoneId.systemDefault`, `TimeZone.getDefault` (java.util and ICU), `Clock.systemDefaultZone`, a `now()` without arguments on the java.time date and time types, and a `Calendar` or `GregorianCalendar` built without a zone. Its `ALLOWED` set is empty, and a class added there needs a comment saying why the account's zone will not do. Take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime` instead.

`app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/screenshot/` holds the abstract `ScreenshotTest` and one subclass per theme and font scale: `LightScreenshotTest`, `DarkScreenshotTest`, `LightLargestFontScreenshotTest` and `DarkLargestFontScreenshotTest`. `ReferenceImages` shrinks each capture to a third in each direction, averaging 3x3 blocks, and compares it with its PNG in `app/src/androidTest/assets/screenshots/`. Record and compare the references only on the AVD `tokkl-api36` (medium_phone, 420 dpi, the android-36 `default` x86_64 image at revision 2), because density and system fonts change the pixels. Two runs on freshly booted tokkl-api36 emulators matched pixel for pixel. Nobody has compared the CI emulator's captures with the references yet (TKA-0087). A change to how a screen looks updates its references in the same commit, after a look at every diff and capture.
Tapping Start or Stop never fails because the server is out of reach. A tap in the app, notification, widget or tile changes the state on the phone without waiting for the server. The notification, widget and tile read the running entry from the phone, so they react at once, and the queue sends the change behind them.
Each offline change waits in a queue on the phone, marked as not sent, and goes out in order when the server is reachable. A timer started offline keeps its real start time. The queue sends in the background when the network comes back, even with the app closed. The app shows how many changes are not sent and when the server last answered (O1 to O5). Some phone makers restrict background work, which can delay sending the queue.
The app has no sync engine and no full local copy of the account. The server is the source of truth. The phone keeps a cache of what it last loaded and the queue of unsent changes. The cache holds projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and about two weeks of history, all readable and editable offline. When the phone and another client both changed an entry, the change that reaches the server last wins. Signing out warns when unsent changes would be lost, then clears the cache and the queue.
Read the timezone, first day of the week and `time_resolution_minutes` from `GET /api/v9/me`, and use the account timezone everywhere (S7). Resolve its name with `time.parseTimeZone`, never `ZoneId.of`. Tokkl accepts what JavaScript's Intl accepts, such as `europe/madrid` in any case and ICU-only names like `IST`, and rejects some names `ZoneId.of` takes, such as `Z` or `GMT+5`. A name it cannot resolve gives null. Never fall back to the device's zone. Screens take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime`, and `NoDeviceZoneTest` fails on any read of the device's zone (see the account settings node). Show stopped entries as the server returns them, after it snaps them to `time_resolution_minutes` (T3). The phone snaps entries it has not sent yet in the account timezone, so their times do not change when the server answers. History and queue code calls `snapUnsent` in `time/Snap.kt`, never `snapSpan` directly. The server cuts both ends to whole seconds before it snaps (`snapToResolution` in `../tokkl/packages/api/src/models/timeEntries.ts`), and `snapUnsent` does the same. With no `time_resolution_minutes` in `/me` it returns the span unchanged. Never pass it the running entry, whose clock is not snapped.
Manual entry accepts times like `9`, `930`, `9:30` and `4pm`, entries across midnight, and durations like `1h 30m`, `90` and `1,5h` (M1). The parsing is a Kotlin port of Tokkl's `parseDuration` in `../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts` and `parseTimeOfDay` in `../tokkl/packages/web/src/lib/timeOfDay.ts`, checked against the cases in the `.test.ts` file next to each. The time-of-day parser lives in the web package, not in `packages/common`. Both ports live in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time`, and their tests copy the TypeScript cases verbatim at a recorded tokkl commit (see the porting practice node). feat(history): show past entries by day in the Timer page's List view

The List view of the Timer page now shows the history, as the web app's
EntryList does: days in the account's timezone, newest first, each with
its total, and under each its stopped entries, newest first, with the
description, project and task, start and stop, tags, a Billable mark and
the duration. The running entry stays out, since the timer shows it.

The days come from the cached two weeks in Room, so they show offline.
When the end of the list scrolls into view, the 14 days before the
oldest loaded day load from the configured server and stay in memory.
On Tokkl, GET /api/app/bounds tells where the account's history starts,
so the list ends with "No older entries." A server without it, such as
Toggl Track, gets pages until one comes back empty, and then more only
on a tap, so scrolling never walks back through empty weeks by itself.
Offline the end says that older days need the server, with Try again.
Nothing loads on a timer.

Entries the server has stopped show its start and stop as returned,
snapped or not. An entry with a change the server has not received
shows snapUnsent of its times, and its snapped start picks its day, so
nothing moves when the server answers. It carries a "Not sent" mark in
words.

The Timer page's list slot no longer has a placeholder. A
SignedInFrame, split out of TokklNavHost, puts a screen above the bottom
bar, so the Timer capture can show a fixed history above the real bar.

Screenshot references, re-recorded on tokkl-api36 in light and dark at
100% and 200%: timer-* now show three days of fixed history on a fixed
day, with no live server data. LargestFontScaleTest waits for the empty
history of the test account instead of the removed placeholder.

    @Test
    fun readsTheServersViewListWhenMissingOrUnknown() {
        val s = setting()
        assertEquals(TimerView.LIST, s.view.value)
        s.refreshed(prefs("""{"timerView":"calendar"}"""), keepsTimerView = true)
        assertEquals(TimerView.CALENDAR, s.view.value)
        s.refreshed(prefs("""{"timerView":"grid"}"""), keepsTimerView = true)
        assertEquals(TimerView.LIST, s.view.value)
        s.refreshed(prefs("""{"timerView":"calendar"}"""), keepsTimerView = true)
        s.refreshed(prefs("""{}"""), keepsTimerView = true)
        assertEquals(TimerView.LIST, s.view.value)
        s.refreshed(prefs("""{"timerView":3}"""), keepsTimerView = true)
        assertEquals(TimerView.LIST, s.view.value)
        assertEquals(StoredTimerView(TimerView.LIST, false), saved.last())
        assertEquals(0, server.requestCount)
    }

    @Test
    fun aTapPostsTheViewAndAStaleRefreshAfterItKeepsTheTap() {
        server.enqueue(ok())
        val s = setting()

        assertEquals(TimerView.CALENDAR, s.view.value)
        val request = server.takeRequest()
        assertEquals("POST", request.method)
        assertEquals("/api/v9/me/preferences", request.url.encodedPath)
        assertEquals("""{"timerView":"calendar"}""", request.body?.utf8())
        assertEquals(StoredTimerView(TimerView.CALENDAR, false), saved.last())
        s.refreshed(prefs("""{"timerView":"list"}"""), keepsTimerView = true) // may predate the tap
        assertEquals(TimerView.CALENDAR, s.view.value)
        s.refreshed(prefs("""{"timerView":"list"}"""), keepsTimerView = true) // the web changed it later
        assertEquals(TimerView.LIST, s.view.value)
    }

    fun anOfflineTapStaysUnsentAndTheNextRefreshSendsIt() {
        server.enqueue(MockResponse.Builder().onRequestStart(SocketEffect.CloseSocket()).build())

        assertEquals(StoredTimerView(TimerView.CALENDAR, true), saved.last())

        assertEquals(2, server.requestCount)
        assertEquals(StoredTimerView(TimerView.CALENDAR, false), saved.last())
    }

    @Test
    fun aStoredUnsentChoiceGoesWithTheFirstRefreshAfterAColdStart() {

        assertEquals(TimerView.CALENDAR, s.view.value)

    }

        assertEquals(TimerView.CALENDAR, s.view.value)
        assertEquals(StoredTimerView(TimerView.CALENDAR, false), saved.last())
        assertEquals(0, server.requestCount)
    }

    @Test
    fun aFailedPreferencesReadKeepsTheView() {
        val s = setting(initial = StoredTimerView(TimerView.CALENDAR, unsent = false))
        s.refreshed(null, keepsTimerView = true)
        assertEquals(TimerView.CALENDAR, s.view.value)
        assertEquals(0, server.requestCount)
    }
}

preferences file, so a cold start opens the last view before the
refresh answers.

server with the next refresh, so the choice that reaches the server
last wins, as for time entries (O3). The one refresh right after a tap
keeps the tap, since its preferences may predate it. A server without
Tokkl's preferences, such as Toggl Track, which Capabilities.favorites
marks, gets no write: the choice stays on the phone and now also
survives a cold start there.

SessionRule clears the stored view with the rest of the session, so
each test starts on List.

When your systemd user manager is running, the emulator runs in a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` and at most 6 GB of memory. If the kernel's OOM killer ends qemu, the script fails and says so, and systemd leaves the session that started it alone. On an emulator it boots, the script also turns on `hide_error_dialogs` and closes open system dialogs, because a fresh headless boot often leaves "System UI isn't responding" in front of the app. It also sets the font scale to 1.0, because the AVD keeps the last scale a test set across boots. # Keep the Timer page's List or Calendar choice in Tokkl's timerView preference

## Problem

The web app keeps the Timer page's List or Calendar choice in the account's `timerView` preference, so the view a user picked on the laptop is the one they get next time, on any device. The app's switch, added by TKA-0157, keeps the choice in saved state on the phone only: it survives a rotation or process death, but a cold start always opens List, and a choice made on the phone never reaches the web app. Users who prefer the calendar have to pick it again on every launch.

## Evidence

- ../tokkl/packages/web/src/pages/TimerPage.tsx:24-25 reads `prefs.timerView` and saves a new choice with `savePrefs.mutate({ timerView: next })`.
- ../tokkl/packages/api/src/models/users.ts:86 accepts `timerView` as `'list'` or `'calendar'` in the preferences.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/TokklNavHost.kt:69 holds the choice in `rememberSaveable`, starting at `TimerView.LIST`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/session/AccountSettings.kt:103 already wraps the `/me/preferences` body (`MePreferences`), which the cache refresh reads for the favorites.

## Direction

Read `timerView` from the `/me/preferences` body the refresh already fetches, and start the Timer page in that view, falling back to List when the key is missing or holds anything else. A tap on the switch changes the view at once and writes the new value to the server's preferences the way other preference writes go, without waiting for the answer. Offline, keep the choice on the phone and send it when the connection returns, or drop it if the server has a newer value; record which. Servers without the key (Toggl Track) keep the phone-only behaviour.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A cold start opens the view stored in `timerView` on a real Tokkl server.
- [ ] Choosing Calendar on the phone sets `timerView` to `calendar` on the server, and the web app then opens the calendar.
- [ ] A missing or unknown `timerView` opens List, and the switch still works.
EOF

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.

The ports in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time` (`Duration.kt` for `parseDuration` and `formatDuration`, `TimeOfDay.kt` for `parseTimeOfDay`, `Snap.kt` for `snapSpan`, and `TimeZone.kt`, which accepts the timezone names Intl accepts) behave like the TypeScript they port, including where Kotlin differs from JavaScript. `JsSemantics.kt` has the helpers. JavaScript's `\s` and `String.prototype.trim` use the ECMAScript WhiteSpace and LineTerminator characters, while Java's `\s` matches only ASCII and Kotlin's `trim()` uses yet another set. `Math.round` rounds halves up and `kotlin.math.round` rounds them to even. JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.
A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.
`DurationTest` and `TimeOfDayTest` hold the cases of the matching `.test.ts` file verbatim, and their header names the tokkl commit they were copied at. To follow an upstream change, copy the cases again and update that commit. `DurationJsSemanticsTest` pins the JavaScript traps in its own file, since they are not in `duration.test.ts` and a later diff against tokkl leaves them alone. Its expected values come from running the TypeScript file in Node 24, where `node file.mts` strips the types.
`formatDuration` uses JavaScript's double arithmetic, and `DurationTest` holds the `formatDuration` cases of `duration.test.ts` too. `jsToFixed` in `JsSemantics.kt` is `Number.prototype.toFixed`, which rounds the double's exact binary value: `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is `1.00` and `(2.55).toFixed(1)` is `2.5`. `Intl.NumberFormat` rounds the shortest decimal string of the double instead and gives `1.01` and `2.6` (Node 24.21). So `jsToFixed` ports a `toFixed` call only, never an `Intl.NumberFormat` one. `sharePercent` in `reports/ReportFormat.kt` uses it for percentages that the web app writes with `Intl.NumberFormat`, and differs from the web app at halves until TKA-0148.
Where the TypeScript throws a RangeError, `snapSpan` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Within hours of the end of a JavaScript Date's range, near the year 275760, the TypeScript can also return an invalid Date. An `Instant` has no such value, so the port throws there too, and `SnapJsDateRangeTest` pins that edge.
The light theme has a sand background, ink text, a sunset orange primary, an aqua secondary, and hot pink and lime for states. The dark theme has a navy background with the neon counterparts.
In the app, `ui/theme/Color.kt` defines the Material 3 roles and the running and billable state colours, each with a comment naming its token in the first `:root` block of `styles.css`. Find a token by name, not by line. `TokklTheme` has dynamic colour off by default. `Theme.Tokkl` in `res/values` and `res/values-night` sets `android:windowBackground` to the scheme's background (`@color/window_background`), so launch shows no flash of another colour before Compose draws. When a token changes, update `Color.kt` and `window_background` together. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, `syncApplicationNightMode` in `settings/ApplicationNightMode.kt` passes the stored theme mode to `UiModeManager.setApplicationNightMode` on every start and every change, off the main thread: light is `MODE_NIGHT_NO`, dark `MODE_NIGHT_YES` and system `MODE_NIGHT_AUTO`. Android picks `res/values` or `res/values-night` for the starting window by that mode, so a cold start shows the chosen theme's colours. `MainActivity` declares `android:configChanges="uiMode"`, so the sync does not recreate it. Below Android 12 the starting window still follows the system's dark mode, and the window theme never knows the wallpaper's colours. So `MainActivity` still repaints the window background and picks the system bar icon colours from the chosen theme each time the setting changes. Wallpaper colours are an opt-in switch on the settings screen, shown only on Android 12 (API 31) and later.

`cache/` keeps what the app last loaded from the server in the Room database `account_cache.db` (`CacheDatabase`): projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and the time entries of `HistoryWindow`, which is today and the 13 days before it, counted in the account's timezone. Screens read the flows of `AccountCache`, which come from the phone and never wait for the network. The account settings are not cached here; `AccountSettingsSource` stays their one source.
One refresh feeds all of this. `AccountSettingsSource.refresh`, called from `MainActivity.onStart`, after sign-in and after an accepted trust prompt, sends `GET /api/v9/me?with_related_data=true` and `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` once. Its `onRefresh`, wired in `TokklApplication`, refreshes the capabilities with the trash probe and then the cache, which adds `GET /api/v9/me/time_entries` for the history window. A feature that needs `/me` data takes it from this refresh instead of sending its own request. `MePreferences` keeps the raw JSON object, and each reader decodes only its own key, `duration_format` for the settings and `favorites` for the cache, so a malformed key fails that reader alone.
Tapping Start or Stop never fails because the server is out of reach. A tap in the app, notification, widget or tile changes the state on the phone without waiting for the server. The notification, widget and tile read the running entry from the phone, so they react at once, and the queue sends the change behind them.
Each offline change waits in a queue on the phone, marked as not sent, and goes out in order when the server is reachable. A timer started offline keeps its real start time. The queue sends in the background when the network comes back, even with the app closed. The app shows how many changes are not sent and when the server last answered (O1 to O5). Some phone makers restrict background work, which can delay sending the queue.
The app has no sync engine and no full local copy of the account. The server is the source of truth. The phone keeps a cache of what it last loaded and the queue of unsent changes. The cache holds projects, clients, tags, tasks, favorites and about two weeks of history, all readable and editable offline. When the phone and another client both changed an entry, the change that reaches the server last wins. Signing out warns when unsent changes would be lost, then clears the cache and the queue.

A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. result_evidence:
`session/AccountSettings` holds the `GET /api/v9/me` fields that decide how the app shows and reads times: `timezone`, `beginning_of_week` and Tokkl's optional `time_resolution_minutes`. It holds no credential. Sign-in stores them from its own `/me`. A `/me` without `timezone` or `beginning_of_week`, or with a week start outside 0 to 6, fails sign-in as `SignInResult.NotTokkl`. Toggl Track and older Tokkl servers leave out `time_resolution_minutes` and do not snap, so it stays null for them. `durationFormat` comes from `duration_format` in `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` and, as in the web app, reads as improved when the key is missing, null or names another format. Screens write durations with `AccountSettings.formatDuration(Long)`.
`session/AccountSettingsSource` is the one place screens read the settings from. `TokklApplication.accountSettings` builds it over `AccountSettingsStore`, which keeps them in the private preferences file `account_settings`, so screens have them offline and after a restart. `MainActivity.onStart` and each sign-in call `refresh()`, so a change made in the web app reaches the phone. A refresh sends `GET /api/v9/me?with_related_data=true` and `GET /api/v9/me/preferences` once and hands both answers to its `onRefresh`, where the capabilities and the cache refresh from them. A second `refresh()` while one runs gets the running job instead of sending another request. A failed request or write keeps what is stored, failed preferences keep the stored duration format, and a refresh drops its answer when sign-in stored newer settings while the request ran.
`AccountSettings.time()` gives a `time/AccountTime`: the account's zone, a clock in that zone, `now()`, `today()`, `local(instant)`, `startOfWeek(date)` and `snapUnsent(start, stop)`. It returns null when `parseTimeZone` cannot resolve the name, as when the server's Intl knows a zone that the phone's tz database lacks. There is no fallback to the device's zone or to UTC. A screen without an `AccountTime` must show no clock times or dates, take no time input and name the zone it does not know. Durations, the running clock, Start and Stop need no zone and keep working.
`NoDeviceZoneTest`, a JVM test, reads the constant pool of every compiled app class through `ClassReferences` and fails on `ZoneId.systemDefault`, `TimeZone.getDefault` (java.util and ICU), `Clock.systemDefaultZone`, a `now()` without arguments on the java.time date and time types, and a `Calendar` or `GregorianCalendar` built without a zone. Its `ALLOWED` set is empty, and a class added there needs a comment saying why the account's zone will not do. Take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime` instead.
