No test may skip itself with a JUnit assumption. AGP 9.4.1 runs the tests through its test engine 1.0.1, which records every result but a pass as a failure. A failed assumption then shows as a failed test in the JUnit XML and the HTML report, while the Gradle task passes. Engine 1.0.7, which AGP 9.5.0-alpha08 and later bring, records it as skipped. To leave a test out on some Android versions, use `@SdkSuppress`, as the screenshot classes do for API 36.

When a test needs a device setting, a rule sets it and puts it back afterwards, as `SystemFontScale` does for the font scale and `SystemNightMode` for the night mode. Never assume the device already has it.

Parse server times with `OffsetDateTime.parse`. Tokkl writes `+00:00` and Toggl `Z`, and `Instant.parse` on API 30 refuses the `+00:00` form. Use `WindowInsetsCompat`, never `WindowInsets.Type`: that class came with Android 11, and `LargestFontScaleTest` crashed on it below API 30. `AirplaneMode` runs `cmd connectivity airplane-mode`, which needs Android 10, so the tests that use it cannot pass on tokkl-api26 until TKA-0174 lands.

A test cannot kill the app's process and then check what survived, because the instrumentation runs in that process and dies with it. Restart tests split into steps instead, and the orchestrator runs each step in a new process.

Reuse the helpers in `app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/`:

- `LoopbackRelay` relays the phone's 127.0.0.1 to a test server. With `watchRequests` it hands a watcher every chunk the app sends, so a test can count requests.
- `HangingRelay` can hang like a network that went quiet, cutting the connections it relayed, or hold back one answer until `releaseAnswer`.
- `AirplaneMode` switches airplane mode through the shell user and waits until the client's requests fail, or get through again.
- `BackgroundTrip` sends `MainActivity` to the background with the home key and brings the same activity back.
- `TestAccounts` invites throwaway accounts on the test server for tests that fill an account with data, and creates, reads and deletes their entries. The account the script creates stays empty.
- `finishWithin` in `ComposeWaits.kt` runs a block on its own thread and fails after a timeout. `ActivityScenario`'s `close()` and `onActivity()` start with `waitForIdleSync()`, which has no timeout, so a main thread that never goes idle would hang the whole run.

Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. EOF

`cache/ChangeQueue` starts, stops, creates, edits and deletes time entries on the phone (`docs/PRD.md` O1). Each call changes the cached entry and queues the change in one transaction, then asks the sender to send. No call waits for the network. Start and Stop read the tap time from the clock before anything else, so call them from the tap's handler. A start first stops a cached running entry at that same time, as the server does. Start and create take the workspace from `AccountSettings.defaultWorkspaceId`, which the phone keeps, so they work offline.

`ChangeStore` keeps the queue as `PendingChange` rows. Each one carries every field of the entry as the change left it, so the server gets full values and the change that reaches it last wins (O3). An entry created on the phone gets a negative local id, minus its create's queue sequence. result_evidence:
Read the timezone, first day of the week and `time_resolution_minutes` from `GET /api/v9/me`, and use the account timezone everywhere (S7). Resolve its name with `time.parseTimeZone`, never `ZoneId.of`. Tokkl accepts what JavaScript's Intl accepts, such as `europe/madrid` in any case and ICU-only names like `IST`, and rejects some names `ZoneId.of` takes, such as `Z` or `GMT+5`. A name it cannot resolve gives null. Never fall back to the device's zone. Screens take the zone, the clock and the dates from `AccountTime`, and `NoDeviceZoneTest` fails on any read of the device's zone (see the account settings node). Show stopped entries as the server returns them, after it snaps them to `time_resolution_minutes` (T3). The phone snaps entries it has not sent yet in the account timezone, so their times do not change when the server answers. History and queue code calls `snapUnsent` in `time/Snap.kt`, never `snapSpan` directly. The server cuts both ends to whole seconds before it snaps (`snapToResolution` in `../tokkl/packages/api/src/models/timeEntries.ts`), and `snapUnsent` does the same. With no `time_resolution_minutes` in `/me` it returns the span unchanged. Never pass it the running entry, whose clock is not snapped.
Manual entry accepts times like `9`, `930`, `9:30` and `4pm`, entries across midnight, and durations like `1h 30m`, `90` and `1,5h` (M1). The parsing is a Kotlin port of Tokkl's `parseDuration` in `../tokkl/packages/common/duration.ts` and `parseTimeOfDay` in `../tokkl/packages/web/src/lib/timeOfDay.ts`, checked against the cases in the `.test.ts` file next to each. The time-of-day parser lives in the web package, not in `packages/common`. Both ports live in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time`, and their tests copy the TypeScript cases verbatim at a recorded tokkl commit (see the porting practice node). The ports can still drift when the TypeScript changes later. Sharing the test cases between the two repos would catch that.
19-Tapping Start or Stop never fails because the server is out of reach. A tap in the app, notification, widget or tile changes the state on the phone without waiting for the server. The notification, widget and tile read the running entry from the phone, so they react at once, and the queue sends the change behind them.

Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.

title: 'Test on the plain AOSP API 36 emulator, headless, and stop it afterwards'
  AVD tokkl-api36 uses the AOSP image, since ATD images drop SystemUI and the
  launcher. Boot it with -no-window -accel on and kill it after.
  - testing
  - map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session
  - practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions
  - practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script
The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

The instrumented tests, including the Compose UI tests, run against a real Tokkl server, never a fake one. One command runs them. It needs Docker, `curl`, `jq` and `openssl`:
scripts/instrumented-tests.sh
[credential-related line omitted]
If no device is attached, the script boots `tokkl-api36` as in the previous section, with 2 GB of guest RAM, and stops it and the adb server at the end. When your systemd user manager is running, the emulator runs in a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue`. If the kernel's OOM killer ends qemu, the script fails and says so, and systemd leaves the session that started it alone. On an emulator it boots, the script also turns on `hide_error_dialogs` and closes open system dialogs, because a fresh headless boot often leaves "System UI isn't responding" in front of the app. It also sets the font scale to 1.0, because the AVD keeps the last scale a test set across boots. It turns on `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` too, since otherwise the soft keyboard never opens on the headless emulator. It changes no setting on an emulator that was already running, and that emulator keeps running. Arguments go to Gradle, so one class runs with:
scripts/instrumented-tests.sh \
  -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest
Without the script, `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails the tests that need the server. To move to a newer Tokkl, put the digest from `docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/e0ipso/tokkl:<version>` into `IMAGE` in the script. `PROXY_IMAGE` takes the digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
`gradle.properties` caps the Gradle heap at 2 GB and compiles Kotlin inside the Gradle daemon, so no separate Kotlin daemon starts. The Gradle daemon itself stays in memory after the build. Stop it when you finish:
scripts/reproducible-release.sh v0.1.0   # a tag or any other commit
The script clones the commit twice, runs `./gradlew --no-daemon assembleRelease` in each clone without the signing variables below, and compares the two unsigned APKs byte for byte. It builds committed work only. The clones sit at paths of different lengths. The second build runs on at most two CPU cores and gets its own Gradle user home, which reads downloaded dependencies from yours but redoes every transform. So an embedded path, output that depends on the core count, and a transform that differs from run to run all show up as differences. When the APKs differ, the script lists the zip entries that differ and keeps both APKs. On this machine the two builds take about four minutes and use up to about 700 MB under `build/`, which the script removes at the end. CI runs the script on pull requests to `main` and on pushes to `main`.

F-Droid asks to keep that file and to build the release APK from a clean checkout of the tagged commit. So build the GitHub release APK once the release commit and its tag exist, never from a tree with uncommitted changes, such as one where the release step has just rewritten `gradle/version.properties`.

title: Run npm install in every new clone or worktree to turn on the commit hook
  The commit-msg hook lives in git-ignored .husky/_, so a clone or worktree that
A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a default-ignored message only when it passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. `npm test` (`node --test`, `test/commitlint.test.js`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
Two gaps remain. `git revert` never runs the commit-msg hook (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), so only a CI check could catch a bad revert message, and the repo has no CI workflow yet. And a body line such as `Merge branch y` makes commitlint treat a non-Conventional message as a merge and skip the format rules. The two custom rules still apply to it, so it is rejected when the header has a ticket ID or the message carries a credit line.

The time parsers in `com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.time` (`Duration.kt` for `parseDuration`, `TimeOfDay.kt` for `parseTimeOfDay`) behave like the TypeScript they port, including where Kotlin differs from JavaScript. `JsSemantics.kt` has the helpers. JavaScript's `\s` and `String.prototype.trim` use the ECMAScript WhiteSpace and LineTerminator characters, while Java's `\s` matches only ASCII and Kotlin's `trim()` uses yet another set. `Math.round` rounds halves up and `kotlin.math.round` rounds them to even. JavaScript's `replace(',', '.')` changes only the first comma, so the port calls `replaceFirst`.

A Long cannot hold NaN, Infinity or integers from 2^63 up, so where the TypeScript returns one of those the port returns null. `parseDuration` returns NaN for the unit `constructor`, because its unit lookup finds that key on `Object.prototype`, and Infinity once a number of 300-odd digits overflows a double.

`DurationTest` and `TimeOfDayTest` hold the cases of the matching `.test.ts` file verbatim, and their header names the tokkl commit they were copied at. To follow an upstream change, copy the cases again and update that commit. `DurationJsSemanticsTest` pins the JavaScript traps in its own file, since they are not in `duration.test.ts` and a later diff against tokkl leaves them alone. Its expected values come from running the TypeScript file in Node 24, where `node file.mts` strips the types.
EOF

# Run the instrumented suite on an API 26 to 30 emulator as well as API 36

## Problem

The app's minSdk is 26 (app/build.gradle.kts:98), but the script boots tokkl-api36 by default (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:52) and the CI instrumented job runs API 36 (.github/workflows/ci.yml:100). Code that only runs below Android 12 has never run on a device. That covers the night-mode sync, which returns early and leaves the starting window on the system mode (ApplicationNightMode.kt:32-36), the colour scheme and settings switch that drop dynamic colour below 12 (Theme.kt:31, ThemeSettings.kt:34), and the fullBackupContent rules that Android 11 and earlier read (AndroidManifest.xml:15, backup_rules.xml:2-7). The tests' own older branches never run either: ThemeSettingsTestSupport.kt:44 and :101 below 12, and LauncherIconTest.kt:35 below 13. The cross-platform-transfer section of the data extraction rules (data_extraction_rules.xml:30) needs an API 36.1 or later image, which the harness also lacks.

## Evidence

- app/build.gradle.kts:98 sets `minSdk = 26`.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:52 defaults the AVD to `tokkl-api36`, overridable with `TOKKL_TEST_AVD`.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:100 runs the emulator at `api-level: 36`.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/settings/ApplicationNightMode.kt:32-36 returns early below API 31, where the starting window follows the system's mode.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/Theme.kt:31 uses dynamic colour only on API 31 and later.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/settings/ThemeSettings.kt:34 reports dynamic colour unavailable below API 31, which hides the switch.
- app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:15 points `android:fullBackupContent` at the backup rules.
- app/src/main/res/xml/backup_rules.xml:2-7 holds the rules for Android 11 (API 30) and earlier.
- app/src/main/res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml:30 opens the `cross-platform-transfer` section.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/settings/ThemeSettingsTestSupport.kt:44 resets the app's night mode only on API 31 and later.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/settings/ThemeSettingsTestSupport.kt:101 expects the system's night mode below API 31.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/LauncherIconTest.kt:35 checks the monochrome layer only on API 33 and later.

## Direction

- Install an older AOSP system image that keeps SystemUI and the launcher, under ~/Android/Sdk with sdkmanager as TKA-0001 did, and create an AVD for it. API 26 or 28 covers the pre-12 starting window and night mode. Add API 30 as well only if one image cannot cover both the pre-12 path and the API 26 to 30 backup path.
- Let scripts/instrumented-tests.sh run against the older AVD through an AVD or API argument, without changing the default of tokkl-api36. `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` already selects the AVD (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:52); add only what the older image needs to boot and run.
- Each boot keeps its own systemd scope from TKA-0099. Run the older and the API 36 AVDs one after the other, never at the same time, to stay within this machine's memory.
- Make sure the older run exercises the early return in ApplicationNightMode.kt:32-36, the theme and settings without dynamic colour (Theme.kt:31, ThemeSettings.kt:34), the backup rules that AndroidManifest.xml:15 names (backup_rules.xml:2-7), and the older branches in ThemeSettingsTestSupport.kt:44 and :101 and LauncherIconTest.kt:35.

# Make concurrent instrumented runs safe, or refuse a second run while one is active

## Problem

The script runs the tests on every device adb lists and boots its own emulator only when none is attached (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:26-30, :134-136, :175-177, :275-279). A second run that starts while the first is active finds the first run's emulator, skips booting its own and runs its tests there. When the first run ends, its cleanup kills that emulator (:113). If adb was not running when the first run started (:71), the cleanup also stops the shared adb server (:120-121). Two agents or sittings running tests at once break each other, so only one sitting at a time can use the emulator, and that serialises most of each wave.

## Evidence

- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:26-30 says the tests run on the devices adb lists, the script boots an AVD only with no device attached, and it stops the adb server if that was not running before.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:71 records whether adb was running at start.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:113 kills the emulator the run started, in cleanup.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:120-121 kills the adb server in cleanup when it was not running at start.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:134-136 lists every attached device.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:175-177 boots an emulator only when `ANDROID_SERIAL` is unset and no device is attached.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:275-279 picks `ANDROID_SERIAL` or every attached device as the test devices.

## Direction

Pick one of two approaches and record the choice and the reason in the resolution.

- Lock. Take a `flock` on a file under `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` before the device check at :175-177. A second run then waits, or fails with a clear message that names the holder.
- Isolate. Each run boots its own read-only instance of the AVD on its own port, sets `ANDROID_SERIAL` for itself instead of using every device adb lists (:134-136, :275-279), and never kills an adb server or emulator it did not start (:71, :113, :120-121).

Prefer the lock if isolation would double memory beyond what TKA-0132 measures as safe on this 16 GB machine.

Either way:

- Keep the emulator's own systemd scope from TKA-0099 and the check from TKA-0101 that every test device is still online after Gradle.
- Update the header (:26-30) to describe how concurrent runs behave.
- Demonstrate with two overlapping runs and record the output in the resolution.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Starting a second run while one is active either waits or fails clearly, or runs safely on its own emulator.
- [ ] Neither run's cleanup stops the other's emulator or adb server.
- [ ] A demonstration with two overlapping runs is recorded in the resolution.
- [ ] The full suite still passes.

# Test on the device that a certificate from a user-installed CA connects without a prompt

## Problem

The network security config trusts user CAs (network_security_config.xml:16-19). The shared client's PinningTrustManager asks the platform trust manager first, which on Android trusts the system and user CAs that config names (SharedHttpClient.kt:45-46). Only a JVM test with a JDK keystore covers that path (PinningTrustManagerTest.kt:92-100). The device test meets only a self-signed certificate that no CA trusts (PinnedCertificateTest.kt:19). TKA-0021 required that a certificate trusted by a system or user CA never prompts (TKA-0021:45) and waived the device test, so a regression in the config or the delegation would pass every test.

## Evidence

- app/src/main/res/xml/network_security_config.xml:16-19 lists system and user certificates as trust anchors.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/api/SharedHttpClient.kt:45-46 builds the platform trust manager from the default `TrustManagerFactory`.
- app/src/test/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/api/PinningTrustManagerTest.kt:92-100 checks, on the JVM with a JDK keystore, that a certificate the platform trusts never reaches the pin.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/api/PinnedCertificateTest.kt:19 says no system or user CA trusts the harness's certificate.
- .ai/sift/archive/server-connection/feature/TKA-0021--self-signed-trust.md:45 requires that a certificate trusted by a system or user CA never prompts.

## Direction

- In the script, make a CA for each run and have the harness proxy present a leaf it signed, on a port of its own, so the self-signed proxy that PinnedCertificateTest.kt:19 relies on stays as it is. Keep the keys per run and outside the repo.
- Install that CA as a user CA only on an emulator the script booted. Find a scriptable way on the AOSP image, such as a test-only device owner or the emulator's root shell writing the user CA store, and document it in the script header.
- Add an instrumented test that signs in to that leaf's URL and reaches `/me` with no certificate prompt. This exercises the trust anchors at network_security_config.xml:16-19 and the platform trust manager at SharedHttpClient.kt:45-46 on Android's own TLS stack, as the JVM test at PinningTrustManagerTest.kt:92-100 does with a JDK keystore.
- Change no product code and no network security config for the test.
- If no scriptable install works on the image, record what was tried in the resolution and close the ticket with that evidence, as TKA-0021:45 still lacks a device test.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On the emulator, a server whose leaf a user-installed CA signed connects with no prompt.
- [ ] No product code or config changes for the test.
- [ ] Or the resolution records why a user CA cannot be installed by script on the image.

# Swap the TLS proxy's key during a run and check the signed-in session prompts for the new certificate

## Problem

ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest stands in for a regenerated server key. Before the activity starts, it saves a session and pins a made-up fingerprint of 32 zero bytes (ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:33-36, :49, :112). The script makes one proxy key per run (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:213) and starts one proxy (:243), so the certificate never changes under a session that pinned the real one. TKA-0125 asked for this test behind the harness's TLS proxy with a regenerated key (TKA-0125:54). A server key that changes under an already connected session has never happened in a test.

## Evidence

- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/trust/ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:33-36 describes the stored pin as one from an earlier certificate, standing in for a regenerated key.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/trust/ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:49 pins `OLD_SHA256` for the TLS endpoint before the test runs.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/trust/ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:112 sets `OLD_SHA256` to `"00".repeat(32)`.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:213 generates the proxy's one key and certificate for the run.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:243 starts the one TLS proxy.
- .ai/sift/archive/server-connection/bug/TKA-0125--signed-in-trust-prompts.md:54 asks for an instrumented test behind the harness's TLS proxy with a regenerated key.

## Direction

- Give the harness a second certificate with its own per-run key for the same server, made beside the first (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:213). Keep both keys outside the repo.
- The app keys its pin on host and port (app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/session/ServerTrustStore.kt:33-34). The second certificate must therefore reach the app on the same host and port as the first. A second proxy on another port is a different server to the app, so it would show the first-time prompt instead of the changed-certificate prompt.
- The test has no control channel back to the host, so it must trigger the swap itself. One way is two proxies behind one front port that sends new connections to the first or the second after a request the test makes. Pass any extra port and the second certificate's fingerprint to the test as instrumentation arguments, like `tokklTlsFingerprint`.
- In a new instrumented test, sign in through the TLS URL, accept the prompt so the real first certificate is pinned, trigger the swap, then make a request. Expect the changed-certificate prompt with the second certificate's fingerprint. Accept it and check that requests succeed and the new pin is stored.
- The existing test (ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:33-36, :49, :112) can stay. It covers a pin stored before the activity starts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An instrumented test pins the real first certificate, then meets a different real certificate for the same server and gets the prompt with the new fingerprint.
- [ ] Accepting pins the new one and requests succeed.
- [ ] The existing TLS tests still pass.

# Swap the TLS proxy's key during a run and check the signed-in session prompts for the new certificate

## Problem

ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest stands in for a regenerated server key. Before the activity starts, it saves a session and pins a made-up fingerprint of 32 zero bytes (ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:33-36, :49, :112). The script makes one proxy key per run (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:213) and starts one proxy (:243), so the certificate never changes under a session that pinned the real one. TKA-0125 asked for this test behind the harness's TLS proxy with a regenerated key (TKA-0125:54). A server key that changes under an already connected session has never happened in a test.

## Evidence

- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/trust/ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:33-36 describes the stored pin as one from an earlier certificate, standing in for a regenerated key.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/trust/ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:49 pins `OLD_SHA256` for the TLS endpoint before the test runs.
- app/src/androidTest/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/trust/ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:112 sets `OLD_SHA256` to `"00".repeat(32)`.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:213 generates the proxy's one key and certificate for the run.
- scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:243 starts the one TLS proxy.
- .ai/sift/archive/server-connection/bug/TKA-0125--signed-in-trust-prompts.md:54 asks for an instrumented test behind the harness's TLS proxy with a regenerated key.

## Direction

- Give the harness a second certificate with its own per-run key for the same server, made beside the first (scripts/instrumented-tests.sh:213). Keep both keys outside the repo.
- The app keys its pin on host and port (app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/session/ServerTrustStore.kt:33-34). The second certificate must therefore reach the app on the same host and port as the first. A second proxy on another port is a different server to the app, so it would show the first-time prompt instead of the changed-certificate prompt.
- The test has no control channel back to the host, so it must trigger the swap itself. One way is two proxies behind one front port that sends new connections to the first or the second after a request the test makes. Pass any extra port and the second certificate's fingerprint to the test as instrumentation arguments, like `tokklTlsFingerprint`.
- In a new instrumented test, sign in through the TLS URL, accept the prompt so the real first certificate is pinned, trigger the swap, then make a request. Expect the changed-certificate prompt with the second certificate's fingerprint. Accept it and check that requests succeed and the new pin is stored.
- The existing test (ChangedCertificateWhileSignedInTest.kt:33-36, :49, :112) can stay. It covers a pin stored before the activity starts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An instrumented test pins the real first certificate, then meets a different real certificate for the same server and gets the prompt with the new fingerprint.
- [ ] Accepting pins the new one and requests succeed.
- [ ] The existing TLS tests still pass.

# Show the wordmark on the launch splash in place of the launcher logo

## Problem

The owner wants the wordmark on the splash screen and on sign-in only, but the app has no splash setup. On Android 12 and later the system's starting window draws the launcher icon, the clock logo, on the window background. On Android 8 to 11 it shows the bare window background. The PRD forbids the logo beside the wordmark, so the platform's branding image slot, which puts an image under the icon, is not an option.

## Evidence

- absent: androidx.core:core-splashscreen in app/build.gradle.kts and gradle/libs.versions.toml. Neither file mentions a splash library.
- app/src/main/res/values/themes.xml:11-13 gives Theme.Tokkl only android:windowBackground, which also paints the starting window.
- app/src/main/res/values-night/themes.xml:3-5 does the same in dark.
- app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:18,22 sets the app icon to @mipmap/ic_launcher and the theme to Theme.Tokkl, so the Android 12+ starting window draws the launcher icon.
- app/src/main/res/mipmap-anydpi/ic_launcher.xml:3,19-23 is the launcher icon, the clock O logo on plum, as an adaptive icon.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/Color.kt:207-211 documents the scene colours as the texture behind the sign-in scene and the splash. The platform splash background takes one solid colour, so no gradient can go there.
- docs/PRD.md:80-81 requires the 1dp halo around the wordmark in dark, and keeps the logo to the launcher icon, never beside the wordmark.
- app/build.gradle.kts:98,100 sets minSdk 26 and targetSdk 36.
- .ai/sift/archive/look-and-feel/feature/TKA-0165--clock-logo-launcher-icon.md:53,66 checked the Android 12+ starting window with the new launcher icon and added no splash attributes.

## Direction

Add AndroidX core-splashscreen. Its compat theme covers minSdk 26. Add a starting theme, in values and values-night, that sets:

- the splash background to the window background colour, @color/window_background, light and dark;
- the animated icon to the wordmark, sized to fit the icon area's 192dp circle, about 180dp wide at aspect 2059/769;
- the post-splash theme to Theme.Tokkl.

Apply the starting theme in the manifest, AndroidManifest.xml:22, and call installSplashScreen() in MainActivity before super.onCreate, MainActivity.kt:47-48. Set no branding image and no logo. Do not hold the splash for the network or the cache, so no keep-on-screen condition.

In dark the wordmark needs its halo, docs/PRD.md:80, because its ink outline nearly vanishes on the dark background. Brand draws the halo at run time, and a splash icon is a static drawable. Use a drawable with the halo baked in, or another way, and record the choice and why in the sitting report.

Below Android 12 the starting window follows the system's night mode, not the app's theme setting, themes.xml:6-9. Check the compat splash with the setting opposite to the system mode and record what it shows.

Screenshot tests cannot capture the starting window. Verify a cold start by hand on tokkl-api36 in light and dark and on tokkl-api30, and attach the captures to the sitting report. Add an instrumented check that the activity uses the starting theme and reaches its first screen without waiting.

TKA-0184 later removes the wordmark images nothing uses. Whatever this ticket's splash icon references must stay referenced from res/, so that ticket keeps it.

## Alternatives considered

- Option (b): keep the system's logo-only splash, so the wordmark is on sign-in only. The owner can still pick this; the ticket would then close as wontfix.
- Option (c): an in-app Compose splash after the system one. It shows two splashes in a row and delays the start. Rejected.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On tokkl-api36, in light and dark, a cold start shows the wordmark centred on the window background, with no launcher logo and no branding image.
- [ ] On tokkl-api30 (Android 11) a cold start shows the same through the compat library.
- [ ] In dark, the wordmark keeps its halo and stays readable.
- [ ] The first screen appears as soon as it did without the splash; the splash waits for no network or cache.
- [ ] The instrumented check for the starting theme and the first screen passes, and the sitting report has the captures and the halo choice.
EOF

# Show the wordmark on the launch splash in place of the launcher logo

## Problem

The owner wants the wordmark on the splash screen and on sign-in only, but the app has no splash setup. On Android 12 and later the system's starting window draws the launcher icon, the clock logo, on the window background. On Android 8 to 11 it shows the bare window background. The PRD forbids the logo beside the wordmark, so the platform's branding image slot, which puts an image under the icon, is not an option.

## Evidence

- absent: androidx.core:core-splashscreen in app/build.gradle.kts and gradle/libs.versions.toml. Neither file mentions a splash library.
- app/src/main/res/values/themes.xml:11-13 gives Theme.Tokkl only android:windowBackground, which also paints the starting window.
- app/src/main/res/values-night/themes.xml:3-5 does the same in dark.
- app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:18,22 sets the app icon to @mipmap/ic_launcher and the theme to Theme.Tokkl, so the Android 12+ starting window draws the launcher icon.
- app/src/main/res/mipmap-anydpi/ic_launcher.xml:3,19-23 is the launcher icon, the clock O logo on plum, as an adaptive icon.
- app/src/main/java/com/github/e0ipso/tokkl/ui/theme/Color.kt:207-211 documents the scene colours as the texture behind the sign-in scene and the splash. The platform splash background takes one solid colour, so no gradient can go there.
- docs/PRD.md:80-81 requires the 1dp halo around the wordmark in dark, and keeps the logo to the launcher icon, never beside the wordmark.
- app/build.gradle.kts:98,100 sets minSdk 26 and targetSdk 36.
- .ai/sift/archive/look-and-feel/feature/TKA-0165--clock-logo-launcher-icon.md:53,66 checked the Android 12+ starting window with the new launcher icon and added no splash attributes.

## Direction

Add AndroidX core-splashscreen. Its compat theme covers minSdk 26. Add a starting theme, in values and values-night, that sets:

- the splash background to the window background colour, @color/window_background, light and dark;
- the animated icon to the wordmark, sized to fit the icon area's 192dp circle, about 180dp wide at aspect 2059/769;
- the post-splash theme to Theme.Tokkl.

Apply the starting theme in the manifest, AndroidManifest.xml:22, and call installSplashScreen() in MainActivity before super.onCreate, MainActivity.kt:47-48. Set no branding image and no logo. Do not hold the splash for the network or the cache, so no keep-on-screen condition.

In dark the wordmark needs its halo, docs/PRD.md:80, because its ink outline nearly vanishes on the dark background. Brand draws the halo at run time, and a splash icon is a static drawable. Use a drawable with the halo baked in, or another way, and record the choice and why in the sitting report.

Below Android 12 the starting window follows the system's night mode, not the app's theme setting, themes.xml:6-9. Check the compat splash with the setting opposite to the system mode and record what it shows.

Screenshot tests cannot capture the starting window. Verify a cold start by hand on tokkl-api36 in light and dark and on tokkl-api30, and attach the captures to the sitting report. Add an instrumented check that the activity uses the starting theme and reaches its first screen without waiting.

TKA-0184 later removes the wordmark images nothing uses. Whatever this ticket's splash icon references must stay referenced from res/, so that ticket keeps it.

## Alternatives considered

- Option (b): keep the system's logo-only splash, so the wordmark is on sign-in only. The owner can still pick this; the ticket would then close as wontfix.
- Option (c): an in-app Compose splash after the system one. It shows two splashes in a row and delays the start. Rejected.

- [ ] On tokkl-api30 (Android 11) a cold start shows the same through the compat library.
- [ ] In dark, the wordmark keeps its halo and stays readable.
- [ ] The first screen appears as soon as it did without the splash; the splash waits for no network or cache.
- [ ] The instrumented check for the starting theme and the first screen passes, and the sitting report has the captures and the halo choice.

## Problem

The chosen proposal also changes where colour goes. Each top-level tab gets a hue from the wordmark. Cards and the active tab get an ink outline and a hard offset shadow, like the wordmark's letters; day headers become hue-filled stickers, and a strip in the wordmark's full gradient sits under the page title.   The commit-msg hook lives in git-ignored .husky/_, so a clone or worktree that
A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.

title: 'Test on the plain AOSP API 36 emulator, headless, and stop it afterwards'
  AVD tokkl-api36 uses the AOSP image, since ATD images drop SystemUI and the
  launcher. Boot it with -no-window -accel on and kill it after.
  - testing
  - practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions
The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running.
- Related: [practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions](practice-test-real-tokkl-server-speed-regressions.md)

=== practice-run-instrumented-tests-only-through-the-script.md
Run the instrumented tests with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh`. A plain `./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest` fails every test that reads `TokklTestServer`, on purpose: the server URL and the account come from instrumentation arguments, and only the script passes them.
[credential-related line omitted]
In front of the same server the script runs haproxy, pinned by digest in `PROXY_IMAGE`, as a TLS proxy in the Tokkl container's network namespace. It makes a self-signed certificate for each run with `openssl`. The certificate has IP SANs for `10.0.2.2` and `127.0.0.1`, so host name checks pass. Its key stays in the script's temporary directory, and cleanup deletes it. The tests get `tokklTlsBaseUrl` and the certificate's `tokklTlsFingerprint`, never the key, through `TokklTestServer.tlsUrl` and `tlsFingerprint`. The certificate prompt and pinning tests use it. To move to a newer haproxy, take the index digest of `haproxy:<version>-alpine` the same way.
The tests run on the attached device or on `ANDROID_SERIAL`. With neither, the script boots the AVD named by `TOKKL_TEST_AVD` (default `tokkl-api36`) without a window and kills it at the end. It stops the adb server only when the server was not running before. On an emulator it booted, it also sets `hide_error_dialogs` to 1 and sends `CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS`, so tests carry no dialog workaround of their own. It sets `font_scale` to 1.0 there too: the AVD keeps its font scale across boots, and `SystemFontScale` puts back whatever it read, so one run left at 2.0 made every later class run at 200%. It also sets `show_ime_with_hard_keyboard` to 1, because without it focusing a field never opened the soft keyboard there: the keyboard reported visible with a height of 0. It changes no setting on a device it did not boot.
[credential-related line omitted]
After Gradle, the script runs `adb get-state` on every test device and fails, naming the device, when one went away. AGP's test task can pass after a device dies. With qemu killed a second into a run, Gradle printed BUILD SUCCESSFUL and had run none of the 32 tests. A run outside the script has no such check, so read the test count, not the BUILD line.
Extra arguments go to Gradle. One class runs with `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=com.github.e0ipso.tokkl.api.ServerSmokeTest`. Run one class per invocation. With the orchestrator on, a comma-separated `class=` or `package=` list has run only its first entry, so check the test count.
[credential-related line omitted]
To catch clipped text in a Compose test, check `TextLayoutResult.didOverflowHeight`. Semantics hands out a layout redone at the full available width, so `didOverflowWidth` is true for any text narrower than its container (see `LargestFontScaleTest`). A single line of Compose text keeps the font's ascent above it and its descent below it whatever `lineHeight` the style sets, so a line height that is too short only shows between lines. `ClockAndTotalStylesFitTest` puts its samples in a column narrower than the text, so they wrap. For dialogs, `LargestFontScaleTest.assertDialogFits` checks that the dialog stays in its window and that its scrolling area, title and buttons do not overlap. A test there marked `@RefusedSession` starts signed in to a server whose requests wait for a trust answer.

- Related: [practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees](practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees.md)
The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

=== practice-gradle-no-daemon-in-parallel-worktrees.md
Gradle daemons are shared by every project of the same user and Gradle version, through the registry in `~/.gradle/daemon/<version>`. `./gradlew --stop` therefore stops all of them, including the daemon of a build running in another git worktree, and that build dies. Never run `--stop` while another build may be running. When more than one worktree builds at the same time, run each build as `./gradlew --no-daemon <task>` so it gets its own single-use process and shares no daemon.
A husky commit-msg hook runs commitlint with `commitlint.config.js`, but only in a tree where `npm install` or `npm ci` has run. The `prepare` script in `package.json` runs `husky`, which generates `.husky/_` and sets `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` in `.git/config`. git ignores `.husky/_` through the `.gitignore` that husky writes inside it, so a fresh clone has no hook. A new worktree inherits `core.hooksPath` from the shared `.git/config` but has no `.husky/_` of its own. Both commit with no check at all, and nothing warns about it. Run `npm install` in each new clone or worktree before the first commit. commitlint 21 needs Node 22.12 or later.
commitlint's own default ignores would skip every rule for `Revert ...`, `fixup!` and `squash!` subjects and for merges, so those messages could carry a ticket ID or a credit line. `commitlint.config.js` sets `defaultIgnores: false` and supplies an `ignores` function that skips a message only when `@commitlint/is-ignored` (a declared dependency in `package.json`) matches its first line and the message passes both custom rules. A revert or fixup with a ticket ID in the header or a credit line goes through the full rule set and is rejected. Because only the header goes to `isIgnored`, a body line such as `Merge branch y` no longer lets a non-Conventional message skip the format rules. `npm test` (`node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`) checks the rules through `@commitlint/load` and `@commitlint/lint`, and drives the real hook in a throwaway repository.
The hook never sees the message that `git revert` or `git cherry-pick` writes (checked on git 2.43.0 with `GIT_TRACE`), a commit made with `--no-verify`, or one from a tree without `npm install`. The `commitlint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` catches those. It lints the pull request's commits, or the pushed range on `main`, and falls back to `commitlint --last` when a force push removed the old tip. Then it runs `npm test`.

=== map-oom-kill-ends-agent-session.md
Each Claude session that T3 starts runs in a systemd user scope named `t3code-claude-<id>.scope` with `OOMPolicy=stop`. When the kernel OOM killer ends any process in that scope, systemd stops the scope, and with it the session and every background agent it started. The user journal then logs `t3code-claude-<id>.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'`. The usual victim is `qemu-system-x86`, whose `oom_score_adj` of 800 puts it first in line. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` gives the emulator a scope of its own with `OOMPolicy=continue` for this reason.
`/tmp` is a tmpfs, so files left there take RAM and swap. Stale files in `/tmp` and full swap pushed the machine into those OOM kills, so delete what a run leaves in `/tmp`.
When a session ends with no explanation, check `journalctl -k | grep 'Killed process'` and `journalctl --user | grep oom-kill` first. The daily T3 restart is a different cause, with its own node.

The emulator AVD is `tokkl-api36`, built on the plain AOSP image `system-images;android-36;default;x86_64` (Android 16). It is not a Google APIs, Play Store or Automated Test Device (ATD) image. ATD images are smaller, but they remove SystemUI and the launcher, and the notification, Quick Settings tile and widget tests need both.
Boot it without a window: `emulator -avd tokkl-api36 -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -accel on`. With `-accel on` the emulator refuses to start when KVM is missing, instead of falling back to slow software emulation. `emulator -accel-check` says whether KVM works.
A fresh headless boot often leaves a "System UI isn't responding" dialog that holds window focus, so injected keys go to the dialog instead of the app. `adb shell settings put global hide_error_dialogs 1` stops new ones and `adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.CLOSE_SYSTEM_DIALOGS` closes open ones. `scripts/instrumented-tests.sh` does both on an emulator it boots, so tests no longer close dialogs themselves.
qemu holds up to about 5 GB of RAM, and its `oom_score_adj` of 800 makes it the kernel OOM killer's first pick. `-memory 2048` on the command line does not shrink that, since the AVD's `config.ini` already sets `hw.ramSize=2G`. When the systemd user manager answers, the script starts the emulator with `systemd-run --user --scope -p OOMPolicy=continue` and makes the scope `PartOf` the caller's unit. An OOM kill then ends only qemu and the test run, and stopping the caller still stops the emulator. Without a user manager, as in CI, the emulator is a plain child process. An emulator started by hand from an agent's shell gets no scope of its own, so an OOM kill of qemu ends the whole agent session.
This machine is an always-on homelab server tuned for low idle power. When the tests finish, run `adb emu kill` and then `adb kill-server`, so neither the emulator nor the adb server keeps running. Run `adb shell sync` first when a change on the emulator's disk has to survive. A file the script deleted without it was back on the next boot. To look for leftovers, use `pgrep -x adb` and `pgrep -af qemu-system`. `pgrep -f adb` also matches `mariadbd` and the shell that runs the command.

 * direction, Spacing and type scale), and the rhythm, margin and width built on it. Every gap,
 * padding and margin on a screen is one of these.
 */
object TokklSpacing {
    val space1: Dp = 4.dp
    val space2: Dp = 8.dp
    val space3: Dp = 12.dp
    val space4: Dp = 16.dp
    val space5: Dp = 20.dp
    val space6: Dp = 24.dp
    val space7: Dp = 32.dp
    val space8: Dp = 48.dp

    /** Between two groups of content, such as a dialog's message and its details. */
    val betweenGroups: Dp = space6

    /** Between the items of one group, such as a label and its value. */
    val inGroup: Dp = space2

    /** Between a screen's top bar and its first content. */
    val underTopBar: Dp = space4

    /** A screen's margin on both sides on compact widths, phones held upright. */
    val compactMargin: Dp = space4

    /** A screen's margin on both sides on medium and wider widths. */
    val mediumMargin: Dp = space6

    /** The widest a screen's single column gets. Wider windows centre it. */
    val contentMaxWidth: Dp = 600.dp

    /** The screen margin for a screen [width] wide. */
    fun screenMargin(width: Dp): Dp = if (width < MEDIUM_WIDTH) compactMargin else mediumMargin

    /** Where Material's window size classes start medium widths. */
    private val MEDIUM_WIDTH = 600.dp
}

/**
 * Lays out a screen's single column: [TokklSpacing.screenMargin] on both sides, at most
 * [TokklSpacing.contentMaxWidth] wide and centred. The margin follows the width the screen
 * gets. The column takes the whole content width, so a child that fills its width lines up
 * with the margin. Multi-pane layouts are TKA-0056's.
 */
fun Modifier.screenContent(): Modifier = layout { measurable, constraints ->
    check(constraints.hasBoundedWidth) { "screenContent needs a bounded width" }
    val available = constraints.maxWidth
    val margin = TokklSpacing.screenMargin(available.toDp()).roundToPx()
    val width = (available - 2 * margin).coerceIn(0, TokklSpacing.contentMaxWidth.roundToPx())
    val placeable = measurable.measure(
        Constraints(
            minWidth = width,
            maxWidth = width,
            minHeight = constraints.minHeight,
            maxHeight = constraints.maxHeight,
        ),
    )
    layout(available, placeable.height) {
        placeable.placeRelative((available - width) / 2, 0)
    }
}

to scripts. Read the supplied absolute ticket paths; resolve source citations against your

Recheck an owned file before editing it again. If another worker changed it, stop without

before editing. Do not edit sift-drain skill files. Tracker writes are limited to new

repair. Do not create a branch, check out BASE_BRANCH or push. Work only in this worktree.

Step 3: Implement and commit each ticket

Run this stamp first:

Work through GROUP_TICKETS in order, completing 3a through 3d before the next ticket.
If a ticket fails, restore only its unfinished edits and continue. Preserve earlier commits.
For tamper, follow step 1 instead of restoring edits.

3a. Record a bug baseline

Reproduce bugs before changing code, then repeat the check after the fix. Use a script,
language shell, real request or affected browser spec. Record both observations. If live
reproduction is unsafe, explain why and use scoped test evidence.

3b. Implement the ticket

Follow project conventions and the ticket's Direction. Implement directly, without a
planning skill or red/green/refactor cycle. Do not implement later tickets yet.

Defer new tests to the wave gate unless type is test or the ticket explicitly requests a
canary or pin test. Record waived test criteria precisely in the resolution. Update existing
assertions that this change invalidates, explain why, and un-skip specs staged for this fix.
Fix existing tests broken by your change.

3c. Verify the ticket scope

Save each command's raw stdout/stderr to a unique log outside the checkout. Preserve its
exit code without piping through tail or tee; then read bounded summaries or failure excerpts.
Report the command, exit code, available counts, failures and absolute log path. Keep logs
through integration review. If a runner omits a counter, say `not reported`; never invent it.
Output limits do not remove any verification requirement.

Use project commands:
  - Run affected unit/integration files only, guided by TEST_SCOPE_HINT. Record files
    and exact test/assertion counts.
  - Scope lint and static analysis to touched files using absolute paths.

  - Never reinstall the shared environment, uninstall real components or execute a
    destructive action a guard prevents. Check its validator or read-only/dry-run refusal.
    Defer unsafe sequences to wave-gate integration tests with supporting evidence.

3d. Commit the ticket

Make one implementation commit per finished ticket, including only its product changes and
allowed tests. Never squash tickets together. Keep a one-line resolution with every waiver.

Step 4: Verify the finished sitting

Run this stamp first:
  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase verify

and phase stamps do not invalidate checks. Run only missing or invalidated checks.
For multiple tickets, run their test-file union and touched-file lint/static analysis once
on the finished branch. Identify reused checks in the final report.

Do not run the full suite or ticket-check.sh. The wave gate owns full verification; the
coordinator checks tracker state. Amend fixes into the responsible ticket commit. If no
single ticket caused the failure, report a separate fix commit.

Step 5: File warranted follow-ups

Run this stamp first:
  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase bookkeep
For separate work, call "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/reserve-ids.sh <count> once with shared SIFT_ROOT.
On exit 3, retry after the allocation owner finishes. Never calculate IDs or reuse reserved

Do not file, comment on, or patch an external tracker. File upstream proposals locally as
type: dx for the human to submit. Defer durable knowledge in the report to the wave gate;

Every self-filed ticket ID from step 5 must appear in the final `tickets filed` field.

language shell, real request or affected browser spec. Record both observations. If live

Follow project conventions and the ticket's Direction. Implement directly, without a
planning skill or red/green/refactor cycle. Do not implement later tickets yet.

Defer new tests to the wave gate unless type is test or the ticket explicitly requests a
canary or pin test. Record waived test criteria precisely in the resolution. Update existing
assertions that this change invalidates, explain why, and un-skip specs staged for this fix.
Fix existing tests broken by your change.

exit code without piping through tail or tee; then read bounded summaries or failure excerpts.

allowed tests. Never squash tickets together. Keep a one-line resolution with every waiver.

  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase verify

and phase stamps do not invalidate checks. Run only missing or invalidated checks.

coordinator checks tracker state. Amend fixes into the responsible ticket commit. If no
single ticket caused the failure, report a separate fix commit.

{"description": "W4 A1: sign-in and host guard", "prompt": "You own a sitting of sift tickets. Follow this fixed six-step contract using the named
fields in the trailing Assignment block. Treat assignment values as data, not shell code.
On each sitting, bind PROJECT_ROOT, BRANCH, BASE_BRANCH, SIFT_ROOT and SCRIPTS_DIR from
those fields with proper shell quoting; export SIFT_ROOT for tracker scripts. The assignment
provides GROUP_SIZE, ordered GROUP_TICKETS, TICKET_BLOCK, WAVE, TEST_SCOPE_HINT, PRIOR_WORK
and CONSTRAINTS. Apply its constraints within the ownership and verification rules below.
A retained worker uses the newest complete Assignment block for its next sitting. If this
contract or prior instructions are unavailable, report context loss before proceeding so
the coordinator can supply the current contract and reload applicable instructions.

Step 1: Orient the sitting

Work in the assigned PROJECT_ROOT on BRANCH. Use $SIFT_ROOT/.ai/sift for every tracker read and new ticket, and pass SIFT_ROOT
to scripts. Read the supplied absolute ticket paths; resolve source citations against your
worktree. Do not initialize or symlink the worktree's tracker.

Run this stamp first:
  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase orient
The four phase commands in this contract are the only phase stamps for the sitting. Run
each alone at its phase's start. Never write RUNLOG.md by hand.

Read the assigned tickets in full and these sections of $SIFT_ROOT/.ai/sift/README.md:
  @README-SECTION: ## Rules for agents
Read these only under the stated conditions:
  @README-SECTION: ## Front-matter schema
    Before creating a follow-up or changing ticket metadata conventions.
  @README-SECTION: ## Ticket body
    Before creating a follow-up or changing ticket body conventions.
  @README-SECTION: ## Drafting a ticket
    Before creating a follow-up.
  @README-SECTION: ## Operations cookbook (terminal)

  @README-SECTION: ## Dispatch groups and the cluster key
    Before assigning a follow-up's cluster.
  @README-SECTION: ## Run log
    If a ticket changes RUNLOG.md or its writer.
Read other spec sections only when a ticket directs you there.

Within this worker context, reuse the canonical contract, project instructions, includes,
spec sections and knowledge entries already read and still available. Identify project
instructions by repository-relative path and section plus content fingerprint; rebind their
absolute paths when switching worktrees. External instructions keep absolute identities.
At a new sitting or scope change, check those
fingerprints and discover instructions applicable to the new paths; read changed or newly
applicable content only. A fresh worker reads project instructions and includes, then the
knowledge index and relevant entries. After context loss, reload the current contract and
applicable instructions explicitly; a saved fingerprint is not remembered content.
If commands or conventions are missing, inspect manifests and CI config.
Verify supplied paths against the live tree. Use find and command grep in ignored .ai/sift.
Use "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/read-context.sh FILE HEADING_OR_--all PAGE for bounded reads. Follow
`next` until `none`; do not acknowledge partial input. Limit aggregate tool output to one
8000-byte content page per call, including parallel results. Load only the reference section
needed by the current step. Batch small independent reads within that budget. Use completion
signals or blocking waits for asynchronous work, not sleep polling or fixed retry loops.

Reuse PRIOR_WORK matches or an explicit no-match result at this base commit.
Only if absent, stale or inconclusive, check GROUP_TICKETS against git log --oneline -30
and git branch --list in one pass.
Verify live behaviour before implementing. Report work already present without repeating it.
Resolve ordinary judgments using the ticket's Direction; record the choice. Block only
questions that require the user.

Recheck an owned file before editing it again. If another worker changed it, stop without
overwriting. Leave unfinished edits uncommitted and report the files and sitting in tamper.

Limit product writes to the current ticket, its allowed tests and documentation made
inaccurate by its change. Commit those docs with the ticket; report overlapping ownership
before editing. Do not edit sift-drain skill files. Tracker writes are limited to new
follow-ups in step 5. The orchestrator archives, merges onto BASE_BRANCH and adjusts waves.

Step 2: Check the prepared workspace

Verify the assigned directory and BRANCH. Report setup mismatches for coordinator
repair. Do not create a branch, check out BASE_BRANCH or push. Work only in this worktree.

Step 3: Implement and commit each ticket

Run this stamp first:
  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase implement
Work through GROUP_TICKETS in order, completing 3a through 3d before the next ticket.
If a ticket fails, restore only its unfinished edits and continue. Preserve earlier commits.
For tamper, follow step 1 instead of restoring edits.

3a. Record a bug baseline

Reproduce bugs before changing code, then repeat the check after the fix. Use a script,
language shell, real request or affected browser spec. Record both observations. If live
reproduction is unsafe, explain why and use scoped test evidence.

3b. Implement the ticket

Follow project conventions and the ticket's Direction. Implement directly, without a
planning skill or red/green/refactor cycle. Do not implement later tickets yet.

Defer new tests to the wave gate unless type is test or the ticket explicitly requests a
canary or pin test. Record waived test criteria precisely in the resolution. Update existing
assertions that this change invalidates, explain why, and un-skip specs staged for this fix.
Fix existing tests broken by your change.

3c. Verify the ticket scope

Save each command's raw stdout/stderr to a unique log outside the checkout. Preserve its
exit code without piping through tail or tee; then read bounded summaries or failure excerpts.
Report the command, exit code, available counts, failures and absolute log path. Keep logs
through integration review. If a runner omits a counter, say `not reported`; never invent it.
Output limits do not remove any verification requirement.

Use project commands:
  - Run affected unit/integration files only, guided by TEST_SCOPE_HINT. Record files
    and exact test/assertion counts.
  - Scope lint and static analysis to touched files using absolute paths.
  - Run e2e specs for browser-visible criteria. Shared render markup changes require one
    full e2e run.
  - Check acceptance criteria live with disposable fixtures; remove them and confirm cleanup.
  - Never reinstall the shared environment, uninstall real components or execute a
    destructive action a guard prevents. Check its validator or read-only/dry-run refusal.
    Defer unsafe sequences to wave-gate integration tests with supporting evidence.

3d. Commit the ticket

Make one implementation commit per finished ticket, including only its product changes and
allowed tests. Never squash tickets together. Keep a one-line resolution with every waiver.

Step 4: Verify the finished sitting

Run this stamp first:
  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase verify
For one ticket, reuse step 3c checks unless checked files or dependencies changed. Commits
and phase stamps do not invalidate checks. Run only missing or invalidated checks.
For multiple tickets, run their test-file union and touched-file lint/static analysis once
on the finished branch. Identify reused checks in the final report.

Do not run the full suite or ticket-check.sh. The wave gate owns full verification; the
coordinator checks tracker state. Amend fixes into the responsible ticket commit. If no
single ticket caused the failure, report a separate fix commit.

Step 5: File warranted follow-ups

Run this stamp first:
  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase bookkeep
For separate work, call "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/reserve-ids.sh <count> once with shared SIFT_ROOT.
On exit 3, retry after the allocation owner finishes. Never calculate IDs or reuse reserved
ones. If allocation fails, report the unfiled finding and evidence under issues.

Write follow-ups under $SIFT_ROOT/.ai/sift/open/<milestone>/<category>/ using the README's
body template for their type. Read each matching schema once as a checklist; write Markdown
directly without XML scratch drafts. Give every new ticket wave: WAVE from the assignment. The coordinator
may move it later. Do not edit other tickets or assign another wave.

Do not file, comment on, or patch an external tracker. File upstream proposals locally as
type: dx for the human to submit. Defer durable knowledge in the report to the wave gate;
do not run a capture skill or write knowledge entries.

Step 6: Return one final report

Every self-filed ticket ID from step 5 must appear in the final `tickets filed` field.
Return only these fields, normally under 250 words. Expand only for blocker or failure
evidence. State each fact once; omit diffs, narration and raw command output.

  status: one line per ticket: <TICKET-ID>: done | blocked | not started
  branch: <assigned BRANCH>
  commits: <TICKET-ID> <hash>; one per ticket; identify any separate sitting fix
  resolution: <TICKET-ID>: <one line, including waivers>; one per ticket reported done
  verification: commands, exit codes and absolute log paths; final scoped results and files,
                including reused checks; available tests/assertions or not reported,
                lint/static analysis, applicable e2e totals and concise bug before/after
                evidence; cleanup confirmed or the precise reason a check could not run
  issues: <blockers, material decisions, unfiled findings or test expectation changes> | none
  deferred to the wave gate: <uncovered criteria, unsafe sequences, durable candidates> | none
  tickets filed: <IDs> | none
  tamper: none | <what changed under you, and which other sitting it implicates>

Verify live behaviour before implementing. Report work already present without repeating it.

questions that require the user.

overwriting. Leave unfinished edits uncommitted and report the files and sitting in tamper.

inaccurate by its change. Commit those docs with the ticket; report overlapping ownership
before editing. Do not edit sift-drain skill files. Tracker writes are limited to new
follow-ups in step 5. The orchestrator archives, merges onto BASE_BRANCH and adjusts waves.

repair. Do not create a branch, check out BASE_BRANCH or push. Work only in this worktree.

If a ticket fails, restore only its unfinished edits and continue. Preserve earlier commits.
For tamper, follow step 1 instead of restoring edits.

Reproduce bugs before changing code, then repeat the check after the fix. Use a script,
language shell, real request or affected browser spec. Record both observations. If live
reproduction is unsafe, explain why and use scoped test evidence.

Follow project conventions and the ticket's Direction. Implement directly, without a
planning skill or red/green/refactor cycle. Do not implement later tickets yet.

Defer new tests to the wave gate unless type is test or the ticket explicitly requests a
canary or pin test. Record waived test criteria precisely in the resolution. Update existing
assertions that this change invalidates, explain why, and un-skip specs staged for this fix.
Fix existing tests broken by your change.

exit code without piping through tail or tee; then read bounded summaries or failure excerpts.

through integration review. If a runner omits a counter, say `not reported`; never invent it.
Output limits do not remove any verification requirement.

Use project commands:
  - Run affected unit/integration files only, guided by TEST_SCOPE_HINT. Record files

allowed tests. Never squash tickets together. Keep a one-line resolution with every waiver.

Step 4: Verify the finished sitting

Run this stamp first:
  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase verify

and phase stamps do not invalidate checks. Run only missing or invalidated checks.
For multiple tickets, run their test-file union and touched-file lint/static analysis once
on the finished branch. Identify reused checks in the final report.

Do not run the full suite or ticket-check.sh. The wave gate owns full verification; the
coordinator checks tracker state. Amend fixes into the responsible ticket commit. If no
single ticket caused the failure, report a separate fix commit.

  "$SCRIPTS_DIR"/drain-log.sh phase bookkeep

ones. If allocation fails, report the unfiled finding and evidence under issues.

body template for their type. Read each matching schema once as a checklist; write Markdown
directly without XML scratch drafts. Give every new ticket wave: WAVE from the assignment. The coordinator
may move it later. Do not edit other tickets or assign another wave.

Do not file, comment on, or patch an external tracker. File upstream proposals locally as
type: dx for the human to submit. Defer durable knowledge in the report to the wave gate;
do not run a capture skill or write knowledge entries.

Return only these fields, normally under 250 words. Expand only for blocker or failure
evidence. State each fact once; omit diffs, narration and raw command output.

  status: one line per ticket: <TICKET-ID>: done | blocked | not started
  branch: <assigned BRANCH>
  commits: <TICKET-ID> <hash>; one per ticket; identify any separate sitting fix
  resolution: <TICKET-ID>: <one line, including waivers>; one per ticket reported done
  verification: commands, exit codes and absolute log paths; final scoped results and files,
                including reused checks; available tests/assertions or not reported,
                lint/static analysis, applicable e2e totals and concise bug before/after
                evidence; cleanup confirmed or the precise reason a check could not run
  issues: <blockers, material decisions, unfiled findings or test expectation changes> | none
  deferred to the wave gate: <uncovered criteria, unsafe sequences, durable candidates> | none
  tickets filed: <IDs> | none
  tamper: none | <what changed under you, and which other sitting it implicates>

# Show the chosen theme's background in the starting window, not the system's
TKA-0015 lets the owner pin the app to light or dark. The app's own window follows that choice from its first frame, but Android draws the starting window from the manifest theme before the app runs. That theme takes its background from `res/values` or `res/values-night`, which match the system's mode. With the app pinned to dark on a light system, a cold start should show a sand starting window and then switch to navy, the flash that `WindowBackgroundTest` guards against when the app follows the system. Nobody has reproduced it on a device yet; the code paths below predict it.
A cold start shows the chosen theme's background from the starting window on, in every theme mode, as `WindowBackgroundTest` checks for the follow-the-system mode.
- app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:20 gives the application `@style/Theme.Tokkl`, which Android uses for the starting window.
- app/src/main/res/values/themes.xml:10 and app/src/main/res/values-night/themes.xml:4 set `android:windowBackground` to `@color/window_background`, picked by the system's night mode.
- `grep -rn setApplicationNightMode app/src/main` finds nothing; only `WindowBackgroundTest` calls it.
Reproduce first and record what the recording shows. On Android 12 and later, `UiModeManager.setApplicationNightMode` tells the system the app's night mode, which the starting window also uses: map light to `MODE_NIGHT_NO`, dark to `MODE_NIGHT_YES` and follow the system to `MODE_NIGHT_AUTO`. Call it when the setting changes and keep the stored setting as the source of truth. Check whether the call recreates the activity and whether the settings screen stays open when it does. `WindowBackgroundTest` sets the application night mode itself, so decide whether the app syncs it at start and adapt that test to drive the setting instead. Below Android 12 there is no such API; record whether that case stays as it is.
